NICETAS OF BYZANTIUM: REFUTATION AND OVERTHROW OF THE LETTER SENT BY THE RULER OF ARMENIA TO SLANDER OUR ORTHODOX FAITH AND THE HOLY AND ECUMENICAL FOURTH COUNCIL, WRITTEN AT THE COMMISSION OF OUR CHRIST-LOVING AND MOST PIOUS EMPEROR. It was written to the ruler in the name of the patriarch.

1. By God's love for humankind, by his divine judgments, and by the [?] of our most pious and orthodox emperors, I have received the high-priestly rank of the imperial city to hold as my charge. So I am eager, with all zeal and readiness, to govern and guide lawfully the rational flock of Christ our chief shepherd. As far as my strength allows, and as speech is granted by the Lord of all in the opening of my mouth, I have also been eager to strengthen that flock often with divine letters. In this way the devil, who sows the tares, may find no opportunity to sow tares, that is, heretical notions, among the guileless and most pure wheat, and to ravage part of the divine flock. That wheat is the sincere and right faith and teaching in which the catholic and apostolic Church stands firm and unshaken. Some people have come within the Lord's fold and been counted worthy to share in our mystery. Then they have been inflamed by rash men, or held fast either by ignorance or by ancestral obstinacy, and so they do not quite rightly hold the exact word of truth and the pure doctrine of the Christians. When this happens, we are eager in some cases to correct them by speaking with them in person, and to establish them firmly on the path of truth and right doctrine. In other cases there are those with whom we cannot

speak face to face, because they live far away, and these we strive to support by letters. Put simply, we are bound to guide, as far as we can, the whole chosen people, which has been called the Lord's royal priesthood, along with those who need the better kind of help. For this has always been a duty laid on high priests. It was in this disposition of soul toward your excellency, our beloved son, that we acted. We have long felt love for him, and many people, as was natural, urged us to write. But it seemed best that we be moved to write chiefly because, I know not how, an incorrect doctrine has for a long time flowed into the regions of Armenia and taken hold there. I mean the doctrine of a certain heresiarch Sis[?]erus, who has ravaged everyone there. So in our letter we used many proofs. I thought these would quickly persuade you too of what is right. Once you had been initiated again into the truth of the blameless and pure faith of Christ's mystery, you would stand with us. Together with us you would rightly glorify the one Christ, our Lord and God, who is from two natures and in two natures and has two natures, but is one in hypostasis. This is what has been held from the beginning, and, one might say, by the whole world under the sun. The five high-priestly thrones of the catholic and apostolic Church gathered at that time in the metropolis of the Chalcedonians. They followed the three earlier holy councils in everything and were of one mind with them, disagreeing in nothing, and in council they defined and decreed this. From that time until today, therefore, those who wish to live rightly and piously with the catholic and apostolic Church gladly receive the council assembled there as holy and ecumenical, the fourth after the other three, and they venerate it always. Indeed, we had more than a slight hope that our letter would persuade you. Then you would very quickly abandon the worse opinion and readily come over to the right doctrine of truth that we hold, namely that in the economy of Christ we must glorify two natures and one hypostasis.

2. But what we hoped for did not come to pass. Instead you took offense at what we wrote. Not only that, you even tried to contradict us and to write arguments in rebuttal. For this reason, kindled by divine zeal and fearing the penalty for silence, we did not think we should leave you neglected and uncared for even now. So we will bring into the open whatever your letter contains that slanders our true confession and is in any way worth discussing, and we will try to overturn it. A little after the preface of your letter, you seem to tighten and bind together the possession of love that follows agreement in one confession of the true and blameless faith, and you are eager that those of like mind be enlightened and perfected in the work of the Lord. Then you write: "Even if some have fled from this true and right confession, which the holy apostles handed down and the three holy councils established [?]..." and so on. By these words you have shown us very plainly

[NICETAS OF BYZANTIUM] that you are exalting your own opinion. You think those are most excellent [?] who have, along with divine love, the one confession of the true faith. But what is this most true confession which the apostles handed down and the three holy councils established, even if some have rebelled against this right faith? No doubt you will say it is your own. Your confession holds that the one Christ, our God, was made up of different natures but is of one nature after the union. It denies that he is from two natures and has two natures while being in one hypostasis. Further on you clearly declare that this was the kind of composition that took place when the divine Word was united to flesh. What an astonishing thing! How can you pour such blame on the eyewitnesses and divine heralds of the truth, and on the holy and God-bearing men who gathered in council at different times? Who that knows how to judge soundly would say that the ministers of the word or the divine Fathers handed down or confirmed the opinion you champion? That opinion says that Christ is of one nature after the union, and that the union was accomplished from two natures. But it refuses to say that he is in two natures, or that he is two by nature after the union. So let Peter, the chief of the apostles, be brought in, and through his own confession let him show that you speak falsely, and through him the whole company of the apostles. For Christ our Lord and God said to Peter, the chief of the apostles: "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it." The Lord said this to Peter when the Lord had called himself the Son of Man and Peter had said to him: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." So both terms were brought together in Christ our Lord and God, and it has been confirmed that he is both God and man. Both terms, I mean the term for the divinity and the term for the humanity, are predicated after the union of our one Christ, Lord and God. And he is one and the same eternal Son. He was begotten of the Father before all ages, timelessly and impassibly. He is one hypostasis of the Holy Trinity, God equal to the Father in eternity, who eternally has the Father's essence and nature in himself. In the last days he was made flesh of the Holy Spirit and of Mary the Virgin and became man. This eternal Son, without change or alteration, became like one of us in all things, yet without sin. He took on our nature, which he did not have before, while the divine nature that he had from eternity remained in him. It is evident, then, that after the union the one Christ, one in hypostasis, is in two natures and has two natures. For the names "God" and "man" indicate natures, since each is predicated of many. Therefore the definition of the holy Fathers of the divine council assembled at Chalcedon rightly expounds the true doctrine of the Apostle's confession concerning Christ. It defines Christ to be one hypostasis of the Holy Trinity, having two natures, a divine nature and a human nature.

3. If you wish to see it, here is a clear example of this. Let three gold coins be set out. One of them is thrown into the fire and heated until it has become fire, yet it remains gold, as it was. Now place the other two gold coins on one side and many burning coals on the other. Then put the heated coin, which has become fire, between the other two coins and the coals. You will see that the coin in the middle has the complete nature of the other two coins, since it is gold just like each of them. It also has the nature of the coals, since it is fire just like each of the other coals. In the same way the eternal Son came down from heaven and took from us not a hypostasis but our nature. He became like one of us, as the divine apostle Paul says, tempted in every way just as we are, yet without sin. So the eternal Son has the nature of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, which he always had, and since his incarnation he also has our human nature. Yet he remains one hypostasis of the Holy Trinity, for the Holy Trinity has received no addition. This is evident even to those who can see only a little. So it is clear that your opinion about one nature of Christ was not handed down by the choir of the apostles. Nor was it handed down by the three holy councils, which were assembled at different times by pious emperors through God's providence, and which you yourself acknowledge and accept in your letter. Those councils were first assembled to put down the false doctrines of Arius, Macedonius and Nestorius. The first two made plain and decreed the right confession concerning theology. We are truly to confess that the eternal Son and Word of God the Father, and the Holy Spirit, are consubstantial with the Father and of one nature with him. The Son and the Holy Spirit share equally in glory with the Father in one and the same Godhead. We are to glorify the three as one God, even though they are believed to be three in their properties, and we must not reduce either of them to a creature. But these councils decreed and defined nothing at all about one nature in the mystery of Christ. Then came the holy council at Ephesus, the first held there and the third ecumenical council after those two. It triumphed over the false doctrine of Nestorius. Nestorius dared to cut our one Christ, Lord and God into two sons and two persons. The wretch shamelessly refused to call the all-pure and holy Virgin Theotokos, the Mother of God, and preferred Christotokos, the Mother of Christ, as though she had given birth to a mere man. He set apart the two natures of Emmanuel, from which and in which Christ was contemplated, I mean the divinity and the humanity. He confessed that each subsisted on its own, and he would not accept a nature without a person. So he brought in as many persons as there are natures, and he confessed only a relational union of God the Word with the one born of Mary. The council therefore anathematized him and decreed and ratified the hypostatic

and essential union of the two natures, I mean the divinity and the humanity, which are to be contemplated in the one Christ, that is, in the one hypostasis. That holy council abolished the opinion of the vain-minded Nestorius, who held two persons in Christ. But it does not in any way follow that it brings in the confession of one nature in Christ. In theology too, the first holy council abolished the opinion of Arius, who confessed three natures, but it did not thereby also abolish the threefoldness of hypostasis. In the same way, when the holy third council at Ephesus anathematized the opinion of two hypostases, it did not thereby also abolish the difference of the natures. In fact, to confirm the hypostatic and essential union of the natures of the one Christ, I mean the divinity and the humanity, it also used the individual man as an example. The individual man is composed of two natures, body and the incorporeal, and is contemplated in two natures, yet he is one hypostasis. The council did not take this example of the individual man to be like the union in Christ in every respect. It aimed only at the wrong thinking of Nestorius. He plainly said that there is no nature without its own person. In his view, it is impossible to see two natures hypostatically and essentially united in one hypostasis without bringing in two persons as well, which makes the union merely relational. For this reason the wretch preached two sons and two Christs. It was to abolish this false opinion that the council used the example of the individual man. Besides, Cyril, who is among the saints, brought before the holy third council at Ephesus many of the God-bearing Fathers. He did so to establish the hypostatic union in one hypostasis, which is Christ, known in different natures. And whatever is known in different natures certainly also exists in the natures in which it is known. The argument has shown, then, that no apostle stated the confession of one nature of Christ, and that none of the three holy councils confirmed it. So you speak falsely, and in vain, when you say that it was handed down by the holy apostles and confirmed by the three holy councils. The argument has shown, rather, that the natures in the one Christ are different. You also said: "Even if some have fled from this" (that is, from the opinion that Christ is of one nature after the union). You meant that those who confess that Christ has two natures after the union have fled from you. What ignorance this shows! Who does not know that it is the part that usually breaks away from the whole, the few from the many, and not the other way round? If those of your opinion were compared with those who hold ours, they would turn out to be the few, the smallest portion. So you should not declare that we have fled from your opinion. You should rather tell the truth, that you have fled from us.

4. Further on in your letter you balk at accepting the holy and ecumenical fourth council because we

counted it among the other three holy councils. You reject it as though you had good reason, and you write as follows: "I know that the character of the fourth council is not hidden from you. In your letter your holiness mentioned this council and ranked it with the other three councils, and you want us to accept it too. But our Fathers and our teachers did not accept it. They knew its empty talk from the other three councils, which discerned and proclaimed to the whole world the one Christ, Son and Lord, united from two natures without confusion, without change and without separation. This council, however, speaks of two separated natures, and of two energies and two wills. It agrees with Nestorius except in the matter of the two persons: he says two persons, while it holds one. And for this reason it mocked the orthodox, [saying] that it does not agree with Nestorius."

I am amazed that you write such things. From your words it seems to me that you have not understood either the intention or the proceedings of the holy fourth council. Nowhere does this holy council appear to hold, in the mystery of Christ, two natures that are separated, subsist independently and exist apart by themselves, even though you unjustly slander it in this way. On the contrary, it banished the opinions on either side of the mean, that is, of the truth. I mean excess and deficiency, which are deviations from the mean and therefore false. And it strengthened the opinion that holds the middle position and clings to the truth. Consider theology. There the mean clearly holds the true doctrine of the catholic and apostolic Church, while excess and deficiency hold falsehood. (Someone might hold three natures because the hypostases are three and different. Someone else might introduce a single hypostasis because the nature is one. Both, it seems to me, have fallen sick, against the truth, with the opinion of excess and of deficiency. This is what happened to Arius and to Sabellius the Libyan, whose errors are diametrically opposed but equal in impiety. The way of truth is a middle way. It banished the three natures of the one and the confused, single hypostasis of the other. In theology it clearly proclaims one God, that is, one essence and nature, and three consubstantial hypostases. This is what the holy and ecumenical first council piously decreed and defined.) In the same way one can see this also in the holy fourth council. Nestorius, because he confessed two natures, also brought in two hypostases, and so he held two sons in the economy. Eutyches, Dioscorus, Severus and his gang, because the hypostasis is one, also spoke of a single nature. It is evident, surely, that the one has fallen sick with the false opinion of excess, the other

with that of deficiency. But the decree of the holy council at Chalcedon walked the middle way of truth. It imitated the holy and ecumenical first council, which confirmed the middle way of truth. It too [rejected] the absurdities on either side. One was the doubling of hypostases, which makes two sons and two christs, and this is the error of excess. The other was the error of deficiency, which gives the nature singleness because the hypostasis is one. The council strengthened the way of truth that holds the middle position. In the hypostatic union of Christ it proclaims that the things that came together are two natures, which have the status of parts in the one Christ, but that the hypostasis is one. For the mean shares something with the extremes and differs from them in something. Where it differs from excess, it shares with deficiency, and where it differs from deficiency, it shares with excess. For example, the mind of the Church differs from that of Arius about the natures and shares with that of Sabellius in holding one nature. It differs from Sabellius about the singleness and confusion of the hypostasis and agrees with Arius in holding three hypostases. In the same way one can see in the economy that the opinion of the middle way of truth shares something with the extremes and differs from them in something. Where it differs from excess, it shares with deficiency, and where it differs from deficiency, it shares with excess. For example, let the opinions of Nestorius, I mean, and of Eutyches and Severus be set out. The one proclaims two natures and two persons, the other holds one nature and one hypostasis. Clearly they will be opposed as excess and deficiency. They are entirely opposed in this way and have nothing in common with each other, either of nature or of hypostasis. Now take an opinion that holds the mean of truth. It must share something with the extremes and differ from them in something. Where it differs from excess, it must share with deficiency, and where it differs from deficiency, it must share with excess. Such is the opinion of the holy fourth council concerning Christ, which proclaims two natures and one hypostasis. It differs from Nestorius about the hypostasis, since he proclaims two and it proclaims one. So it shares with Eutyches and Severus, since they too confess one hypostasis. Again, it differs from Dioscorus, Eutyches and Severus about the nature, since they proclaim one nature in the economy and it proclaims two. So it shares with Nestorius in holding two natures, and only two, in Christ. We must not reckon sharing in some respect as sharing without qualification. Nor must we treat someone who shares something with another as being of one mind with him, count him the same as that person and abhor him. Otherwise the true mind of the Church will also be condemned, because, as the argument has shown, it shares something with the extremes, I mean Arius and Sabellius. And who could bear such blasphemy? In the same way one can piously see in the case of the holy fourth council at Chalcedon that because it shares something with Nestorius, it is [not] thereby of one [?]…

…shall we grant that it holds such views? By no means. So this council, holy as it is, which proclaimed the middle way of truth, must not be slandered and rejected out of malice and ignorance. Rather, whoever has confessed its doctrine should accept it and count it with the other three holy councils. The argument has therefore shown that the holy Fourth Council introduces no empty babble alongside the other three holy councils. If the truth must be told, it shows rather the greatest agreement with them, because it too walked the middle way of truth, as they did.

10. One may also see from the council itself what it means to proclaim about Christ. Following the Fathers, as it says itself, it states word for word: "It teaches us to confess with one accord one and the same Lord Jesus Christ." By "with one accord" it cuts off in advance the suspicion that the definition before us was not produced by all the bishops gathered there, but only by some, who alone were pleased with what was said. After this, as if curing the most comprehensive error (I mean the division of Nestorius's impiety, which was being brought into the spotless economy), it says that we are to confess one and the same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. By the designation "one and the same" it tears out root and branch the notion of division, and especially by the masculine form. For it said "one" in the masculine, not "one thing" in the neuter, and by this too it signifies the whole composite and not a part of it, which the other form would probably have indicated. In this too it imitates Gregory among the saints, who signifies the whole by "one and another" in the masculine, and the parts by "one thing and another" in the neuter. After this, to ward off the suspicion of the bad opinion on the opposite side, it says: "The same perfect in divinity and the same perfect in humanity." I think it is saying nothing other than this: no one should suppose, because of the designation "one," either that the Godhead carried out the economy bare of human nature, or that it underwent a change into human nature. Rather, the same one exists perfect in both, I mean in divinity and in humanity, as a whole recognized in his own parts: truly God and truly man, of a rational soul and a body. He is not [?] simply God or man [?], but the same one is consubstantial with the Father according to the divinity and consubstantial with us according to the humanity. For those who pay proper attention to these words, nothing more remained for the council to explain about the spotless economy. Yet it foresaw what was to come: that some would dare to confess that the divine and spotless body of the Lord was impassible, immortal and incorruptible from its first conception, and in this way would overturn the whole economy. So it says: "Like us in all things apart from sin." These words come from holy Scripture, and placed here at the right moment they muzzle those who think such things. Neither bodily suffering, nor death, nor dissolution (which we think is properly called corruption) is sin. And apart from sin alone, that spotless and all-holy body is of the same nature as ours in every other respect. It is clear, then, that God, who was pleased to take on our poverty, took on such poverty as could rightly be called poverty, all

…are themselves shown to be heirs of the Fathers' blessings. For this reason we too, the last and least of all, have set ourselves to explain a few of the discourses of Gregory the Theologian, which are hard to express and hard to contemplate, or rather spoken by God: their more secret passages, which the many cannot see into. We fix our mind on Gregory, whom we honor above all elders and teachers, as the guide of our soul, and because we are more abundantly built up by his theology. In doing so we honor the divine Father with sacred acts of remembrance. At the same time, through interpreting his text, we are of necessity joining or stretching our own mind to his God-wise mind, even though the undertaking is truly bold. Through him we are guided toward the breadth of his knowledge of the truth. In this way we may also give no small benefit to other educated people by explaining theological doctrines. First, then, there lies before us for examination a verse On

…those who believe they have grasped the highest summit of worldly wisdom pride themselves on tracing all things that exist and come to be back to three most sovereign and primary causes and principles. They call these mind, matter and form. They posit them as equally without beginning and as joint causes of all things, which by no way of thinking could ever have received, or will ever receive, a beginning or an end. Mind they have also named God, on the grounds that it passes through all things and beholds all things. Matter, they say, is the set of four so-called elements, together with a fifth, the heavenly body. Form is what is peculiar to each thing and completes its substance; some have named it essential quality, others idea. These three causes of what exists and comes to be, then, always stand equally without beginning and equally eternal, having neither beginning nor end, and they lay down that each is to be considered separately by itself. From them, from an efficient, a material and a formal cause, humans and all animals and all individual plants are forever being brought into the world, now one, now another, through generation, and they pass away through corruption, in a fortuitous, endless and indefinite cycle of succession. Thus, without beginning and without end, [?] … vanity. To recall it briefly: they posit things truly worthy of their godlessness, anarchy and disorder, and they lay down as doctrine that the formless disgrace, matter, and the unsubstantial form always coexist with equal power alongside the most sovereign principle and cause of all things. The most shameful and irrational part of this irrational vain wisdom has been refuted well enough by the theologians, so we will pass over it and attach ourselves [?] to the [teaching] of the great Gregory

Again, because the followers of Nestorius did not believe the spotless Virgin was the Mother of God, it added: "Begotten from the Father before the ages, and in the last days the same one, for us and for our salvation, born of Mary the Virgin and Mother of God according to the humanity." These are a few passages from the Fourth Council, chosen with the length of the discourse in mind, since anyone who wishes can collect a great many from it. In them it appears most clearly that the council disagreed in nothing with the three holy councils, but [agreed?] with them in all things. It proclaims the same one Christ, our Lord and God, from two natures and in two, and that there are two natures after the union. It banishes the absurdities on either side of the middle, whatever they may be, and remains firm and immovable in the middle of the truth. The holy Fourth Council defined, declared and proclaimed these things about the mystery of Christ in these very words. Who, then, being of sound mind, would say that the Fourth Council agrees with Nestorius and is carried away together with his heresy? 6. Perhaps the duality of the natures troubles you. Perhaps hearing the number two at once leads you to think of the things as divided, and you reason that every number indicates things that subsist on their own. That is the mark of someone ignorant rather than someone who knows. So let us set out briefly how one should think accurately about the number two and every other number. Number is spoken of in two ways: in one way simply and in itself, in another as considered in a relation and in a thing, just as "white" means both whiteness and the thing that has been whitened. The nature of number, taken in itself, neither joins nor divides, for it has no underlying things. Number by itself neither joins nor divides, but it admits both through a particular relation. Take two and four, for example. If you consider the units of which a number consists, it is divided into them. If you look for the unity of those units, it is joined together from them. Two and two, say, are joined into four, and four is divided into two and two. So it is truer than anything to say that the nature of number has nothing fixed in it, neither separation nor union, and that these exist in the combining and composing of things. It is ignorant, then, to lay down that division of things necessarily follows from the nature of number. Rather, number is made a sign of the quantity of its subjects according to their united or divided nature, and it is some other principle, not number, that divides and joins them. We speak of ten cubits of a continuous piece of wood, say, without dividing by the number the unity that is in the ten-

-cubit piece of wood. And again, when we speak of ten measures of grain, we understand them as divided. So it is with other things too. If a number is applied to natures, it does not primarily present their quantity, but their difference in kind. When we say that horse, man and ox are three natures, we do not signify that they are divided in quantity, but that they differ in form. But when we say three men, say Peter, Paul and John, we present rather their division, and that they are so many, not that they are of such a kind. So too in the economy: when we speak of two natures, we indicate their difference of form, not their separation. We exclude from them, even if they are not enhypostatic, the number of hypostases. We know very well that even in the case of things separated in hypostasis and substance, such as this horse and this ox, the word "nature" signifies not division but difference, just as "hypostasis" signifies division. Much less, then, in the case of things that do not appear by themselves but exist and come to be together and in one another, will "nature" indicate separation rather than difference, whether in theology, in the economy, or in any matter whatever. Put another way: even if we number the two natures of Christ and call them two, we do not introduce a division in actuality of the natures and properties. For every number is a number of differing things. It is impossible to number things that differ in nothing, and in whatever respect they differ, in that respect they are also numbered. Peter and Paul, for example, are not numbered in the respect in which they are united. Being united in the principle of their substance, they cannot be called two natures; but since they differ in hypostasis, they are called two hypostases. So number is of differing things, and differing things are numbered in the same manner in which they differ. The Lord's natures are united without confusion according to hypostasis, but divided indivisibly by the principle and mode of their difference. In the mode in which they are united, they are not numbered, for we do not say that the natures of Christ are two according to hypostasis. In the mode in which they are indivisibly divided, they are numbered, for the natures of Christ are two by the principle and mode of their difference. United according to hypostasis and interpenetrating one another, they are united without confusion, each preserving its own natural difference. Since we number them only by the mode of their difference, they are not divided in actuality and existence, as you suppose. Another point to the same effect: not every number indicates things that subsist on their own, and this is clear from the following. Whatever subsists on its own is in every case in number, but not everything that is in number subsists on its own. Take the elements of composites, to say no more. They complete one thing and are combined into a single continuity, yet they have no existence of their own by themselves. Once they have become what completes one thing, they show their proper existence in the combination. "Animal," "rational" and "mortal," for instance, are not seen to exist by themselves; but in the whole, I mean the man, they clearly show their own

existence. And though they are numbered by the principle and mode of their difference, they do not introduce a division of the man. They might be called parts of a man, but they certainly do not have existence by themselves. So it is clear that not every number indicates things that subsist on their own.

7. You also found fault with the holy and ecumenical Fourth Council over the division of the natures and properties. You claim that by speaking of two natures and of properties of the natures it agrees entirely with Nestorius and creates a division of the natures, and that for this reason we should not accept this council. In its defense, and to clarify what is meant by division and property, we say this. Consider the natures of Christ, I mean the divinity and the humanity, from which and in which the one hypostasis is contemplated as a whole. If someone divides the properties along with the natures in thought and by reason, but not in existence and actuality, he would not be acting unreasonably. Nearly all the Fathers, one might say, have cried this out expressly. Hear Gregory the Theologian, for one: "When the natures are distinguished in thought, the names are divided along with them." So the phrase "in thought" is used in contrast to division in actuality and existence. The Fathers banish that kind of division as far as possible: they say that the natures exist and are named in actuality, but they took their division to be in thought, positing as divided in reason things that are not divided in reality. They did so because of the unchanging difference and property of the things united, even after the union. So it is clear that one may speak of a division of the natures and properties, the kind called "in thought," and we would not stray from reason in doing so. The holy and ecumenical Fourth Council said nothing about this, but we say it nonetheless. When we look at the wholeness of Christ's hypostasis and consider the whole, the whole is composed of parts and is contemplated in its parts. This is especially so when the whole is composed of unlike parts, which are of course preserved without confusion in the union. Since the parts that exist in the whole are reckoned as belonging to the whole, the properties of the parts will also be reckoned as belonging to the whole, even if reason, dividing in thought, judges them to be proper to the parts. Here is what I mean. Sight naturally takes place in the sense organ, that is, the eye, and walking likewise in the legs. Yet we do not say that the eye sees or that the legs walk; rather, the man who has these as his parts is said to see and to walk. So it is with the hypostasis of Christ. When we look at its wholeness, we say that both the miracles and the sufferings belong to the very One of the Holy Trinity, that is, the Son of God. This is so even though he undergoes the sufferings in one part, the human, and performs the signs in another, as consubstantial, of course, with God the Father and with the Spirit. But when we consider instead the parts of which the whole is composed, which are of course preserved without confusion in the union, and the difference is found within the union (where

[?] difference, number is certainly introduced there as well. That is, we say that there are as many parts as [the terms] of the difference, and we make no mistake. For union is one of the relatives. 8. Again, you say that the fourth council agrees with Nestorius: it speaks of two natures, and he likewise speaks of two natures, so it shares the mind of Nestorius. They differ only over the two persons, since he speaks of two persons and the council holds one. You also say that for this reason it mocked the orthodox by claiming that it does not agree with Nestorius. Your own words furnish the clearest refutation of this at once: they show that the council does not share the mind of Nestorius, as you falsely charge. For if he holds two persons, he clearly also confesses the two natures as separated and self-subsistent, and that is why he calls their union relational. But the holy council, by your own account, decrees one person and one hypostasis, so it would clearly say that the natures are united in the one person essentially and hypostatically. Otherwise it would not be possible to speak of two natures in one person and one hypostasis, unless they are united hypostatically and essentially. If so, your own words have clearly shown that the holy and ecumenical fourth council does not speak of the natures and operations in Christ as separated, but as united hypostatically. The same point can be made another way. The nurslings of the Church differ from Nestorius because of the union alone, namely the hypostatic union, and not because of the two natures, as Cyril among the saints also says. You yourself said that the council differs from Nestorius over the one person versus the two, the one producing the union of the natures and the two their division. So it is clear that the council differs from Nestorius in keeping with the right faith of the Church [?]. If this is so, it clearly does not agree with him either. You slander it unjustly, then. To see that this is true, listen to Cyril in his letter to Eulogius, in these very words: “Some are finding fault with the statement of faith that the Easterners have drawn up, and they say: ‘Why did the bishop of Alexandria tolerate it, and even praise it, when they name two natures?’ And those who hold the views of Nestorius say that he thinks the same way, carrying off those who do not know the exact truth. But to those who

find fault we must say this: not everything the heretics say is to be shunned [?] and rejected. They confess many things that we also confess. For example, the Arians say that the Father is Creator and Lord of all things. Must we run from such confessions on that account? So it is with Nestorius too. Even if he speaks of [two natures?] [?] … after the union, that is, by estranging them, not by enumerating them.”

9. You declared [?] that the holy fourth council [?] …, and for that reason shares the mind of Nestorius. You did not simply assert this. You also [adduced] passages from Leo among the saints, from the letter through which the fourth council [was confirmed?] [?] … the letter, and that the fourth council holds the same confession as Nestorius. Come then, let us set these passages before us and examine whether they [?] express what agrees with the mind of Nestorius or not. Word for word, the passages read as follows. Nestorius writes in the first chapter of his teaching discourse: “I confess the two natures of [the Word] of God: true God from true God, and perfect man from the seed of David and Abraham.” Leo writes in his letter: “I confess [him] God, according to ‘In the beginning was the Word’; and man, according to ‘The Word became flesh.’” [?] … the passage of Nestorius, whether it is rightly expressed or not. To say “two natures of the Word” does not seem to be rightly said. Before the incarnate dispensation the Son and Word of God was of the [divine] nature alone. After the incarnation [?] … and [?], not

[?] in the one Word, that is, in the one hypostasis of Christ. Instead he said that the Word was related to the flesh by reference and by a relational union, that is, by dignity, identity of will, or good pleasure. By treating them separately in this way, he claimed that the Word was one and the one from Mary was another. When he spoke of a personal union, he did not mean the person that is identical with the hypostasis, which is what applies to an individual. He held it in a different sense, to suit his own purpose. It is as when someone takes on the role of another and makes speeches on his behalf in his place. This should not be regarded as union in the proper sense; the whole thing is a relational union. Some people call the relation of certain people to one another “persons,” and ordinary usage knows this sense of the word “person.” We say, for instance, that a governor represents the person of the emperor. In this sense Nestorius championed the personal union. For this very reason he has justly been placed under anathema. Pope Leo, however, confessed our one and the same Christ, Lord and God, as existing in one hypostasis, being both God and man. He is God as coeternal, begotten of the Father outside time, and consubstantial with God the Father and with the Holy Spirit. In the last days, for our salvation, he became flesh, that is, became man, and was born of the Holy Spirit and Mary the Virgin. So the theologian’s tongue proclaims, the rest of the oracles testify, the voices of the apostles teach, and the teachings of the God-wise Fathers make clear. It is evident, then, that Pope Leo stands with the truth and does not agree with Nestorius. Again, Nestorius writes: “It was not the Word of God that was clothed in swaddling clothes by the hands of Joseph, but the body of the Lord.” Leo writes that the one shone forth through signs, while the other was subject to sufferings. In this passage Nestorius plainly makes God the Word one and the one from Mary another. He confessed that the latter had a person of his own, and he called him Jesus. If he had spoken rightly, he ought to have said: “The Word of God was not clothed in swaddling clothes by the hands of Joseph insofar as he is the Word, incomprehensible, uncircumscribed and coeternal with the Father. He was clothed in swaddling clothes by the hands of Joseph insofar as he became man for our salvation, like us in all things except sin, and an infant.” [Having spoken as he did,] he clearly introduced a division [?] of the one hypostasis, cutting it into persons, and for this reason he has been placed [under anathema]. But when Leo says that “the one shone forth through signs, the other [was subject to] sufferings,” he does not speak of two wholes, so as to bring in two persons and two hypostases each subsisting on its own. He speaks of [parts] that complete [the whole]. [?] (and so that [?] … the addition, the “one” and the “other,” clearly [?]) he says: the one, the completing

part, taken up into his composition, shines forth in the miracles; the other, likewise completing the whole and taken up into his composition, is subject to sufferings. Whoever understands it in this way, as Pope Leo among the saints said it, will meet with nothing absurd or blasphemous. Again, Nestorius writes: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Leo writes: “Wisdom built herself a house; for the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” The accursed Nestorius did not put forward these passages from his own resources, and Leo did not compose them either. Both took them from divine Scripture and set them in their own writings. But Nestorius took the Gospel saying according to his own perverted understanding, not according to the mind of the Church. “The Word became flesh” has this pious meaning: the divine Word himself, one hypostasis of the Holy Trinity, remained unaltered and unchanged, God as he was, and assumed flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul. He united it to the divine nature in his own hypostasis, that is, the hypostasis of the divinity, effecting an essential and hypostatic union. So he is believed to be one hypostasis even after the incarnation, that is, after he became man. The Holy Trinity did not admit the addition of a person, and he is understood to be, and is, [one] together with flesh. This is the sense in which the Church’s exact understanding interprets the Gospel saying. The Theologian rightly added at once “dwelt among us.” He did so in order that you might understand two things signified, the one who dwells and that in which he dwells, and not think that he was changed into flesh. Rather, you should understand that he dwelt in flesh, using the temple from the holy Virgin as his own body.

10. Since the evangelist spoke of God the Word tabernacling, that is, dwelling, in his own flesh, we must determine in how many ways God is said to dwell in us. The saints too are called a temple of God in which God dwells, but right reason would say that in their case this is said by operation. Again, the Virgin too is called a temple of God, for God the Word dwelt in her essentially. This is more than in the other saints, and incomparably more. But God the Word is said to dwell in his own flesh, which he used as his own body, the temple from the holy Virgin, by being united to it essentially and hypostatically. This is the pious mind of the Church. Nestorius, however, took the saying in a perverted way. He said “The Word became flesh” in the sense of appropriation, by reference of dignity, or identity of will, or good pleasure, because he makes two sons: God the Word is one, and the individual man from Mary is another. Likewise he said that “dwelt among us” was by operation or good pleasure. Hence he also confessed Jesus to be a mere man, and for this reason he has justly been placed under anathema. But Leo, saying “Wisdom built herself a house; for the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” piously

understood it according to the mind of the Church, which we stated above. He is not carried away into Nestorius’ perverted understanding, and for this reason he does not share his mind on these points either. Nestorius writes, separating the two natures of Christ: “The nature is double, into one dignity.” Leo writes: “To hunger, to thirst and to grow weary is human; but to feed five thousand men from five loaves and to grant living water to the Samaritan woman—this belongs to the divinity.” Nestorius has not been condemned for saying “The nature is double.” Very many of the God-bearing Fathers, or rather all of them, declare this of Christ, that he was double. Listen to Gregory the Theologian saying: “He was double, since he grew weary and thirsted and underwent everything that belongs to the law of the body.” Nestorius is to be rejected because he added “into one dignity.” By this he plainly indicated that the natures are separated, made them self-subsistent, and held that the human nature has only a relational union with the divine Word, that is, a union by reference of dignity. But Leo, in orthodox fashion, said that Christ thirsted, hungered and grew weary according to the human, and he attributed the working of miracles to the divine part. This is how the catholic Church teaches us to think of Christ, attributing the lowly things to the humanity and the lofty things to the divinity. So Leo has been shown to be pious and not in agreement with Nestorius, even if you slander him unjustly. If this is so, you are making excuses for sins in vain when you do not accept the holy fourth council and the right doctrine it defined about the dispensation of Christ. It does not divide the one Christ into two or create a separation from God, as you plainly and falsely claim. Rather, it unites, and it makes whoever gladly accepts it an heir of the kingdom of heaven. Together with the three holy councils, it too taught with right mind and clearly set out the mystery of Christ.

11. You have tried to slander the holy fourth council by setting the passages of the vain-minded Nestorius beside those of Pope Leo among the saints, though your argument proved unpersuasive and incoherent. But you have not stopped there. You have also taken garbled sayings from the council itself, and from Saint Cyril as well, and you want to show disagreement between them by setting them side by side. Come then, let us again set these passages before us and show most clearly that the council and Saint Cyril agree. As you wrote, the council says, word for word: “The council of Chalcedon writes that he did not alter the difference of the natures through the union, but preserved the property of each nature.” Saint Cyril writes in his first letter to Succensus: “We speak of one Son and, as the Fathers said, one nature of God the Word incarnate.” “What fellowship, then, does the council of Chalcedon have with Saint Cyril? He united the two and [spoke of] one nature [?], in accordance with the holy council at Ephesus; but the

council of Chalcedon spoke of two separated natures.” Here you seem to present Cyril among the saints as discordant with the council at Chalcedon and at odds with it. As it seems to you [?], he spoke of one nature of the Word after the incarnation, while the council proclaimed two natures after the union. But as reason shows, this passage puts Cyril in agreement with the holy fourth council rather than in disagreement. Whenever anyone said that there are two natures of Christ, Nestorius would immediately seize on the expression for his own purpose and infer two persons. For he said: “There is no nature without a person,” that is, without a person of its own. Cyril among the saints foresaw his perversity and therefore spoke of one nature of the Word, and that incarnate. He did not mean that the Word, united with flesh hypostatically, had become one nature as a whole. If he had said it with that meaning, as you claim, he would perhaps be inconsistent and at war with himself. Here he would be saying that there is one nature of God the Word after the incarnation in the sense that divinity and humanity came together and both produced one nature, composite according to you. Elsewhere, however, he appears again clearly proclaiming Christ in two natures and two natures after the union. He does so not only in the second letter to Succensus, but, one might almost say, in everything he wrote about the dispensation and the mystery of Christ. Nor is that all: he would also be opposed to the other Fathers, which would be a false and slanderous thing to say. Almost all of them have explicitly cried out that Christ, that is, the one hypostasis [?], is in two natures and is two natures after the union, since the same one is perfect God and man after the union. Cyril, however, used a circumlocution: by calling the whole, that is, Christ, one incarnate nature of the Word, he displayed the whole by means of its parts. The one nature of the Word is the same as that of God the Father and of the Holy Spirit. The addition of “incarnate,” which means animated by a rational and intellectual soul, as he himself says, certainly signifies our nature. This shows that Christ has two natures, divine and human. If this is so, he clearly agrees with the holy fourth council instead, since he too showed by circumlocution that the one Christ, one in hypostasis, our Lord and God, has two natures. Now listen to what Cyril among the saints says in the second letter to Succensus, defending himself for having spoken of one incarnate nature of the Word: “If we had said ‘one nature of the Word’ and then fallen silent, without adding ‘incarnate,’ as though we were setting the dispensation aside, their argument might perhaps not be implausible when they pretend to ask: ‘Where is the perfection in humanity? Or how has our substance come to subsist?’ But the perfection in humanity and the indication of our substance have been brought in by saying ‘incarnate.’ So let them stop

leaning on a staff of reed.” See, the teacher says that “incarnate” was introduced to indicate our substance. So the one nature of the Word, together with the indication of our substance through “incarnate,” presents two natures, of divinity and of humanity. A little further on in the same letter he says: “Most rightly [your understanding] sets out the account of the saving passion. It does not assert that the Son of God himself, insofar as he is understood to be and is God, suffered the things of the body in his own nature. Rather, he suffered in the earthly nature. Both must be preserved in the one true Son: that he does not suffer as God, and that he is said to have suffered as man, for his flesh suffered.” Observe how he holds that a divine nature and an earthly nature are preserved in the one Christ even after the union. Are you indignant, then, and will you not concede that the divine nature and the earthly nature are two? Hear Cyril again, elsewhere, in the discourse on the Trinity: “The most wise Paul, or rather the whole choir of the saints, know and teach a twofold account concerning the Son after he [came] in the flesh [?].” Do you say, then, that the twofold account concerning him is according to hypostasis or according to nature? If according to hypostasis, look: that is the thinking of Nestorius, and it is impious. If according to nature, I agree, and here too Cyril agrees with the holy fourth council, which said that there are two natures of Christ. In almost all of the saint’s writings [?] one finds him saying that Christ is double after the union, according to nature [?]. Let Gregory, renowned for theology, be brought in again. In his discourse on the Son he speaks in harmony with the holy fourth council: “He would be called God, not of the Word, but of the visible one. For how could he be God of the one who is properly God? In the same way he is Father, not of the visible one, but of the Word. For he was double, so that the one title applies properly in both cases, and the other not properly.” The same author, in the oration on the Nativity, says: “He was sent, but as man; for he was double.” Let us also bring in Ambrose, bishop of Milan, writing to the emperor Gratian, a passage that was adduced at the council in Ephesus against Nestorius: “Let us preserve the distinction between the divinity and the flesh. The Son of God speaks in each, since each nature is in him.” These passages suffice to show that the holy fourth council agrees with Cyril, with the other Fathers, and with the council in Ephesus. If the length of the discourse did not prevent it, we could perhaps show the agreement of the holy fourth council with the [three] holy and venerable [?] councils, and with [?]. We could do so with many, almost countless, testimonies from the scriptural oracles and the writings of the Fathers, and with demonstrative syllogisms. Since, then, the argument has clearly established this, stop disparaging the holy fourth council, if indeed you [long for] your own salvation and that of those [?]

…of the time, the sovereigns who decreed that that great and crowded synod should be assembled, and who ordered that everything done in it be done lawfully: I mean Marcian and Pulcheria, who greatly adorned the imperial authority with orthodoxy as well as with good order in everything else. Such was Pulcheria's reverence for the all-pure Mary, the Theotokos, whom she faithfully called both Mother of the Lord and Theotokos and venerated with great faith, that in the imperial city above all she built in the name of the Mother of God churches that were very large, very beautiful and splendidly adorned. Each took its name from the place where it was built, and through them she showed everyone the warmth of her faith toward the all-pure Mary, the Theotokos. For this reason you must not disparage her as though she held the views of Nestorius, since you yourself also confess the Mother of the Lord to be Theotokos.

12. Your letter, magnanimous lord, also stated: "We had many testimonies to present concerning the confession that is our doctrine, namely that of the one nature of Christ after the union, and much to say. But because your holiness's letter contained no testimonies of the God-bearing men, we did not include any either." Nevertheless, to set your eminence right, we now say this on these matters too: you must not collect testimonies of the Fathers on faith and doctrine haphazardly and at random. Otherwise you would both expose the divine Fathers to accusation and fail to keep yourself unharmed in the matter of faith. For the Fathers said many things by catachresis, that is, by metaphor, or homonymy, or inversion, or in some other way

…one should collect the passages of the divine Fathers in which they are found legislating about particular matters, laying down definitions, and disclosing their own opinion. An example is the distinction between the terms "essence" and "hypostasis" received from the great Basil, according to which they differ from each other as the common differs from the particular. Or one should collect the passages in which the Fathers, having used terms loosely in one place, clarify in their proper sense in very many of their other writings what they had used loosely elsewhere; or the points on which most of the Fathers have agreed; or what was ratified by a synod. But one should not collect them from a chance [?] remark, in which someone often misuses words because he is rather careless in his exposition, being led to this by other [?] considerations, or not

having the right expression ready to hand, or because he is opposing certain heterodox people, or for other reasons pays no attention to precision in terms.
