13. Further on in your letter, as though annoyed with us because we wrote that those who say there is one nature in Christ are Eutychianists and fall under the same anathema and condemnation, you write as follows: "And we say, master, that in this you did not judge rightly." You therefore also try to set out the opinion of Eutyches and to make clear that he holds a confusion and commingling in the economy and says that God the Word took nothing from the holy and immaculate blood. You thus try to show that you yourself are not a confuser of the natures, and that although you hold one nature in Christ, it is in a different way, and so for that very reason you are not justly subject to the same anathema. But if your argument aims to show the difference between the two opinions, I mean that of Eutyches and your confession, so that you are not dragged under the same anathema with him, our demonstration will nonetheless show that when you say there is one nature in the union of Christ, even if at first you are not found to hold that view, what you say will lead you entirely into the mode of confusion. This will be clear to you from what follows.

Three principal opinions have been put forward about the union of the natures in Christ: the dividing, the confusing, and the one properly called unifying. The first two have been the playthings of the children of heretics, and let them stay that way. For the divine Gregory anticipated them and rightly denounced them. The dividing opinion is merely relational and does not join the natures at all to begin with. It leaves the realities separated from each other, neither giving nor imparting to them what is proper to each. Hence two natures are defined as wholly separate from each other, except that with dignity, will and identity of will it disguises the separation of the natures and deceives the foolish. Such is the opinion of the vain-minded Nestorius. The diametrically opposite opinion, the confusing one, obliterates and confounds most things, and fashions and imagines a single spurious thing. It does not preserve purely in either of the united natures what is proper to it, but makes this into that and that into this, and so allows neither this nor that. For everything that results from confusion turns out to be spurious, having nothing pure and nothing established in its own abiding property. The union that lies between these, unconfused and undivided, recognizes that the united [?] realities possess their own properties without any deficiency, because they are immutable. Yet through the essential union itself it makes them common and the properties of one subject. So what is properly peculiar to one becomes common to the whole, and what is common to the whole is peculiar to one, because the property of each is preserved unconfused in it. For there would have been no exchange of properties unless the property of each had remained unmoved in the union. Such a union is therefore more unifying than the wholly divisive opinions, and richer

NICETAS OF BYZANTIUM

than the wholly confusing ones, so that it makes the united things neither wholly the same as each other nor wholly different. If, then, it shows that what results from the union is neither wholly the same nor entirely different, we must ask in what respect the word of truth knows it to be the same and in what respect different. It is the same with respect to hypostasis, and different with respect to nature. For it is the reverse of how things stand in the Trinity, according to the divine Gregory. But if our opponents find this unacceptable, let them draw the consequence themselves. For if the sameness is not by hypostasis, they will certainly grant it by nature. And if so, there will surely be one and the same definition of divinity and humanity because of the union. And if that is so, union and nature are the same thing, for the predicate is common to both. Just as things whose nature is one have the same definition, so necessarily, according to them, things that are united together and in the same subject must have a common nature. Therefore the reverse also holds: things whose nature is one have different hypostases. And since one nature circumscribes one person, what follows from this? That there is one nature of the flesh and the divinity, and therefore confusion, but two hypostases. But if the things that came together are one neither by nature nor by hypostasis and number, where is the identity of the united things through the union? And if they are one with each other both by nature and by hypostasis, how will the principle of immutability and non-confusion be preserved in the union? So for those who say there is one nature in Christ, the mode of confusion follows inescapably, even if they do not want it.

Another argument to the same effect, showing that those who say there is one nature in Christ fall into the mode of confusion. We must ask you: do you recognize the things that came together as unconfused in the union, or not? You will certainly say they are unconfused, unless you wish to Eutychianize. And even according to you the things that came together are two, I mean divinity and humanity. On what grounds, then, do you not recognize as two after the union the things that were not confused in the union? And if you do recognize them, how is it that you do not confess them? And if you confess them, how is it that you refuse to count them, when you know that their natural property remains unconfused even after the union? "For what they confess," says the divine Basil, "let them also count." If you do not count them, clearly you do not confess them. If you do not confess them, neither do you recognize them. If you do not recognize them, you do not say that the things that came together are two. And so the nature of one of the things that came together has been changed into the other.

Another argument to the same effect. Every whole takes its constitution either from unlike parts or from like parts. If it is from like parts, it is entirely of one kind [?], that is, it is also incomposite. But if it is constituted from unlike parts and different natures, it will certainly be composite, since things put together from different natures are composite. Now the whole that is Christ has been composed from unlike, that is, different natures, I mean divinity and humanity, and these have remained different also in the union. And where things are different, there at the very least the number two certainly follows. If so, clearly it is also counted. But if, according to you, the difference of the parts is not counted in the union of the whole, clearly it does not even exist. And if it does not

exist, it is clear that the parts in which no difference is found have been confused. It is evident, then, that it follows for those who say there is one composite nature in Christ that they are saying the natures have been confused, even if they do not want to. So much for these matters [?].

14. In your letter you abhorred [?] the confusion of Eutyches, as your exposition shows, and you attempted to set out [?] your own confession in a few words, so as to show that you are thereby beyond reproach and seemingly revere [?] the correct doctrine of the Church. That is why you write as follows: "Now we will state the confession in simple words. We say one nature in Christ, which is plain to all. This one nature is understood and spoken of in two modes: the one simple, incorporeal [?] and without composition, namely Michael and Gabriel; the other with composition, like Adam and Noah." Having set these modes aside, [you say] that neither fits the union in Christ. The first, that of the simple and incorporeal one nature, does not fit because it would follow that the Lord had not become man but was bare, without incarnation. The second, the composite one, does not fit because according to it Christ would not be God but a mere man. So you posit a third mode, that of one composite nature, which you confess applies in the same way to Christ. That is why you take man as an example and write by way of illustration: "And man becomes an example, as the Fathers said, and they declared [?] what belongs to the body and what belongs to the soul. But man is not said [?] to have two natures. If someone objects and says there are two natures in man, then Christ too has three natures, two of the humanity and one of the divinity. Now, then, which of these three do we say should be removed from what has been stated [?]? If the body, we Eutychianize; if the human soul, we become like Apollinarius; if the divinity, we become like the Jews who say, 'You, being a man, how do you make yourself God?' So we now state plainly that there is one nature in the union of two unconfused natures."

You have come as if to some impregnable fortress, taking man as an example for your confession. Therefore, since you set out to explain the mode of the one nature according to which you confess Christ to be of one nature after the union, before we take up our counterarguments against you, let us define nature and essence, hypostasis, [?], person and "hypostatic," and explain how the teachers of our mystery and those outside our faith distinguish these terms and to what meanings they assign them, so that no confusion or error may spring up anywhere as we set out doctrine. For almost all those who strengthened the heresies, so to speak, understood these terms wrongly and not in the Church's sense,

and so they went astray. Indeed, Holy Scripture everywhere, the holy synod at Nicaea, the synod at Constantinople after it, and the first of the synods at Ephesus have handed down to us that essence and nature mean the same thing and refer to what is common and universal and predicated of many. Through these synods the faithful everywhere hold and cherish the all-holy Creed, which has handed down to us one nature and essence of the all-holy Trinity and three persons and hypostases. They teach that nature and essence are the same, and again that person and hypostasis are the same, referring to what is particular and individual. The Fathers likewise took the term "form" to refer to essence and nature. That is why the great Basil, interpreting "being in the form of God," said that it means the same as "being in the essence of God." And "having taken the form of a servant" signifies that our Lord was in the essence of humanity. The "hypostatic," however, they treat as different from hypostasis. For in defining hypostasis they said: "A hypostasis is [essence] with a property or properties, considered as subsisting on its own and being a whole in itself. The hypostatic, on the other hand, is essence with a property or properties that does not subsist on its own and in itself as a whole, but is part of some whole."

Those outside our faith define the term "nature" in the same way as the Church, as referring to something universal. They say that nature is one thing and having a nature is another, and by "that which has a nature" they mean the individual, which among us is called hypostasis and person. This, namely the hypostasis, they say is the subject. That is why it is called hypostasis: not, as some supposed, simply because it subsists, that is, exists, but rather because it stands under, that is, under the nature, as its subject, while the nature resides in the subject, that is, is predicated of some hypostasis. They also define nature as follows: "Nature is the principle of motion and rest, primarily and in itself." The term "essence," on the other hand, they apply both to the common and to the particular, that is, to the universal and to the partial. John, surnamed Philoponus, followed them and turned out to be a tritheist. Severus, for his part, uses the term "essence" in the same way as the Church, for something common. But with the term "nature" he went his own way, following neither the Church's usage nor that of those outside. He held that it refers both to something common and to something particular, that is, to the universal and to the partial. By speaking of a common and a particular nature he fell into many absurdities, which the discussion will set out with proof as it proceeds.

15. Now that we have clarified and distinguished these matters in this way, it is time to examine what you wrote here too. It runs as follows: "And man becomes an example, as the Fathers also said, and they declared what belongs to the body and what belongs to the soul. But man is not said to have two natures. If someone objects and says there are two natures in man, then Christ too has three, two of the humanity and one of the divinity," and so on. See how very plainly you lay down the doctrine that Christ is of one composite nature,

and how, wishing to show this, you used man [?] as an example. Just as man, composed of different natures, is of one composite nature after the union, so too, you say [?], the Fathers declared that this example applies in the same way to the union of Christ. And as if to establish the example, you add that man is of one nature: "But man is not said to have two natures. If someone objects that he does, it follows that Christ too has three." So you think you are bringing out some absurdity against us who hold that there are two natures in the union of Christ. It is nothing strange, my friend, that once one absurdity is granted, countless others follow. If every composition were said to be composed not from the things immediately composed but from the remote ones, perhaps what you write against us would have some force. But no one of sound mind would say that a composite is composed from the remote things. It is said to be composed from the things that are joined immediately and directly, which serve, as it were, as parts or elements in the whole. So what you write is feeble and empty. Otherwise, by your reasoning, one would have to say that man is composed of at least five natures: the four elements and the soul. Likewise one would have to say that electrum is composed not of two things, gold and silver, but of many more: gold and silver, the four elements, and further back still, matter and form. For when we ask how many things something is composed of, we do not consider the parts of the parts, but the things that serve immediately and directly as its parts. So even if we say that man has two natures and that the divinity is one, what you want to conclude against us does not follow. For here, in our Lord Jesus Christ, we must not consider the parts of the parts, that is, the body and soul of the humanity, but the things immediately and directly combined, I mean the divinity and the humanity. For if, by your reasoning, we who say that man has two natures will be forced to say there are three natures in Christ, then you too, who say that man is from two natures (even if you say he is not two natures or in two natures but one nature), would nevertheless be teaching that Christ is from three natures. In this way you will be overturned by your own argument. But this is not the case. Therefore, when we say that Christ has two natures, "three" cannot be inferred against us, even if we say that man has two natures.

Another argument to the same effect. Man is either universal or partial, that is, individual. That the individual man is composed of two natures, I mean body and the incorporeal, no one who knows how to judge well will deny. For the body is not immortal but corruptible, and the soul is not mortal but immortal. The body is not invisible, and the soul is not seen with bodily eyes. The soul is rational, intellectual and [?], while the body is dense, visible and tangible. Things that are opposed to each other are not of one nature; therefore soul and body are not of one essence. And again: things whose definitions differ also differ in nature. The definition of the body differs from that of the soul; therefore the nature of the soul also differs from

the nature of the body. These are preserved unchanged in the individual man, so the individual man will be said to have two natures. For each preserves its natural property even after the union, and its definition is contemplated from and in that property. As for generic, that is, universal man: when one breaks it down into the things from which it was composed, I mean soul and body, these too being generic and universal (since nothing generic can ever be produced from two individual and particular things), one would say that universal man has two natures. But when one contemplates the whole itself, taken beforehand from two universal essences, and regards man as a single generic thing completed in its fullness, because many individuals fall under it that do not differ in species and share equally [?] in the same definition, one would then confess that universal man is one essence and nature. And whenever it is taken into the composition of something else, it will be taken as one thing, one nature and essence. The eternal Son, our Lord and God, having become man, is therefore not said to have assumed the individual man, lest the Nestorian madness creep in, but rather the universal man, which he also individuated in his own hypostasis. And this has been shown to be of one nature when considered in relation to [?]. It is clear, then, that Christ, whom we hold to be from two natures, in two natures, and having two natures, is rightly proclaimed so. Nothing absurd or blasphemous will follow even if we say that man has two natures, since all composites are said to be composed from the things that immediately compose them, and not from the things of which those in turn are composed. It is in vain, therefore, that "three" is inferred against us when we say that Christ has two natures and that man likewise has two.

16. Moreover, even if man, from two different natures united without confusion, is completed as one nature, it is not possible for Christ to be completed as one nature, even though he too is composed of different natures, I mean divinity and humanity. This is clear from the following.

1. Everything composed of different natures is completed as one nature when the composite admits neither the names nor the definitions of its components. For example, man is completed as one composite nature because he does not properly admit the names and definitions of his parts. One cannot say that man is properly called soul or body, nor does he admit their definitions, even though he is said to have a soul and a body. But Christ our God, composed of divinity and humanity, does admit both the names and the definitions of the parts. For the same one is by nature God and man and admits their definitions. Therefore he cannot be completed as one nature.

Another argument. 2. Everything composed of different natures and completed as one nature is something other than the things from which it was composed. But Christ is the very things from which he was composed, for the same one is both God and man. Christ, therefore, is not of one

[?] after the union. 3. If everything that is made into one nature after the union is produced either by way of confusion or by way of unconfused union, its parts are co-hypostatic. For example, man, being made one nature, has co-hypostatic parts. Christ, however, is not so, but [?] hetero-hypostatically; not as an accident [?], for accidents are everywhere [said] to be in a subject [?], whereas humanity is seen in others, for instance in [?] or in Thomas, as subsisting individually. Therefore the Lord's man did not subsist in the hypostasis of God the Word as an accident, but as an essence, together with the assumption of the properties that separate Christ [?] from the rest, having come to be hypostatically. And not [?] hypostasis. 4. Further: in all things composed of different natures according to hypostasis, not co-hypostatically but [?] individually, that is, hetero-hypostatically, what is produced is one hypostasis of the things united [?], not one nature. If so, it is clear that God the Word, [united] to human nature not co-hypostatically but having it subsisting in his own hypostasis, is not made one nature. 5. Further: everything that is seen in common and in many, existing not more in one and less in another but equally, and that completes the things of which it is predicated, is called a [?] essence according to the Church. Every man is composed [?] of soul and body, and man does not differ from man in respect of any [?] of nature insofar as he is composed of soul and body; rather, by their constitution [?] all men are brought under one [?] definition, and in this respect they are said to be of one nature. But in the case of the hypostasis of Christ we cannot speak of one nature (for the natures are preserved even after the union), and there are not [several] Christs to be found; for no other Christ came to be from divinity and humanity, but he is God and man, one and the same. If all this holds, then Christ is not made one nature after the union. 6. Further: the 'one' according to the species of man and the 'one' according to the essence of soul and body are not the same. For 'one' according to the species of man shows that there is no variation among all men, while 'one' according to the essence of soul and body destroys its very being and leads it to complete non-existence, for body is not the same as the incorporeal in the definition of essence [?]. It is therefore necessary that those who speak of one nature in the case of man, not because the essential quality of soul and body is the same, but because the individuals [?] brought under the species do not vary, [? not] speak of one nature in the case of Christ as well, where there is no [?] species comprehending hypostases. 7. Further: no things that come about paradoxically [?] produce a nature. We do not speak of a nature of a bush that is in contact with fire and is not burned up, nor of a nature of a human body preserved in fire; we say these are paradoxical things that happen to a [?] hypostasis. But God the Word was united to human nature beyond nature; for this reason what is produced, in one hypostasis, is not a composite nature but a hypostasis. 8. Further:

No nature that is one becomes receptive of contrary essential differences; for how is it possible for the same nature to be at the same time created and uncreated, mortal and immortal, comprehensible and incomprehensible? But Christ has this. Therefore Christ is not of one nature, even if man is of one nature. 9. Further: if, as you say, Christ is of one nature after the union, it will certainly follow that you call this one nature either divine only, or human only, or divine and human at once, or neither divine nor human. If this one nature is divine only, then Christ will be God and not man. If this one nature is both divine and human at once, then it is the nature neither of the Father nor of the Holy Spirit, nor indeed of men. On both counts the charge of blasphemy will attach to whoever thinks this, and he will [?] a sound mind. And if this one nature is neither divine nor human, then Christ is neither God nor man. Wherever, then, we turn the arguments, we are led to say that Christ is one hypostasis of the Holy Trinity having two natures, a divine nature and a human nature. And for this reason both sayings met in him: his own, when he said of himself, 'Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?' and Peter's, when he answered, 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.' 10. Further: if Christ is of one nature after the union, the nature by which Christ is of one nature must be either common or particular. If you say and grant that it is common, it follows that it is predicated of several. But it is impossible to find other Christs, or that there came to be other Christs, of whom this common nature will be predicated. If it is particular, it will be the same as the hypostasis. And if so, by your account it is entirely necessary that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be counted as three particular natures, and that three gods and three godheads be confessed. That is the most extreme of all blasphemies, or rather a denial of all Christianity. For one cannot say without qualification that nature is hypostasis or hypostasis is nature. Otherwise all Christians would have to say either that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are three natures, which is to say three hypostases, or that they have one hypostasis just as they have one nature, and both are foreign to the faith of Christians. 11. Further: [God] brought the parts of man, who is of one nature, out of non-being into being at the same time, and had them for the completion of the universe. Things that come into being at the same time can make one composite nature, since they receive from the Creator such a limit and natural law that by the law of nature like things come from like in succession. But in the case of the Lord, of the natures that were united, one is without beginning and timeless, while the other had a beginning and is subject to time. They did not come to be a species for the completion of the universe, since God rested from his works on the seventh day. Nor did they spring up naturally, nor are they subject to the limit of nature, so that from Christ there should be born and produced a species

of Christs comprehending many hypostases. Rather, they make one composite hypostasis, out of two natures and in two natures and having two natures, each nature keeping its own limit and law, and its difference from the other, even after the union. 12. Further: hypostases of different species are compared or distinguished not by hypostatic but by natural difference, and hypostases of the same species are compared or distinguished not by natural but by hypostatic difference. Just as it is impossible for things that differ by hypostatic difference to be of one hypostasis, so it is impossible for things that differ by natural difference to be of one nature. Therefore one cannot speak of one nature in the case of our Lord Jesus Christ. Rather, the hypostatic union came about out of two perfect natures, divine and human, without change, without confusion, without alteration, without division and without separation. We confess one composite hypostasis of the Son of God, the same also incarnate, produced in two natures that exist perfectly. We say that the hypostasis of his divinity and of his humanity is the same. We confess that the two natures are preserved in him after the union, not setting each apart on its own, but united to each other in the one composite hypostasis. We speak of an essential union. It is essential not because the two natures produced one composite nature, for this has been shown to be altogether impossible, but because they were truly united to each other into the one composite hypostasis of the Son of God. And we define that their essential difference is preserved: the created has remained created and the uncreated uncreated, and likewise with the remaining antitheses. 13. Further: if Christ is of one nature after the union, tell us, of which? And what became of the other? But if both exist, how is there one? Unless, on your view, one composite nature was produced from both. But in that case Christ is of a different essence from the Father, who is not composite, and likewise from the Spirit. That is blasphemous and foreign to the portion of Christians. 14. Further: man is produced as one composite nature from different natures, and becomes something other than the things from which he was composed. No one could ever call him consubstantial or connatural with the things from which he was composed, for his definition differs from that of his parts. Nor indeed are the individuals who fall under the same nature of man connatural or consubstantial with the souls that fall under the common nature, nor with the bodies that fall under the common nature. Christ, however, being one hypostasis of those who fall under the divine nature, is connatural and consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and is properly God and God by nature. He is also consubstantial and connatural with us and with his Mother, as properly man and man by nature, and he is one of the Holy Trinity. For the same hypostasis admits the definitions of the two natures. Whatever account one gives of divinity, one will find the same in Christ, and whatever account one gives of humanity, one will find the same fitting Christ too. So it follows of necessity that Christ is not of one

nature, but that there are two natures of the one composite hypostasis of Christ, even if man is of one nature. [15.] The argument has shown, from common notions and as many natural arguments as possible, that Christ is not of one nature after the union, and that the composition of man is not like the composition of Christ, since man is united co-hypostatically, while Christ has the union of the natures in another way. It is therefore clear that you hold an erroneous confession, which you must abandon. 16. The things said about the economy of Christ are said in Holy Scripture in three modes. Some are said by way of synecdoche, that is, naming the whole from the part. An example is 'Christ died for us': clearly the Apostle says this [?] from the part, namely the humanity, even though the name Christ signifies the two natures; this, however, is a peculiarity of Scripture. Or, conversely, the part is named from the whole, as when the same Apostle speaks of 'the inner man' and 'the outer': from the whole, I mean the man, he signifies the soul and the body. Others are said by way of exchange, because of the mutual interpenetration of the parts and the hypostatic and ineffable union, and because the one who performed both divine and human acts was one and the same. By the mode of exchange, then, the divine nature imparts its own properties to the flesh, and the human nature in turn imparts its own to the divine nature, being hypostatically united in the divine Word, and the two existing together inseparably. That is why the Lord of glory is said to have been crucified, although his divine nature did not suffer, and why the Son of Man is said to have been in heaven before the passion, as the Lord himself said: 'No one has ascended into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man.' Yet we do not say that the flesh came down from heaven; we say that it was formed from the [pure] and spotless blood of the Virgin. So this too is said by way of exchange. Others again are said by way of appropriation, as when we say, 'A few drops of the blood of God sanctified the whole world,' and again, '[?] the Jews,' since the flesh became the Word's own and subsisted in his own hypostasis. The Word therefore appropriates the sufferings of his own flesh and reckons them as his own. In your treatise you yourself went through these modes as used by divine Scripture of Christ, although [?] you thought . . . . . also in the case of the composition of man. Likewise [you claimed] that in Scripture the three modes, I mean synecdoche, exchange and appropriation, are found [in the case of man] just as in the case of Christ, as if you could infer from this that the composition of man is like the [?] of Christ [?]

[?]. That is why you said that Christ is of one nature after the union, just as in the case of man. But in doing so you have unwittingly spun together what cannot be spun together and mixed what cannot be mixed. For one cannot find Holy Scripture speaking of the union of man in the way it speaks of the economy of Christ and the union in him. One can indeed find Scripture using the synecdochic mode of man, naming the whole from the part or the part from the whole, as you yourself said: it signifies the whole man from the soul alone or from the body, or the part from the whole. But the mode of appropriation you could not demonstrate even in the case of Christ, let alone in the case of humanity. And your account of the mode of exchange, which says that the things of the body are imparted to the soul or those of the soul to the body, was mistaken. The mode of exchange or of appropriation is not found used of soul and body, as you claimed through your examples. You said that in divine Scripture 'soul' is used instead of 'body' when the Lord says, 'Do not be anxious for your soul, what you will eat or what you will drink.' But it is clear that eating and drinking belong not to the body but to the two together, I mean the [?]. The wise have said that some things are proper to the soul alone, such as thinking, while others belong to the two together, that is, to the living being, such as eating, drinking, moving, sleeping, waking and similar things that exist because of it. So too the great Basil: 'Some things are proper to the body, such as being cut or burned; others to an ensouled body, such as growing weary; others to a soul that uses a body, such as grieving or being distressed.' These belong to the two together by synecdoche. And the saying 'Do not be anxious for your soul, what you will eat or what you will drink' means 'you yourselves.' Likewise with everything else you went through on this subject: things said by synecdoche you transferred to the mode of exchange, [?] ignorantly and without discernment. So much for these matters. 18. Again, in your letter, as if clearing yourself of a charge because [we] had written [?]: 'If you hold one nature of Christ, it would follow either that this is divine only, or human, or that the divine has been changed into the human, or the human into the divine; or, Christ being of one composite nature with the natures of course preserved, [?] that the nature [?] is [?] composite, because even after the union Christ is connatural and consubstantial with God the Father and the Holy Spirit; or that the Son is not connatural and consubstantial with God the Father after the union; and one might perhaps infer many absurdities from this argument [?]' [?] as if marveling at the writing, and [?] yourself outside [?] . . . 'I marveled [?]'

[?] after a little: 'For if we spoke of a confused mixture in the natures of Christ, as water mixed with wine is wholly confounded [?], or as gold, I mean, and unstamped [?] melted in a crucible are wholly confounded, there would be a likeness to what we say. But if the mixture we speak of between the Word of God and his own body is outside these, like light with its ray, or fire with gold, or spirit with body, without variation and without separation, then you [?] us unjustly, trampling on justice,' and so on. And to confirm the unconfused union of the natures, you brought forward Gregory the Theologian saying this very thing, and his peer and like-minded Gregory the Wonderworker. On this point alone we too agree. So you seem to escape the refutations, since you think the union of one nature in Christ came about without confusion, which you indeed confess. But what you write by no means lets you escape the refutations; rather, you will be found caught by your own feathers. This is clear from the following. Everything that is composed and produces one nature from the composition evidently comes about either by blending, that is, by confusion, or by unconfused union. By blending, for example, come our bodies. And further, whatever [?] is produced as one thing and of one nature from four elements subsists as a whole, the parts that came together having suffered joint destruction in the union. Yet these parts have not entirely departed from their own nature in coming together, for otherwise it could not rightly be called a composition or union of parts that came together if they were entirely destroyed. Rather, in one respect they will seem to be destroyed and in another to be preserved. The whole that comes from them is said to be from so many things that came together, but it will in no way properly be said to be in them or in so many as existing in actuality, unless one means this potentially. Our body, as we said, coming from four elements by blending, that is, by confusion, is said to be from four, but it will be said to be in four, or to be four, potentially, not actually. And although the body is said to have four elements, it will in no way itself be called connatural and consubstantial with the things from which it was composed, because the whole in no way admits either the names or the definitions of the parts that came together into the composition. [?] Nor indeed could individual human bodies be called connatural or consubstantial with the things that fall under the universal elements. But if, again, the composite becomes one nature by unconfused union, as in the case of man, for two things, I mean body and soul, came together without confusion and produced the whole, then this, having a different union, also has a different mode of union. It may rightly be said to be from so many, namely from soul and body, and in so many, since the things that came together are preserved undiminished in the union, existing in actuality; and man may be said to have so many parts

by those who judge rightly. But man is in no way said to be so many, that is, to be two natures, since the natures are in no way predicated of the whole. For the composite has become something other than its components and not the same as them. Nor could the whole itself, namely man, ever be called connatural or consubstantial with the things from which he was composed, I mean the soul and the body, since he does not properly admit their names or their definitions. Nor could individual men, such as Paul or Peter, be called connatural or consubstantial with individual human souls or human bodies, because the universals are not of the same species either. Therefore, if anyone were to say that man, united without confusion from different natures, is connatural and consubstantial with the human soul, it would necessarily follow either that the soul is composed of itself and the body, or, if not that because of its evident absurdity, that the soul is not consubstantial and connatural with the one composite nature of man. We did something of this kind in our Letter, where we said: 'If you speak of one nature in the composite union of Christ, you must necessarily say either that it is divine or that it is human only, or that both have been changed into each other. Or, if the nature of Christ is one composite nature, it is necessary either that the nature of the Father be found composite, so that Christ's connaturality with him after the union may be preserved; or, if not that because it is blasphemous, the Son will not be consubstantial with the Father.' And that is itself the highest of all blasphemy. You, then, thinking to escape the refutations, brought forward the difference between union by confusion and union of another kind, as if on this account you were being unjustly maligned by us. Now our statement that one nature has been changed into the other applies equally to unions by confusion. But then there is our statement that it follows either that the nature of God the Father is found composite, because after the union Christ is, and is believed to be, connatural and consubstantial with God the Father, or, if not that because it is blasphemous, that the Father is not consubstantial with the Son after the union, which is itself beyond all blasphemy and absurdity. The argument, by the illustration of man, has shown that this applies also to [a nature] united by unconfused and unchanging union, and it leads to the absurd and the blasphemous. So you could in no way escape our refutations by teaching that Christ is of one nature and holding that the union is unconfused, for the argument has shown that either way leads to the absurd and the blasphemous. Likewise, the examples you adduced to demonstrate the one nature you hold, produced by unconfused union, were not rightly chosen. They serve rather to overthrow the one composite nature [?] of your doctrine. Take gold mixed with fire: the gold, receiving the fire in its own hypostasis, certainly makes a composite hypostasis having two natures, that of the gold and that of the fire. Very many illustrious and God-bearing Fathers [used] this to demonstrate the two natures in the one Chri-

[651 – Nicetas of Byzantium – 652]
[...]ist, that is, to the one hypostasis, they have set down in their own writings. But these examples are far removed from the unconfused and unchanging union of the natures in Christ. For no one of sound mind would say that the one is composed together with its own ray. Nothing that exists is ever said to be composed with its own activity, or with the effect that comes from it. Nor is the union of soul and body in a human being an unconfused union like the one in Christ. This too has already been shown: the soul's union came about with both parts coming into existence together, but the other came about differently.

19. Again, in your letter you raise an objection and write: “Why were the Fathers in disagreement when they spoke of mixture and of union? Mixture has no separation, and union has no division. But by these words the Fathers meant that, just as things that are separated are not called mixed, so things that are mixed are not called separated; and just as the properties take away the union, so the union fuses the properties. If, then, he was not mixed without confusion with the body, why do they say that he became flesh? And if he was not united with humanity, why do they say that he became man?”

These objections deserve no consideration, since we have already refuted them sufficiently above, and we need hardly concern ourselves with them. All the same, so that no one may think we are treating them with contempt, we shall say a few words about them. When the holy Fathers taught as dogma an unconfused and unchanging union and mixture in Christ of the two natures that came together, divinity, I mean, and humanity, they plainly meant a union brought about hypostatically and essentially in the one Christ. They opposed those who set the two natures apart and separately in activity and existence, namely Nestorius, who is hateful to God, and they rightly placed him under anathema. For things united hypostatically and essentially cannot be separated individually and apart, just as things separated in existence and activity and apart cannot have the hypostatic and essential union. We, therefore, do nothing of that kind when we hold two natures, and two properties of the natures, in the one Christ, contemplating the parts. For number by itself does not divide things, nor does it show that they subsist on their own. We number the natures solely on the basis of their difference, and we hold their activities and wills in correspondence with the natures. But we do not on that account speak of a division of the natures and properties in activity and existence, which would give your charge some ground. And if nothing you write touches us, you are shifting your argument this way and that to no purpose, slandering the truth. So much on this point.

20. We also stated in our letter that the holy synod at Chalcedon proclaimed one person and one hypostasis for this reason: that both the sufferings and the miracles are reckoned as belonging to the one of the holy Trinity, that is, God the Word,

and are referred back to him. You yourself, not [?] ... how thoughtlessly you laugh at what we say and contradict what we wrote, and in your astonishment you write something like this: “And we have learned of another marvel in your letter: that the synod of Chalcedon spoke of [?] and two natures in Christ for this reason, that [they are] reckoned to the one Word of God [?] ... it duly made its defense [?].” Truly you mix what cannot be mixed, and you treat as alike things that have nothing at all in common in meaning. And whether you do so willingly or [unwillingly], God alone knows, you will not understand the difference between what we wrote and the malice of Nestorius. Nestorius thought that nature, person and hypostasis were the same thing. He did not know how they differ, and he reckoned every nature to be self-subsistent. So he objected to the hypostatic union, as though the natures were being merged in the union of one person. He therefore held a dangerous view about the divine Word. Against him Cyril, who is among the saints, gave the example of a human being, in whom two natures are contemplated in one hypostasis: body, I mean, and what is incorporeal. If a man is said to suffer something, such as being burned or cut, he says, “I have suffered this in the body,” while the soul is kept without share in it and impassible. One can see the same thing in the case of God the Word. When God the Word suffers bodily, he himself remains impassible as far as he himself is concerned, since he is God without beginning and incorporeal. It was because Nestorius understood things in his own way that he wrote in opposition to Cyril.

But the aim of the holy fourth synod was something different, not that of the accursed Nestorius. The synod clearly knew how nature differs from hypostasis, as the synods and the Fathers had defined it, and it did not reckon every nature to be self-subsistent. It understood precisely the hypostatic and essential union in Christ, and that the eternal Word gave subsistence to our nature in his own hypostasis. It knew well that he did so by reason of the appropriation that is natural, I mean, and essential, which is contemplated in the hypostatic union. This is not the appropriation that is personal and seen as a relationship, the kind Nestorius proclaimed that the Word had toward the man, but rather, as we said, the natural and essential one. Glorifying the eternal Son as having become man, the synod said what Athanasius and Cyril, the hierarchs of Alexandria, and all the Fathers have said: that he formed for himself from the all-pure Virgin Mary flesh animated by a rational and intelligent soul, and made the human flesh and the human soul [?] his own, belonging to his own hypostasis. And just as Peter, or anyone else, is a man because he has a human body and a human soul, in the same way the eternal God [?] ... having in his own hypostasis a human body and a human soul, and having made them [his own],

his own, and not belonging to some other human hypostasis. Since he has these in this way, he certainly has human nature, which belongs not to his hypostasis alone but also to every human hypostasis. This is why the synod says that the eternal Son, who is one of the Trinity, has two natures in one hypostasis. It does not mean that each nature stands in the same relation to his hypostasis. Rather, the divine nature belongs both to him and to the Father and the Holy Spirit, while the human nature belongs both to him and to individual human beings. His hypostasis, however, is marked off as distinctively his alone, as distinct from the Father and the Holy Spirit. And his body and soul both belong peculiarly to his hypostasis, as distinct from all other human beings. Therefore whatever the flesh of the eternal God, and his human soul, underwent and suffered, the eternal Son himself is said to have undergone and suffered. It truly happened to him and is ascribed to him, just as whatever Peter's flesh and soul suffer happens to Peter and is truly ascribed to him. For this reason, confessing the true faith, we say that the eternal Son himself hungered and thirsted, was in agony and grew weary. His face was struck, he was spat upon and scourged. The hands and feet of the eternal Son were nailed, and he himself hung on the cross, died, was buried, and rose on the third day. All these things happened to the eternal Son. But he suffered them in the way in which suffering was possible for him, that is, in his own human flesh and soul, not in his divine nature. All these things, then, happened to the one Word by reason of the natural and essential appropriation, not insofar as he is the Word, as we said. That is why the holy fourth synod defined one hypostasis and two natures in Christ. Nestorius, however, understood the sufferings of the Word in a different way, as we said above, and that is why Cyril of Alexandria rightly opposed him. This argument of yours, too, has been shown to be stale and entirely without force.

21. Let us see what you write next. Your letter goes on like this: “But let us raise an objection and argue from the contrary words that they themselves use, as we read in the letter. If they separate the natures and, in uniting the persons, speak of a blending, then there must be a blending, and a person must come about. For the Apostle writes of two persons, that ‘being in the form of God, he took the form of a servant.’ So he said ‘form’ and ‘form.’ Now which of the two do they choose to load onto the person they speak of? If they choose the divinity, they will be sick with the sickness of Sabellius. If they choose the humanity, what was it that they truly saw when they saw the Lord in human form?”

Here you frame your argument as if it were brought against us from contraries. You seem to be trying to drive us into an absurdity, since we say that there are two natures and one hypostasis in Christ. By leading us into absurdity, you hope to establish your own doctrine, that Christ is of one nature. What you argue against us, then, comes to this, though you have put it senselessly. You mistakenly suppose that the terms nature and hypostasis, that is, person,

mean the same thing in the case of the incarnation, and you grant that there are as many hypostases, that is, persons, as there are natures. So whenever we speak of two natures and one hypostasis in Christ, you immediately conclude, as it suits you, that a blending of the persons necessarily results. And if it is absurd to speak of a blending of persons, then, since he is of one hypostasis, he must necessarily also be of one nature. Oh, the ignorance of those who say such things! They understand neither what they are saying nor what they are asserting. Who of sound mind would say that the common, that is, the universal, is the same as the particular, that is, the individual, which is the person or hypostasis? The universal is customarily predicated of many, as “man” is predicated of Peter and of Paul. The particular is predicated of one, as person and hypostasis are. Nature and person are not necessarily convertible with each other. If someone speaks of a hypostasis, a nature must be present, since a person, or hypostasis, is nothing other than a nature with a property, or with properties, spoken of as a whole by itself. But if someone speaks of the universal, that is, of a nature, the individual, that is, the person or hypostasis, need not also be present. For universals, contemplated in particulars, help to complete those particulars, but particulars are not contemplated in universals in that way. So it is not because we speak of two natures and one hypostasis in Christ that a blending of persons results. No argument compels this, since nature and person are not the same, and they do not convert in such a way that there are as many persons as there are natures. In many cases one can see two natures contemplated in one hypostasis, and, though there are two natures, there is no blending of two persons into one person. This is so in the individual human being, in iron heated red-hot, and in very many other things: two natures are found united without confusion, but not two persons that might become one by being blended.

Likewise you have also misunderstood the saying of the Apostle: “Who, being in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” As for the word “form,” the great Basil says that it can mean the same as saying that the Son is in the essence and nature of the Father, and that the Lord assumed the form of a servant, that is, the nature, and became man. And all the Fathers who interpreted this saying understood the term “form” to signify essence, that is, nature. But you think that it means the same as person, just as it means nature, and you draw your conclusion ignorantly and without proof.

Another point on the same subject. Suppose we taught that the natures were separated, that is, self-subsistent and existing by themselves. Suppose, for example, that God the Word existed individually with his divine nature [?], and that a man pre-existed by himself and was formed, and that we then spoke of the union of the natures, confessing that they are two

and that there is one hypostasis. Then the two persons would necessarily have been merged into one person. But if this is foreign to the orthodox faith of Christians (for this is the thinking of Nestorius, which we abhor), you draw such conclusions against us to no purpose. What we say is this. God the Word, having the divine nature perfect in himself, then united the human nature, with its distinguishing properties, to his own hypostasis. He made the Lord's humanity subsist in his own hypostasis. This humanity was united to him from the very moment of conception and was not formed beforehand in the Virgin's womb. Rather, the moment it was brought into being, three things took place together: its assumption, its existence, and its deification by the Word. And so the holy Virgin is understood and called Theotokos, the Mother of God, not only because of the nature of the Word but also because of the union with the human element. Both the conception and the existence of that human element were miraculously brought about together: the conception of the Word, and the existence of the flesh in the Word himself. This happened through the Mother of God herself, who in a way beyond nature granted the Fashioner to be fashioned, and granted God, the Maker of all, to become man, as he deified what he had assumed. The union preserved the things united just as they were: I mean not only the divine element of Christ, but also the human, that which is above us and that which is like us. If this is so, it is pointless for you to say that, because we hold two natures and one hypostasis in Christ, a blending of persons follows.

We have set out here our answers and objections to the reproaches against us, and to the abuse and slander directed at the correct dogma of the great and ecumenical synod at Chalcedon. These show all who share the mind of that holy synod to be guiltless, at least to those who wish to think rightly. Let them end here.

22. It remains to examine also what concerns your own confession. You understand and maintain it wrongly, not so much out of wickedness as under the tyranny of preconception (for it would be unpleasant to say out of ignorance and love of strife). You have not fallen away completely from the right teaching of the faith, but only in part. [?] That is, unless someone should want to apply to you that proverbial saying, “He who despises small things will fall little by little.” And everything that leads to a fall, and to a fall away from God, deserves hatred and aversion. In agreement with the ecumenical and orthodox Church, you rightly hold that the Son and Word of God exists before the ages together with his Father, who is without beginning, and with his all-holy and life-giving Spirit. You also rightly hold the indwelling of God the Word in the womb of Mary, ever-virgin and Theotokos, which came about by the good pleasure of God the Father and with the cooperation of the all-holy Spirit. You hold the unconfused and inseparable union of our nature, in which God the Word remained unchanged in his own nature, that is, his divinity, and his humanity, that is, his human nature, was kept unchanged. He assumed everything [?] human except sin alone, that is, body, soul

and mind. Since you confess these things, the one and the same Christ our God is shown to be perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity. If, then, even you confess that God the Word, united to humanity and having perfect divinity, preserves his humanity perfect, on what grounds do you not believe that he is both from two natures and in two natures, and that he has two natures? Why do you proclaim him to be of one nature? If you confess that the same Christ has appeared perfect in each nature, it is clear that you also count these natures, the divine, I mean, and the human. You number them in the mode of their difference, and not by a distinction of existence. That is how we define it, and how the holy fourth synod defined it, and if you confess the two natures in Christ in this way, you are within the truth [?]. But suppose you confess that in the one Christ himself the divine and human nature are one [?], and so do not number these natures according to their difference, and yet you say that Christ is in two natures and has two natures. Then you are clearly inconsistent with yourselves, confessing in one respect and denying in another. For by not numbering the difference you abolish the natures. By abolishing the natures you abolish the absence of confusion and change after the union. And if you abolish that, you also abolish his being consubstantial with the Father in his divinity and consubstantial with us in his humanity. Whoever at one point declares that the same thing has [two] natures [?], and at another insists that it is not as he said before, is either out of his mind or acting maliciously. We pray that neither of these may happen to you. For the first is wretched and pitiable [?], and the second deserves punishment [?]. Yet you think you show yourselves [free] of such charges [?]. You confess that the Son of God has divinity [?] [consubstantial] with God the Father, and [is consubstantial] with us in his humanity. You number the natures, plainly saying: Christ has two natures, and is in two natures, and is of two natures after the union in one hypostasis. You revere with us the synod at Chalcedon, which decreed this, and so you are confident that your way of life is orthodox. [?] to say, and we do not confess the union of the natures, divinity, I mean, and humanity, as a simple union. If you say that the composite, which is of one hypostasis, has two natures, you will truly be reckoned to speak rightly and truthfully. But if you confess that what is made up of different natures results in one composite nature, just as one nature results in a human being from soul and body, then clearly you abolish your own confessions. For it was shown earlier by many arguments that things composed without confusion that produce one nature are neither consubstantial nor connatural with the things from which they were composed, nor with the individuals that fall under what those things have in common. If this is so, then Christ is not consubstantial with God the Father in his divinity, nor with us in his humanity. But if you wish to preserve his consubstantiality also in the union, then throw away the belief in one nature in Christ. These, then, are the absurdities that follow from what you confess about the incarnation of the Son of God, because you do not follow

[?] Niketas of Byzantium [?] … to you in the orthodox exposition of the Christian faith issued by the most holy and ecumenical fourth council at Chalcedon. And because of this very thing, because you shamelessly reject its precise doctrines, or rather understand them ignorantly, you also err about what is said concerning the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ. These are the points.

23. As for what is called "concurrence": the usage of the many, the vulgar crowd, applies it to two or more people competing with one another, whether on horseback or completing the course on foot. But wise men mean "concurrence" to signify not only this, but also the swift and undivided coming together into one of two or more things, without any interval of time, as we know happened in the case of the paralytic. For as soon as the Lord said, "Rise and walk," "immediately," says the evangelist, "he got up and walked." So the wise call the swift fulfilment of the Lord's command, together with the paralytic's healing, a concurrence, for the man's health ran together with the Master's command. It is the same with Peter's mother-in-law, with the rebuking of the sea, and with other such cases. So when the Fathers speak of a concurrence of the two natures in the same one Christ our Lord, they plainly mean nothing other than this: without any delay and without any interval of time, at the very moment the power of the Most High overshadowed the ever-virgin Theotokos, it brought about the union of the two natures. But you take the union of the divine nature with the human in the first sense of "concurrence". You then slander the Fathers as having said that the union is divisible and that each of the essences subsists by itself. Mistaking your own ignorance for blasphemy on the Fathers' part, you have strayed far from the truth and, which amounts to the same thing, from salvation. Now that you have learned the meaning of this concurrence too, and how useful it is for understanding the incarnation of the Son of God, give up the slander that springs from your ignorance, and put forward the term, as we do, to express the exact union of the two natures in Christ. Two things will follow for you from this: first, you will appear wise and knowledgeable; and second, you will be known as truthful in what you teach. Some heretics may have taken the term "concurrence" in its first sense to serve the malice of their own doctrine, and for this reason you reject it when it is applied to the union of the divine and human nature of our one Lord Jesus Christ. But now that you have understood its second meaning, and learned the security it gives concerning the union, do not forbid it any longer. For when things that are not really such share a name with things that properly are, the latter are not harmed by it. And since you confess that the lowly and the lofty things recorded in the Gospel belong to the same one Lord Jesus Christ, with

his body and his bodiless nature preserved in him without separation and without confusion, to which of the natures that came together in the one Christ will you assign the lowly things: to the human or to the divine? I mean advancing in stature, being struck, being bound, being pierced with nails, dying, and things of that kind. For the one who endured these things is truly one and the same, God and man. Yet no one with any sense will say that he endured them in his divine nature, for the divine nature cannot suffer and is not capable of growth. Nevertheless the same Lord truly suffered these things. Will not the very stones cry out, then, even if you keep silent, that he underwent these things in his human nature, being perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity, one Lord Jesus? And if he underwent these things in his human nature, it is clear that our Lord Jesus Christ, who is one in person and in hypostasis, is seen in two natures. The charges brought against the accursed Nestorius you foolishly apply to us, who acknowledge one person and one hypostasis in the one Christ our God. We confess the hypostatic union in Christ. We glorify his one person and one hypostasis after the union. We praise in hymns his dwelling in the womb of the ever-virgin. We glorify his all-blameless Mother as Theotokos in the proper sense. And we confess one and the same Son of God and of the Virgin. That worthless man confessed none of these things, so how could you judge us deserving of the same charge as he? Unless perhaps you want to deflect the reproach that fits you for your ignorant departure from right doctrine, and choose to do so by irrational slander against us who think rightly. Our blameless and unimpeachable belief, both about the theology of the Holy Trinity and about the right teaching on the incarnate dispensation of the Son of God, is shown by the most sacred and divine Creed that we confess. It began with the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers of the council of Nicaea and was confirmed by the remaining six holy and ecumenical councils, though perhaps you will misunderstand this too and try to disparage it. But this has gone beyond measure, since too much talk is hostile to the ears.

Niketas of Byzantium, the Philosopher: [Refutation] of the Book Forged by Muhammad the Arab [?]

1. All the excellences of the most God-beloved emperor are great and far beyond what we deserve. Because they are so great, we are utterly unable to honour them in words, and because they are boundless, we cannot measure them out. Yet the amazement that disposes every mind to wonder, and urges even those of lofty mind to proclaim and announce them clearly, has compelled us, who creep along the ground, to do this work. We will not treat all of his excellences, for that would be quite impossible, but only one of them, and we do not even aim to crown him with praises. For where would I find such a wealth of golden words, so that I might write in gold of the splendours and delights of his virtues, which bloom like a meadow full of flowers? Where shall I place his all-wise steering of the empire? Where the peaceful and untroubled life of the Church? Where the

universal good order of the state? Where the sea of his forbearance and gentleness? Where the showers of his kindness and benefactions? Where the orthodoxy of his doctrine of the faith? Where his preaching of the Gospel of Christ, which one might call apostolic? He is not content merely to rout the bodies of the wretched barbarians; he also wants to cleave their God-fighting souls with the two-edged word of truth. So he calls the Arabs too to true religion, shooting down their irrational and deluded impiety by refuting it with words of truth. He trusts in Christ our God, the giver of victory, whom they blaspheme, that victory will follow both in the refutation of their blasphemy by true arguments and against their lawless armies through his stratagems. Hence we, sluggish as we are, have been led to treat in words what the God-minded emperor has accomplished in deed; and what he achieves every day by his actions, we too have been eager to trumpet loudly in bare words. May the Lord, the steward and provider of every good, lavish on the Christ-loving emperor what saves both soul and body, and grant that by length of life he may refute the barbarians' impiety [?]. Amen.

CHAPTER ONE

A constructive exposition of Christian doctrine, with demonstration, drawn from common notions, dialectical method, natural arguments and an abundance of syllogisms. Also a rebuttal, overthrow and refutation of the most irrational and most abominable book forged by Muhammad the Arab, that is, of the falsely named faith of the Hagarenes.

3. Every day our most Christian emperor, who loves the good, accomplishes many virtuous deeds that tend to the glory of God, especially in the pious worship of God. One form that this zeal has taken in his most serene majesty is the wish that the deluded and most irrational doctrine forged in the so-called book of Muhammad the Arab be refuted. He therefore urged our unworthy self, as someone with some learning and loyally devoted to his God-supported reign, to expose that doctrine publicly as far as we are able. We are to show that it is far from the truth, not only in clear conceptions about the divine but also in matters easily known to the common race of humanity. So we have called upon the prayers of this same Christ-loving master of ours and great emperor, prayers that are acceptable to God and save the world. With the power of the Holy Spirit, fortified with the breastplate of faith, grasping the shield of hope and putting on the helmet of salvation, we have been led to carry out his exhortation. Rebuttal has two parts: one establishes one's own position, and the other overturns the opposing one. First, therefore, we shall set out our pious Christian faith, with demonstration, from natural reasoning as far as that is possible. After that we shall try to refute the things that seem to support his impious doctrine. We shall do this partly by natural reasoning, from the common notions about God, and partly from Scripture, using what the forger of this book himself seems to accept. I shall begin here.

4. The all-wise, good-loving, infinitely powerful and all-holy God brought the world's structure and being out of non-being. Either he created and produced it as one who is powerful in power, or as one who is not powerful in power. If not in power, then the precise and common notions about God that are customary among people, which they both speak of and hold firmly, are false. And how would he have bound together and fitted together the things of this world and brought them into being? Or how could he be producer and creator? How could the name of creation, that is, of such an activity, be firmly applied to him, if he is confined to a nature that is powerless and weak, and is reckoned and believed to be a powerless God? For the name "God", in my view at least, would signify and represent nothing other than creative activity, since the

[?] Niketas of Byzantium [?] Divine is unnameable, inexpressible and beyond interpretation as to what it is. The many have taken this name "God" as referring specifically to the divine nature, like a proper name, though this is not its natural sense. Even so, from this name the idea of power necessarily springs up in our minds, since every activity involves power, and the facts bear witness. If God did not produce the world in power, as was supposed, it is clear that he lacks the ability. Whatever lacks the ability also lacks the capacity to produce. And whatever lacks the capacity to produce and create also lacks being God and being called God. It follows, then, that God is not God, which

5. Another argument. If making involves power, then what is not in power is not by nature able to make. What does not make and is not by nature able to make does not produce either. And what is not by nature able to produce from non-being is not God. So God is not God, which is full of every blasphemy. The argument has shown that it is impossible and blasphemous for God to produce without power. It remains, then, that it is true and certain that he is powerful in power, and the evidence bears witness to this [?]. God produced the world in power and governs the whole by his wisdom, as even those descended from Hagar would surely say. So it is clear that he is powerful. Everyone who is powerful has a power by which he is powerful, through which he acts as one who is powerful, and because of which "being able" is said of him. It follows, then, that God, who made the world in power, has a power by which he is powerful and through which he acts, and because of which "being able" is said of him. If this is so, the power that is possessed would in some way be other than the one who possesses it. For nothing that exists seems to possess itself and be possessed by itself in the same respect, just as the same thing is not both seeing and seen, striking and struck, knowing and known, writing and written. So it is clear that in some way God himself is not called the power by which he is powerful, as one who has power, and through which he, the maker and creator, makes. If this is true, as indeed it is, did God bring the whole world into being and create it by one single, simple power? And was that power finite or infinite? Or did he do it by several powers, and were these finite or infinite? Suppose he did it by one single, finite power. Consider the absurdity: God produced the things of this world and preserves them by a finite power. But whatever produces by a finite power must be bounded and measured along with the quantity and quality of the things that come to be. If that is so, it will also give out along with them, for what is finite cannot endure through infinite time.

6. Another argument. If God creates all created things by one finite power, it is clear that [?] (thō, that is, "I construct and make") the maker of all things and the cause of the construction of all things becomes [?]

and he is defined in his being by a finite power. If so, he is not eternal either. It follows, then, that God is not eternal, which is absurd. Suppose, on the other hand, that God produces all created things by several finite powers. Then the Divine is in no respect infinitely powerful, and both hypotheses come to the same result [?]: it follows that the Divine is in no respect infinitely powerful. Now eternity is, as it were, an infinite power, or as it were an infinite extension, as the learned hold and as the truth confirms. So it is clear that what is eternal is also infinitely powerful. One may therefore reason as follows. If what is eternal is infinitely powerful, then what does not have infinite power is not eternal either. On neither of these two hypotheses does God have infinite power, so he is in no respect eternal. And if he is not eternal, he is necessarily subject to time, for some beings are eternal and others are subject to time. But how can the creator of the ages be subject to time? If he were, he would have both a beginning and an end, and something else would be the cause of his being and existence. We would raise the same difficulties about that, and so on to infinity, which is absurd. It remains, then, that one of the other two hypotheses is true: either the one that says one infinite power, or the one that says many infinite powers. But it is unfitting to say of God that there are several infinite powers through which he creates the world, because God is utterly simple. So it is clear that there is one power, infinite and in every respect infinitely powerful. This is also nearer the truth and in keeping with the common notions about God. The argument has thus shown, from common notions customary to us and through scientific arguments, that God's being powerful comes from one single, simple power that is in every respect infinitely powerful. Through it he does what he does, by it he brought the world into being and produced it, and because of it "being able" is said of him. This power, then, is either in God at some times, or always. If at some times, then God is at some times powerless and lacks the strength to create and produce. For those to whom power is at some times not present are also at some times prevented from acting. If so, his being able does not go together with his willing [?]. And how will he differ from created nature, if being able is not always present to him? But it is not for nothing [?] that the common notion rests on this and firmly holds that God can do all things, both when he wills and when

7. Another argument. If God, as we said, has his power only at some times, it is clear that he receives it as something acquired, since God always exists. Whatever receives something as acquired receives it after its own being; it receives it by way of progress and because it was lacking. It follows, then, that God will at some time be imperfect and be perfected by progress, which is blasphemous both to say and to think of God. Another argument. If God's power is present to him only at some times, he received it later. If so, he received it either from himself

[?] Niketas of Byzantium 680 [?] or from another. Suppose he received it from himself. Then either he received it as one who had power, or as one who did not. If as one who did not, he will never receive it, for what is incapable of doing something cannot do it. If as one who did, then first, since he was eternal, what prevented him from having the ability all along? Second, there would turn out to be a power of the power, and many powers in God, which has clearly been refuted. So he did not receive it from himself, and it remains that he received it from another. But if from another, it was either from an equal, from a lesser or from a greater. That it is from none of these is clear from the following. What is perfected is perfected by something greater. The lesser is inferior, and the equal is merely alike. And again, there is nothing greater than God. If anyone granted that there were, there would be a God of God, and then another God, and so on to infinity. So God did not receive his power from another.

8. God, then, receives his power neither from himself nor, still less, from another. It is clear, therefore, that it is innate in him. He himself always exists, and his power, by which he is powerful and through which he acts, always exists. If it always exists, it is also eternal; if eternal, it is also everlasting and timeless. Everything that always exists is eternal, everlasting, timeless, uncreated and unoriginated. It follows, then, that God's power, by which he is powerful, through which he acts and without which he does nothing, is unoriginated and uncreated. Now one unoriginated thing will not differ in nature from another unoriginated thing in respect of not having come to be, nor one uncreated thing from another in respect of not having been created. If they do not differ at all, they are the same; and if the same, then of the same nature and consubstantial, and whatever else is like these. God is unoriginated and uncreated, and so is his power. And what is unoriginated and uncreated is one in nature, as the common notions precisely maintain. It follows, then, that God's power, by which he is called powerful, through which he acts and without which he does nothing, is consubstantial with God and of the same nature as he. If so, it too is God. As the argument proceeds, it will show that even on these premises there are not two gods, as they irrationally accuse us of holding. It will declare plainly that the Spirit too is in God, of the same nature and consubstantial with God and with his power, which is also called the Wisdom and Word of God. God's power, by which he is called powerful, through which he acts and without which he does nothing, is also called the Word and Wisdom of God, as your own scripture testifies too. This power is not of a different hypostasis, as an accident, as you say. It is of the same nature as God and consubstantial with him, being unoriginated and uncreated, and this is [shown] as follows [?]:
9. God is utterly simple, beyond all composition and every notion of composition, as the common notions also declare to us. And every accident

[?] flux. Every accident, taken together with the thing in which it inheres, is composite and is regarded as composite. If so, it can also be broken up, either actually or potentially, that is, either in thought or in reality. So one can reason as follows: God is supremely simple; no accident taken together with the thing in which it inheres is simple, or is regarded as simple; so it follows that God cannot receive an accident. But he has power, as has also been shown. So this power is not an accident either. The conclusion can also be drawn like this: God cannot receive an accident; God has power; so it follows that the power of God is not an accident. If so, it is also hypostatic: it has being in itself and needs nothing else. It is also eternal, as has also been shown. What is eternal has neither a beginning nor an end in time, and whatever is hypostatic and has neither a beginning nor an end in time is uncreated and unoriginate. So we find that the hypostatic power of God, which the divine Scriptures also plainly call Word and Wisdom, is uncreated and unoriginate. And the common notions are not accustomed to call anything else "uncreated" and "unoriginate" except God.
