So the power of God, which we also call his Wisdom and Word and Son, is true God and like the God and Father in all things. This is what Christians of right belief believe and hold. The argument has shown with exact proof that the power of God is God, the power by which he is called powerful, through which he acts and without which God does nothing. It has also shown that this power is consubstantial with the God and Father and shares his nature. All this is clear.

10. It can be made clear in the following way that this power is also Son of God, Word and Wisdom, and is rightly confessed and believed as such by us Christians. God is true God, and the right-minded call him so, believe in him, glorify him and proclaim him. So he is known either from what belongs to him in himself, that is, from his essence, by which he is glorified, proclaimed and believed to exist, or from what surrounds him, that is, from his creatures. But the common notions also teach us that he cannot possibly be known from what belongs to him in himself, that is, from his essence. Even the angelic powers cannot know him in this way, let alone human nature. For both the divine Scriptures and the common notions teach that God, with respect to his essence, cannot be named or expressed by us and has no name. If one cares to look, there is a clear proof of this: none of his names reveals his essence itself. We take each of the names as guidance toward the divine nature, and each of them carries its own particular meaning. Among the names most fitting for God, you would not find a single word that lacks some definite notion. If, then, he cannot possibly be known from his essence, as we said, it is clear that he is known from what surrounds him, as right reason also shows: "For from the greatness and beauty of [Patrologia Graeca 105]

created things their Creator is known by analogy." For suppose someone refuses to grant even this, namely that he is known from what surrounds him, that is, from what is in us. Since we have never known him with respect to his essence, we would necessarily be left in total ignorance of God, which is absurd. If, then, God is [known?] from what is in us, it is clear that we describe him from the more worthy and more honorable things among us. We leave out the incidental features that happen to us, since we exclude these from what is said of God. That is why we affirm of him everything we affirm of the better things in us, and, more properly, we deny all of them of him. We do not think that the affirmations conflict with the negations, because the two are not made with respect to the same things. To make our argument clear, I will put it this way: [?]

11. Among us there are many different things, and some of them are understood in a way as opposites. Some are worthier and better, while others belong among the worse. So it is surely clear that whenever we are guided from the things in us toward God, we describe and affirm him from the things that are better and more honorable to us. In us there are light and darkness, life and death, mortality and immortality, justice and injustice. Some of these are ranked among the better, such as life and immortality, justice and love. Others are ranked among the worse, such as death, mortality, injustice and enmity. So it is clear that we ascribe to God life and immortality, justice and love, and whatever corresponds to them, and through these we describe and affirm him. To speak more properly, though, we deny these things of him, since God is beyond light, beyond immortality, beyond justice, and beyond everything like them. Likewise there are sight and blindness in us. Setting blindness aside, we will say that God sees, but impassibly, that is, without the affections that accompany sight in us, for God is impassible in all things. Even if we had never received Scripture, we would track God by such traces and ways. In us, then, there are the fruitful and the barren, generation and sterility, fruit and fruitlessness, sprouting and the lack of it. The better ones are generation, fruitfulness, sprouting and the like. The worse ones are barrenness, sterility, fruitlessness and the lack of sprouting. And we describe and affirm God through the better things, without the incidental features that happen to us, as we said. So it is clear that we will say he has fruitful generation, a shoot, fruit and the like. If anyone wants to argue on this point, I will argue as well that death is better than life and darkness better than light, which is ridiculous. So it is clear that God is fruitful and begets a Word.
For with every objection silenced, generation is more honorable than sterility and fruitlessness. If so, it is clear that God has a Son. For one can reason as follows:

12. From the better things in us, we fittingly describe God as begetting, fruitful and bringing forth. Everything of this kind has a relation to a son, a shoot, a fruit or an offspring. So it follows that God, when fittingly described from the things in us, has a Son. We rightly believe and glorify this Son: the Word begotten from him hypostatically, impassibly and without flux. If so, it is clear even to those who can see only dimly that the hypostatic power and Wisdom of God is Son of God, Wisdom and Word, and that we Christians rightly confess and believe it to be so. This is the power by which he is powerful, through which he acts and without which he does nothing. The argument has shown it to be consubstantial with the God and Father and like him in all things except generation. If this is true, as indeed it is, as has been shown, then the barbarous and irrational Muhammad mocks us in vain in the book he forged. He calls us "associators" and "partner-makers", as if we were bringing in the Son of the God and Father from outside as another God, besides the one God who is God by nature and in truth. The argument used common notions and logical methods to show plainly that the power of God is hypostatic, consubstantial with the God and Father and like him in all things, and that this same power is Son, as we rightly believe. This is the power by which he exists as one who has power, through which he acts and without which he does nothing, and which also is and is called Wisdom and Word of the God and Father. If, then, the argument has shown this, it has very plainly banished [the charge] far away and shaken it off. It has shown you to be false, you who [?] us, who confess in the Godhead the [distinction] in property, that is, in hypostasis, together with the oneness of nature. And you do not accept that the Father and the Son are consubstantial and the same in all things, except for being unbegotten and being begotten. So our constructive argument would seem complete to us. It lacks nothing for those who wish, as far as possible, to accept proofs from common notions and natural arguments for things that are beyond nature. It has shown that the God and Father has a Son like him in all things, whom he has begotten impassibly, timelessly and without flux. This Son is also the hypostatic Word, Wisdom and Power of God, and we rightly believe in him.

13. The Spirit too proceeds from the God and Father. Together with the Son it gives life to the world, refashions it and transforms it into a better life. It shares the nature of the Father and the Son, is consubstantial with them and equal to them in honor, being by nature one hypostasis of the one true Godhead. And so we Christians rightly believe and proclaim it. Come, then, let me make my argument about the Spirit as well. I will present the proofs chiefly from common notions, and also from sayings of Scripture, so that the

confession of faith in the Holy Trinity may be firm and [secure?] and may not lead anyone of another faith astray. This is the faith in the Trinity according to its properties, or hypostases, and in its one Godhead, lordship, authority and monarchy. We will begin our treatment of this as follows. The use of common notions has been laid down for us as a clear proof. Above it stands the inspiration given to the prophets through the divine Spirit. This inspiration clearly tells us that God guards and cherishes the whole creation and gives it life. It also tells us that he grants divine inspirations, kinds of gifts and sanctifications to the worthy. Your scripture also speaks in agreement with these things. So it is clear that God is holy long before all else. In divine holiness he guards and cherishes the world and leads it toward a better state. Anyone foolish enough to deny this would be saying that God is completely without holiness. Yet he places the wealth of divine grace, without favoritism, in all who wish to draw from it. How could he do so if he himself had no share in holiness? If he has no share in holiness, he will not sanctify either. Nothing that exists will give anyone what it does not possess, or enrich others with what it lacks. If God has no share in holiness, then clearly the whole creation would be far more lacking in grace and divine [?]. But creation is not wholly lacking in grace, holiness and stability, for how else would it hold together? Clearly God, who bestows these on it, is far more filled with essential holiness and orders the world in sanctification. God, then, is holy in holiness. He sanctifies and orders the world and fills it with divine inspirations, initiations and gifts. If so, it is clear that he has holiness. Whatever has holiness has it either by conferral or by nature. If he has it by conferral, a syllogism lets us see the absurdity: God has his holiness and inspiration by conferral; whatever has something in this way is perfected by progress; so it follows that God is perfected by progress. But it is blasphemous to say this of God.

14. Here is another argument. If God has his holiness and inspiration by conferral, then clearly he has received it from outside. Whatever has something in this way has received it from someone else. For nothing that exists both gives a thing to itself and receives it from itself, or both sanctifies and is sanctified, just as the same thing does not both teach and get taught. If God received holiness from another, he received it either from an equal, or from a lesser, or from a greater. But it is clear from what follows that it cannot come from any of these. Whatever takes a share of holiness from something takes that share by being sanctified. And what is sanctified by receiving takes its share from something greater and is sanctified by it. Of these, the worse and the equal [are ruled out?]. And nothing is greater than God, as the common notion holds. So God has not received his holiness from another. And if not from another, clearly not from outside

either. And if not from outside, then not by conferral, since whatever is such by conferral is such [from outside].

15. Here is another argument. If God has holiness by conferral, then clearly it is an accident in him. Every accident is limited, and clearly it has its being in a created nature. So it follows that God is created and has a created nature. If so, he was created either by himself or by another. If he was created by himself, then the same being will at once produce and be produced, create and be created, make and be made. But nothing that exists is like this. So God was not created by himself. Nor was he created by another. If anyone grants this, there will be a God of God. We will then raise the same difficulties about that God, and so on to infinity. So God does not have his holiness and the inspiration of gifts by conferral. The argument has used many proofs to show that God cannot have his holiness and inspiration by conferral. So it is clear that he has it by nature. If he has it by nature, he has it either of necessity or for the most part. But it is clear that "for the most part" does not apply, because "for the most part" implies a failure of nature. Nature sometimes fails in the rarer cases, while it succeeds in what holds for the most part and in what holds of necessity. But failure is foreign to the divine nature, since all failure involves passion, and God is removed from all passion. So God does not have his holiness "for the most part", and the remaining option is that he has it of necessity. If he has it of necessity, it is also eternal, since that is what things of necessity are like. If God's holiness and inspiration is eternally in him, then it is either hypostatic and has being in itself, or it exists in something else and is an accident. That it does not exist in something else as an accident is clear from the following.

16. God is supremely simple and beyond all composition and every notion of composition, as the common notions also hold. Every accident, taken together with the thing in which it inheres, is composite and is regarded as composite. So one can reason as follows: God is supremely simple; no accident taken together with the thing in which it inheres is simple, or is regarded as simple; so it follows that God cannot receive an accident. But he has holiness and inspiration in himself, and this is also called the Spirit of God. Your scripture, that is, the book of Muhammad, also testifies to this. So this holiness is not an accident. If it is not an accident, it is hypostatic and has being in itself. It is also eternal. Whatever is hypostatic and has being in itself, being eternal, has neither a beginning nor an end in time. Whatever is like this is entirely uncreated and unoriginate. So it follows that the holiness and inspiration of God, which the divine Scripture also calls the Spirit of God, is unoriginate [so the manuscript] and uncreated. And the unoriginate

is the same in nature as the unoriginate, in that it has not come into being; and the uncreated is the same in nature as the uncreated, in that it has not been created. What is the same in nature also shares the same nature and is consubstantial. So it is clear that the hypostatic holiness of God, which the divine Scriptures also plainly call the Spirit, is true God, consubstantial with the God and Father and with his Son.

17. The God and Father, then, is hypostatic, is eternal and has being in himself, as all the common notions imply. It has been shown that the power of God, by which he is powerful, through which he acts and without which he does nothing, and which also is and is called the Word and Wisdom of God, is eternal and hypostatic. Likewise, the holiness that is also called the Spirit of God is hypostatic and eternal and has being in itself. [?] So you will find the eternal and the eternal, and the hypostatic and the hypostatic, to share the same nature and to be consubstantial. And this is our God: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Father is the begetter and the one who sends forth, and I mean impassibly, timelessly and incorporeally. Of the other two, one is begotten and the other is sent forth. For the Father is true God, and so are the Son and the Holy Spirit, since the same one Godhead is seen in them undividedly, as in divided things, so to speak. Yet they are not three gods. As I promised above, I will try to show that this is true. Every number indicates the quantity of the subjects, not the nature of the things counted. It counts them, moreover, not as the same but as different. Likewise every counting-together, that is, every gathering into one number of things that are in some way different, insofar as they are different, is a composition and a gathering. This is clear if someone takes gold and cuts it into five coins. He will not say "five golds" to indicate its nature. He will say "five gold coins" to show the quantity of the subjects, counting them not as the same but as different. Likewise, when these coins are counted together, that is, gathered into the one number five, they introduce a composition of their differences, insofar as they are different. For number would embrace and include different things insofar as they are different.

18. With these points established, consider what is being argued. The divine and blessed nature is seen whole as whole, undividedly, in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, as the argument has shown. It is predicated of them equally and with equal glory, not more of one and less of another. Nor does the predication present one as prior and another as later; it applies to them at once, co-eternally and in the same manner in every respect. For wholeness is conceived either as prior to the parts or as existing in the things that participate in it. In the latter case, it is seen either whole as whole and undividedly in the one, or also in the others. By wholeness I do not mean what is put together from parts and is composite; far from it! I mean the nature as it is seen in its own

hypostases. So it is clear that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are identical in one Godhead, authority and lordship, and are one, since by nature they belong equally to the same one Godhead. The God and Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit equally possess the one Godhead and authority, and in this respect they are one and are believed to be one. It has been agreed that every number indicates the quantity of the subjects and not the nature of the things counted, and that it counts them not as the same but as different. It has also been agreed that every counting-together, that is, every gathering into one number of things that are in some way different, insofar as they are different, is a composition. So it is clear that when we call the Father God individually, and likewise the Son and the Holy Spirit, we do not introduce three gods by counting the nature. Otherwise number and counting-together would apply to the nature, and not to the quantity of the subject things. They would count the same things as the same, and not the different things as different, which has not been agreed. So when we confess Father, Son and Holy Spirit, we do not proclaim that they are one insofar as they are Father, Son or Holy Spirit, since these are different. We proclaim them one insofar as they are seen to be one Godhead and authority and one God, even though they are believed to be three in hypostases.

19. It can also be shown in another way that we do not introduce three gods into the one Godhead, even though we confess three hypostases. We have shown precisely that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit co-eternally possess the one uncreated and unoriginate Godhead. One nature is predicated of the three, not one nature of one and another of another. If so, it is clear that when we speak of three hypostases, we do not also introduce three gods. Anyone who attributes this to us is saying nothing other than this: that one and many are the same thing at the same time, that contradictory statements are true together, and that narrower terms are predicated of wider ones and made equal to them. This agrees neither with the methods of logic nor with the truth. To make our meaning clear, we will take human nature as an example, together with the things of which it is predicated, and so make our meaning plain to you. Suppose that human nature is predicated of only three hypostases, say Peter, Paul and Thomas. This nature is predicated whole as whole and undividedly of Peter, Paul and Thomas, since each of them is a rational, mortal living being, capable of mind and knowledge. Clearly, then, those who share in the nature are one and the same insofar as they share in the same one nature. Insofar as they differ in hypostases, they have received the number three. The word "man" indicates the nature. In the case of the three hypostases it is one and the same, and is predicated of them undividedly. Suppose someone then counted the three together and necessarily counted this word "man" along with the hypostases, speaking of "three men". He would be saying nothing other than that three natures are to be seen in the three hypostases, because the word "man" indicates the nature. And if so,

…it will be found that the same thing holds in the same respect [?]. In other words, human nature would be both one and not one, and the contradictory statements would be true together, which is absurd. And not only that: the lesser terms, the hypostases, would also end up being predicated of the broader terms, the natures, and being equal to them in extent. This too is clear, as follows.

20. Human nature is predicated of the three hypostases. But they are not predicated of it in turn, and the statement does not convert, because human nature is broader than each hypostasis. If something is Peter, it is also a human being; but it does not follow that if something is a human being, it is also Peter. Some predicates are coextensive with their subjects, and these convert. Take "human being" and "capable of laughter": if something is a human being, it is capable of laughter, and if something is capable of laughter, it is a human being. Other predicates are broader, and because they are broader they are not predicated in turn. If something is a human being, it is also an animal; but it does not follow that if something is an animal, it is also a human being. Human nature, then, is broader than each one of the three hypostases. The number three is predicated of the three hypostases, not absolutely, but according to how many subjects there are. That number is what we call the counted number, the number that is counted rather than the one that counts. Suppose you predicate this same number of the word "human being" too, equally with the number of the hypostases. Then each hypostasis will be found equal to the one nature, and will be predicated of it in turn. For "three" and "three" when counted are not [?] but equal. If there are two things and one is predicated of the other, as "capable of laughter" is predicated of "human being," and the predicate is shown to be coextensive, then the predication necessarily converts, and "human being" is predicated in turn of "capable of laughter." So [?] if someone counts the name of their nature together with the hypostases, he concludes that the lesser terms are predicated of the broader ones and are equal to them in extent. As we said, this agrees neither with the methods of logic nor with the truth.
21. The same holds for the divine nature, so that, guided by this example, we may grasp what is true and reject what is false. We confess three hypostases in the divine nature, but because of the absurdities shown above we are not obliged to introduce three gods as well. So it has become clear to us [?] that when we confess three hypostases in the one divine nature, distinguished by their properties, we do not introduce three gods but one God. There is one Godhead, and what comes from it refers back to one. The names Father and Son do not signify a nature. They signify a relation: how the Father stands toward the Son, or the Son toward the Father. Among us these names signify genuine kinship; there they signify that the begotten shares the nature of the one who begot. In the same way the name Spirit does not signify a nature, any more than the others do. It is the difference in how they relate to one another that has made their names [different] [?]. So when we look to the Godhead and to the first cause, in keeping with the single rule of one principle, what we perceive is one; but when

we look to those in whom the Godhead is, those who come from the first cause timelessly and with equal glory [?], there are three who are worshipped. These are the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, in whom we believe, into whom we have been baptized, and whom we serve.
[22.] The people of Hagar may argue: "Strictly speaking, the name of the nature is not counted together with the hypostases. Yet in common usage it is loosely counted, as when we say three men or three horses. So by your own account, let the Trinity you revere be called, in a loose sense, three gods, like three men or any other things counted together." To them we reply that the name of a nature is loosely counted with its own hypostases when those hypostases do not interpenetrate one another but stand far apart, have different wills, operations and purposes, and differ greatly while sharing little. But where there is one mind, an undivided will, identity of nature, one authority, one willing and one operation, and everything is shared except the single difference of the hypostatic properties, and where the hypostases never depart from one another and interpenetrate one another, there the name of their nature is never counted together, whether strictly or loosely. That is why, though we confess the Father as God, and the Son and the all-holy Spirit likewise, we do not introduce three gods. Nor are we required to count them together, strictly or loosely, because they interpenetrate one another, never depart from one another and are never separated, and share one mind, will and operation and the rest that we have mentioned.
They may object again that the name "God" does not indicate the divine nature but an operation, and that names of operations are counted together: we say three orators, three philosophers or three carpenters. To this we reply that names of operations are counted together where differences of opinion creep in, where wills differ, where want drives people to their needs, and where the operation is not one but varied and divided. But where there is one natural and undivided operation, names of operations are never counted together. The supersubstantial Trinity, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, which Christians believe in reverently and [?] and worship, has one operation that cannot be separated. So even if the name "God" indicates an operation, there is no room here for counting together. Our faith is therefore above all slander and accusation, as has been shown.
23. We can also set out the doctrine of the consubstantial and

holy Trinity in another way, by a scientific and inescapable division, presenting the proofs briefly, as follows. If God is truly God and is believed to be so, then he is one of four things. He is one in nature and in hypostasis; or one in nature but many in hypostases; or, conversely, one in hypostasis but many in nature; or many in both nature and hypostasis. If he is many in nature and in hypostasis, the absurdity is obvious. To be like that is to be ruled by many. Rule by many breeds faction. What is factious is without rule and disorderly, and disorder is the beginning of dissolution. If so, such a God would decay and perish. If, on the other hand, he is one in hypostasis but many in nature, that too is absurd. Such a being is necessarily composite, since everything that is made one out of different natures is counted among composite things. What is composite can be broken up; breaking up is followed by decay, and decay by nonexistence. It would follow that God is subject to decay and does not exist [codex, second hand: "exists"], which is utterly absurd. Both "many in nature and in hypostasis" and "one in hypostasis but many in nature" have now been refuted, so one of the two remaining hypotheses must be true. If the argument shows that "one in nature but many in hypostases" is true and certain, then clearly the remaining hypothesis has been refuted along with the others, and the truth is this: one in nature, many in hypostases.
It is clear from this that a nature is either something common or something particular. If it is particular, it is individual, and if it is individual, it is also indivisible, a single individual. It would follow that a nature is a single individual. In that case, when one individual is destroyed, the nature must be destroyed with it, since when one of two identical things is destroyed, the other must be destroyed with it. So when Moses died, human nature would have been destroyed. Yet when Moses died, the nature was not diminished at all. A nature, then, is not something individual; and if it is not individual, it is not particular either, since that is what being particular means.
24. And again: if a nature is a particular thing [?], it must be predicated of one subject only. But it is predicated of many. "Rational mortal animal" is predicated of Peter, Paul, Thomas and every individual human being. So it is not a particular thing, and if it is not particular, it is common. Another argument: suppose a nature is a particular thing. A hypostasis is also a particular thing, and a nature has hypostases of which it is said. Then a particular thing would be found to have something particular under it, which is never found. So a nature is not particular, and if it is not particular, it is common. Another argument: if being predicated of many is what makes a thing common and universal, and a nature has this property, then a nature is a common and universal thing. The supersubstantial, uncreated and unoriginate essence is a divine nature. So it too is clearly something common and universal, since it has been shown that a nature is something common and universal. If, then, the divine and blessed nature is something common and universal

since it too is a nature; and if what is common is not common to one alone (the nature of angels or of human beings belongs not to one but to many); and if, as the methods of logic declare, the universal is likewise what is said of many; then the divine nature clearly belongs to many, since it is something common and universal. That much has been agreed.
25. The divine nature, then, belongs to many, as something common and universal. Every nature, being common and universal, is common to nothing other than the things in which it is contemplated and of which it is predicated, and these are its own hypostases. It follows that the divine nature, being common, is predicated of several hypostases and contemplated in several. This is true, and it agrees with the meaning of the Scriptures. The argument has shown that "one in nature but many in properties, that is, in hypostases" is true. Clearly, then, "one in nature and in hypostasis" has been refuted.
The divine and blessed nature is one in nature but many in the hypostases in which it is contemplated, being something common and universal. Yet it transcends every created nature, and it is marked more by oneness than by multiplicity. The difference in God is slight and faint: there is oneness and identity, unvarying in every respect, except for being unbegotten, begotten and proceeding. In creatures, conversely, there is much otherness and little identity. It is clear, then, that the several hypostases in which the one unvarying nature is contemplated are not an infinite multitude, for the infinite is not akin to the one but foreign to it. Nor do they simply unfold beyond the number three. Multitude in itself stands apart from the one, so infinite multitude is plainly altogether foreign and unlike it. If the first principle were multitude, what shares in it directly would have to be more of a multitude than what is further removed. But since the one is the first principle of the divine nature, the multitude of divine hypostases joined to it must be the smallest possible and the furthest removed from multiplicity. That is the triad. It is not the dyad, because the dyad is not [a number] (8); nor is it any other number, because no other is the first. It is clear from all this that God, who is one in nature, is known in three hypostases, and that orthodox Christians rightly believe in him and glorify him. For us this is the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.
FIRST REFUTATION. Against what Muhammad held [?] in the [?] book.

26. The argument has now presented, by scientific method and syllogistic demonstration, the consubstantiality and identity of the Holy Trinity, its one Godhead and single rule, as far as is possible with things that are beyond reason both in their being and in our belief,

and it has established its own doctrine. So it is now time to examine the utterly abominable and lying book forged by Muhammad the Arab, and to ask whether its contents are true and on target. I shall begin with them as follows. Muhammad's utterly irrational book leaves itself open to refutation from many sides. The whole of it is rotten and easily knocked down, like a rotten house built clumsily out of perishable material, with no firmness or solidity anywhere. So let us first bring to bear the refutation that pulls out the foundation [codex: "pit"] which seems to hold the whole together, intending to overturn it by the power of the Holy Spirit. That is what people do when they set out to demolish houses like this: they first remove what seems to support the building, and then bring the whole thing down to the ground at once. The first siege engine brought against this rotten structure is a comparison with the divine Scripture. Muhammad passed over every other kind of discourse and threw it behind him, and claimed for himself the highest of all, God's own spoken address. So we too must first set his writing beside the Scripture that everyone agrees was spoken by God. The precision of the comparison will expose how strange and incoherent his writing is, and the rest of it will then be shown to be false and empty, and therefore blameworthy [?].

27. Each book of divinely inspired Scripture is arranged individually and stands on its own. All of them look to one aim, piety, yet each is clearly marked off by the subject it covers, part by part. That subject is shown by the meaning of its title together with the [?] aim of the book. So the name of each writing alone is enough to draw even the uninitiated to listen, let alone the initiated. Take, for example, the five books of Moses, Genesis and the rest. Each fittingly presents a whole sense that matches its title, the force of the discourse runs in step with it, and everything in it suits it. Genesis covers what belongs to the genesis of things; Exodus, what happened at the exodus; Deuteronomy, what was legislated a second time; and so on, each appropriately and, so to speak, naturally delimited. If you look, you will find the same in the Prophets, the Wisdom books and the Books of Kingdoms. In this too, I think, the guiding Divine Spirit of the Word shows how unerring and wise it is. The tutor of the mind must first set in faultless order whatever produces unerring knowledge, so that, having tasted its correctness through the perception of the intellect, the learner may then gain certainty about more remote matters.
28. Muhammad the Arab's most pitiful and irrational little book, by contrast, is full of blasphemies against the Most High, and with all its disorderly

and rubbishy abomination it does not even keep the logical order [codex: "list"] found in ordinary writings. It shows no form of prophetic discourse, nor of history, law or theology, nor any other kind that comes from a sound and sensible mind. Its whole [so the codex] composition is chaotic and disorderly, and even the titles set over its sections do not match the discourses under them (10). He falls short even in what we see everyone use with ease. How, then, will he be able to establish that arrogant and supposedly superhuman glory, I mean the claim that the book was sent from heaven (11)? It falls as far short of human understanding as human understanding is set apart from the nature of irrational animals, to say nothing of that incomprehensible strength and wisdom beyond the mind, in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. He is eager to claim that God wrote it, yet from what he writes he cannot show when or how this happened: whether in a vision or some other appearance of God, and with whom as witnesses, as the more than six hundred thousand were with Moses; or whether it was written on tablets, as the law given to Moses was written on stone. He himself says that he received it unwritten, not on paper nor in any work of human hands (12), plainly for fear of being unable to produce it if asked. He is thus deprived of wisdom both divine and human. Worse still, he fearlessly tells lies about that blessed and divine nature, attributing to it things unworthy of it, utterly foreign and alien to it, indeed hostile to it. What is more hostile to God's goodness than to say that he rejoices in the destruction of human beings and counts their ruin as nothing? What adequate answer will he give to show that this does not come from an abominable and demonic inspiration?
29 [?]. Every deed and every word falls into one of three classes: divine, human or demonic. The Arab is deprived of two of them, the divine and the human, and so is necessarily driven round to the third. That he lacks human wisdom as well as divine illumination is clear from what follows and from many other places. Human wisdom either does theology, or studies nature, or treats of ethics, or narrates history, or something of the kind, and does so in a worthwhile way. But the author of this nonsensical writing has had no honorable share in any of these, not even enough to arrange his book under a heading. Stammering somehow, he wandered into theology and blurted out (13) this godless statement: that the divine is spherical,

NICETAS OF BYZANTIUM
or rather, as he himself put it, that God is wholly spherical (14). He must think God is a body, for otherwise God could not take the shape of a sphere. Since on his view God is a material sphere, he will neither hear nor see (intellectually, that is). Nor will he act, except perhaps when something else moves him, and then above all he will roll mindlessly downhill. Be merciful to us, O God, as we repeat this man's words, even though they are against you. If, on the other hand, he calls heaven itself God, as many of the Greeks foolishly did, then too our account will be true that called him demonic. On the study of nature, he either knew nothing to say, or, when he dared to peep into it, he says (15) that a human being comes from a leech (16), and that the sun sinks into hot water as it moves toward evening (17). On ethics, what does he say? "Gather your souls together, and be hostile to everyone, just as everyone is hostile to you" (18). On history, you who read can see for yourselves how many lies he tells about Moses, and about our Lord Jesus Christ himself, claiming that he did and said this and that. He says that the Mother of Christ was the sister of Moses, and that the Christians were with Moses in the desert (19). I do not want to seem to be dismissing all these things without proof by listing them all now, so I shall keep them for the refutation of each one that will be given later, by God's grace. For now I [have touched on] them only briefly [?], just enough to show that this boastful mind is empty of divine and human wisdom and lacks the gifts God gives to human beings.

30. This whole little book has been put out in a hundred and thirteen chapters. In the first discourse, the writing that seems to serve as a preface, he exhorts those who [?] … [?] sounds [?] generative seed), and with slight [?]

has been falsely written. To make the deception look plausible (21), he orders that this book too be accepted along with the earlier holy Scriptures. The barbarian does not realize that this works to his own undoing. Then, again and again, he offers a defense to those who refuse to believe his worthless words, and this defense is full of blasphemy against the good God who loves humankind, who swore by himself that he does not desire the death of the sinner so much as that the sinner turn and live. The defense is this: God gives those who believe this writing the understanding to believe (22), while he himself prevents those who disbelieve from believing (23). In truth it is the other way round: God does not want those who trust this empty thing to be deceived. To put it more plainly, his excuse comes down to this. Those whom God wants to save, he makes ready to obey his every commandment. Those whom he does not want to save, he does not give the understanding and power to listen and to do what pleases him, and so he hands them over to punishment.
From this one can see the host of absurd blasphemies involved. God hinders those who are set apart for the good. He gives laws that contradict himself: he does not want to save everyone, yet he sets saving commandments before everyone, so that they serve to convict them rather than to help them win the prize. He must be doing this out of envy, or because he is too poor to pay everyone their wages, or because he is making sport of his own works, having no one to fear for the sake of such truth. Or he simply delights in the destruction of human beings, or bears a grudge because of his anger at our forefather, or is by nature the cause of evils and cannot help doing evil [?].

31. These and similar things are the opinions of this utterly ignorant barbarian, who thinks he can resolve right from the preface the difficulty of why God did not will that all [be saved, but that some] [?] should be carried away by deception. One thing must be noticed throughout that boorish little book. The man who babbled it knew that his fabricated mythology and barbarian religion would be very hard for Christians and Jews to accept. So he plundered the divine promises found in the divine Scripture, and not even all of them, but only paradise, and falsely promises it as an inheritance to those who obey him. And he does this most wretchedly with women [?] [?], according to [I think: after] the writing that seems to serve as a preface. [?]

711 · Niketas of Byzantium. …he says, keeping company with white-clad and fair-eyed women (24); and, more horrifying still, in the very presence of God (25). For God, he says, is not ashamed (26). So he makes their resurrection a marvel that is wholly fleshly and material, differing in no way from the present life, with them making use of food and drink and privies (27). Those who do not obey him he threatens with the Gehenna that the Gospels threaten against those who [blaspheme?] God, so that by combining desirable and hateful things in what he mentions he might become acceptable. One must also be aware of this piece of trickery: he does not simply refuse to mention the names of the holy prophets (28), so that the honored name of those venerable men may keep the deceit of this God-denying Hagarene [?] religion from being suspected. He merely names them. But the truth they proclaimed he tries openly, through his deeds, to expose as a deception, as though the law were not able to save those it trained unless they were persuaded by him. He also mentions our Lord Jesus Christ himself in various ways, and declares him one of the other prophets. Christ alone, he says, has as his special distinction, being the Word of God, birth from a Virgin through the Holy Spirit, and, with [?], the ascension into heaven (29). It is clear that he did not know what he was talking about and made use of these things in this way as a ruse (30), since in fact he openly disparages him. For he says (31) that Christ was asked by the Father whether he was God, and that he had proclaimed himself God and then denied it. For he supposes that Christ's Father was quite likely ignorant of this (32).

32. Besides this, it is safe to recognize that everything he cites from the Old Scripture and from the New is distorted. And not only that: he also cites things that are not written at all and do not agree with divine Scripture, so that his stupidity is plainly stripped bare and paraded in triumph. He has also collected a great many monstrosities of Manichaean abomination: names of certain demons, oaths sworn by them over blasphemous things, invocations addressed toward the places of the demons, and confessions that apostles and prophets have very often been appointed from among them as well, [rather than?] by the God proclaimed in such a scripture. There is also a letter set down by way of sorcery (33), and numbers transcribed by him [?] the expulsion from paradise, so that God may not judge him: "I know that you said the word, and that the Samaritans enter into paradise, not to enjoy it, but [?] the produce and the…

…happen to differ (34). His own work clearly testifies to the cowardice he feels about the failure of his vain scheme, for in almost every discourse he begs not to be disbelieved when he claims that he brought this God-reviling writing from God. This is what happens to those whose words are not confirmed by deeds. The wretch did not know how severe the punishment is that awaits him for this audacity; but he did know that he was openly fighting against God and could not escape people's notice. So right away, in that same first discourse, thinking to confirm that these things were sent from God, he says this (35): "If you are in doubt about what we sent down upon our servant, bring an ode (36) from those like him"—meaning, of course, the prophets—"and bring your witnesses"—meaning the same prophets—"or else those able to examine whether a word is true or false. Apart from God," he says, "[nothing] will be true (37)." It is as if he were saying, "I too proclaim God, as they do." But the camel-driver failed to notice that simply proclaiming God does not make someone a true herald of the true God; what matters is whether he truly is a herald of the true God [?]. "What benefit," I would say to this barbarian and enemy of God, "does the ode of David, or the prophecy of Isaiah, or of Ezekiel and Daniel, and those of the other prophets gain from your godless proclamation of God, through which your proclamation [is set up?] to overthrow theirs? Where else, then, will you find proof, now that the proof you trusted in has been extinguished? For does not the whole divine and primordial Scripture foretell that God would become incarnate? And this has clearly been shown to be Christ, even though he suffered in the flesh. Isaiah calls his generation indescribable, using the word 'generation' and so describing the Son's procession from the Father, since the word indicates this very thing. But you, being ignorant, do not accept it."

33. Next in his mythical composition (39) he presents God taking counsel with the angels about the creation of man, and being hindered by them on the ground that man would be unjust. But God, he says, made Adam and made him wiser than they were, and it was God who taught him the names of things. Such is the account of man's origin given by the one who urges people to accept the Arabian dreams alongside the divine Scriptures that came before him. Then (40) he says that Moses was commanded by God to point out to the people a heifer that they were to sacrifice. Since they did not know what kind of heifer it might be, he besought God about it many times, and so he learned, and taught them by means of — Isa. 53:8. [?] 5.

…signs, that it is "neither old," he says, "nor young, but between the two, saffron-yellow in color, wild and untamed"; and with difficulty he persuaded them to sacrifice it. Such is the nonsense of his fabrications. These things have been set out to show that his writing has no agreement at all with divine Scripture, the very agreement by which he hoped it would be believed to be true.

34. The godless man, behaving shamelessly against the glory of God the Father and raving like one possessed to seize it for himself, as though he were the one who spoke with Moses and sent forth our Lord Jesus Christ, says (41): "We brought the scripture to Moses, and sent apostles after him; and we brought the manifestation to Jesus son of Mary, and strengthened him through the Holy Spirit." In writing this, what did you think you were establishing? That this barbarian scripture too, as coming from the same God, would be accepted as divine? He did not realize how badly he would miss his aim, and that he would not achieve what he hoped. For how could he? Someone might say to him: "What fault did you have to find with Moses, that you sent forth Jesus?" And if he gives the reasonable and truly genuine answer, "We had nothing to find fault with; we wanted to bring to perfection the elements laid down through him, and moreover to change the burdensome, habitual practice of fleshly observances into the lightness and fitness of the Spirit," then one may say to him again: "Then what fault did you find with Jesus, that you have issued this newer, third scripture? Was it to teach the same things, equal to his, or greater things, or lesser ones? To teach greater things is impossible for human nature. For what is greater than, for the sake of God's commandment, to hate the world and the body, and even to carry one's own soul over plainly to things above nature? But it is obvious that nothing of the kind is contained in this barbarous scripture, nor anything at all lofty and worth mentioning. On the contrary, the whole of it is full of every kind of beastliness and godlessness. If, again, you say it teaches equal things, then what need was there for it, when law and Gospel both stand—the law, I mean, being deficient, and the Gospel bringing it to perfection? It would make those who serve either of them unstable, so that neither could take confidence in salvation, one side blaming the imperfection, the other rejecting the loftiness as beyond human strength. Yet neither of the two is found in it with any exactness in its own right. It remains, then, that it was given to teach lesser things. But if it was given for this, it is utterly laughable that they should abandon the lofty and the middle things to pursue things that wholly grovel on the ground and surpass the irrational animals in nothing. Besides, the least things, being by nature at the extreme opposite of the greater, stand hostile to them. This is in fact true of this scripture, for it is arranged in every respect in opposition to the Gospel of Christ. If, then, the Gospel does not overthrow the law but rather establishes it, since it is what perfects it, and the barbarian scripture tries to overthrow the Gospel, then it clearly tries to overthrow

the law as well. But to overthrow both what perfects and what is perfected is not the work of God. Therefore the God-fighting writing of the barbarian is not the Scripture of God. It remains, then, that it belongs to the adversary of God, that is, to the Anti[christ?].

35. After this he mentions Solomon and insists that he was never led astray, though divine Scripture plainly shows him practicing idolatry in his old age; so he thinks contrary to Scripture at every point. He also mentions two angels who he says came down in Babylon, named Arioth and Marioth. He says they are teachers of evil to anyone who wants it, and further that they dissolve the unions of husbands and wives and do harm. He pretends, though, that even they wait for God's permission. But the text of divine Scripture knows nothing of these angels, unless perhaps one were to say that they are demons belonging to his father Satan and known to him alone. One must also observe this about the barbarian's empty babbling: he plainly knows the demons by name and declares their names, yet he pretends, of course, to call them accursed, and their chief the devil. He does this so that he can ensnare simple people, persuading them that his myth-making comes not from the evil spirit but from one who rebukes demons. Going on a little from this nonsense (41bis), and thinking to present himself as preferred above all the godless and [?] condemnation, and as teaching these things for correction, he maligns Jews and Christians as opposed to one another, each insisting that those of its own belief rather than the other's have been deemed worthy of closeness to God and of the delights of paradise. Then he says that both fail in their hope because of the error of each doctrine, and declares, though no one asked him, that he alone is heir of paradise. He has acted like someone who, when certain people are disputing among themselves over a talent, let us say, pushes himself into the middle and says: "It belongs to none of you, because you are quarreling with each other. It has been assigned to me, since I have done nothing and fought with no one." What he condemned in each party for disputing with the other, he himself is not ashamed to do against both.

36. What sort of proof he has that he brought this book from God need not be said. He even dares to call down curses on himself, and in this alone he truly does well. He pronounces condemnations and countless reproaches upon himself if he has not been sent by God, evidently thinking to cover up the suspicion of falsehood. He also swears by the sun and moon and stars, by shining creatures and running dogs and plants, and by other unknown barba[?]…

…rian names (and I certainly think that they too are names of demons), that he is the God of Abraham and Isaac, who dictated the New Testament for the fulfillment of the law, and who also brought this Manichaean abomination upon Muhammad. Yet the [?] man is quite unable to see in what respect it agrees with those scriptures or disagrees with them. Throughout his whole mythical discourse the persons in it are jumbled together and do not fit with one another, as though the one who composed it forgot who was speaking and who was listening, and whom they were speaking about. They are switched around: sometimes the speaker becomes the listener, sometimes the listener becomes the speaker, and the one they were speaking about becomes both. This is the peculiar affliction of a madman out of his senses. He says (42) that a temple was built to God by Israel and [?], a temple that never existed and is never mentioned in divine Scripture. For if the man who saw God did not pass over the anointing of a single stone anointed as a pillar to God, how could he have kept silent about a whole temple?

37. To those who find fault (43) with the people he has fashioned for praying turned toward the south, he says one need give no other answer than this: it is done to show reverence toward Muhammad and to distinguish them from those who do not do it. Well done, divine wisdom, for setting them apart in this too, and exposing them as worshippers of what is truly darkness! And so that his deceit may become evident: he prepares the wretched barbarians to worship the idol situated at [Bakka?], which he himself calls "the place of worship of observance." "For wherever you are," he says (44), "set your faces straight toward the side of the place of worship of observance." He also says that two barbarian names, Zapha and Maroua (45), are among the sacred things of God—his own god, surely—and he commands those he has deceived, when they arrive there, to circle around the polluted house of prayer there. As we learned from one of them who came over to the Christians, a stone idol sits there in the middle of the house. Those who carry out the command of this demonic man bend their wretched necks, stretch out one hand upright toward it, hold their ear with the other, and whirl round in a circle until, from dizziness…

[?] to those deceived by him (49). "Eat," he says, "of the things on the earth, for they are clean and good; and do not follow in the footsteps of Satan. He is your manifest enemy." By Satan, clearly, he means the one who laid down the distinction between clean and unclean according to the law. Do you see how openly he calls God Satan? The wretch did not understand what he was saying, for shortly afterward he says: "Those who dispute about the scriptures are in a long apostasy." Can anything more shameless and senseless than this be found? An ape that pretends to a lion's charge is exposed when it makes an ape's leap and not a lion's. In the same way this wretched man, who claimed for himself the dignity of supreme lawgiver, has been shown to have nothing more than the most pitiable stupidity. He has put on only the outward form of piety, or rather its bare name, and not the reality itself. So, thinking to give ordinances about fasting to the wretched barbarians, he says this (50): "The month of Ramadan is the one in which the reading was sent down to you; fast during it. The night of the fast will be permitted to you for intercourse with your wives, for they are coverings for you and you are coverings for them. For God knew that you would do violence to your souls in the fast, and [?] for you. Have intercourse with them for comfort, and eat in the evening and drink until [?] the black dye appearing from the darkness through the day [?] star; and then complete the fast until evening. And do not have intercourse with them while you are frequenting the place of worship. This is the legislation of God; do not approach them." Does an ape fall as far short of a lion as this abominable and [?] man falls short of the One who gave the law of divine Scripture? Having [laid down?] this unlawful fast of his, he rouses them to war against us, saying: "Kill them wherever you meet them." Then, setting them limits of love, it seems, he says (51): "And whoever bears a grudge against you, be hostile to him just as he was hostile to you." And [directing?] them falsely toward [?] and chastity, he says (52): "Your wives are your fields; go into your fields however you wish; and come together with your souls"—that is, fulfill every desire of your souls. Then, speaking of the divorce of wife and husband, he says this to the barbarians (53): "If anyone divorces his wife, she is no longer [lawful] for him after she has been divorced, until she is joined to another man. And if the second man divorces her, there is no condemnation on them if they return to each other. For these," he says, "are the laws of God." Oh, the profligacy of the barbarians!

40. To provoke the barbarians to manslaughter, he saw fit to set a story from Scripture before them as encouragement — Sura 2 [?]. (55) [?]

Niketas of Byzantium. …to set before them. Confusing the persons, as he always does, he transferred the events of Joshua son of Nun to Gideon, and those of Gideon to Saul, and he says that David lived at the same time as they did (55). He said that the ark was carried by angels and not by men. That is how well the godless man knew and taught divine Scripture [?]. But the Lord, providing for those who are devout toward him, made his godless heart futile, so that it did not [?] as it intended. For concerning forced denial in matters of faith he says this (56): "Do not compel anyone into the faith, for the [right way] has been made clear from error." Inserting things into his myths as usual, he presents Abraham holding silly conversations and arguing with God about the resurrection of the dead. He says that Abraham received faith in the resurrection through four birds which he placed on four mountains and which were brought back to life. The divine and most ancient Scripture says nothing of this. Not only does he shamelessly charge headlong into evils (58), but he also appears to condemn usury and the robbing of orphans, and urges people to show compassion, so that by seeming to be a good counselor the wretch may escape notice while doing harm in the matters that count. And here too, having prayed for victory over us (59), [he ends] the first…

REFUTATION 2

41. The second discourse of Muhammad's myth-making is entitled "Of the [Family?] of Amran." Right at the outset he declares that this writing was given by God (60), and he adds the reason: it confirms the things sent down before it. And the things sent down before it, he says, are "the law and the Gospel, a guidance for mankind and salvation." Consider, then, whether in keeping with this claim it confirms the law and the Gospel. What follows will show it through the facts: whether it ratifies those books as good and blameless, as is written, or fills up what they lack. If neither of these, nor anything of the kind, is seen in it, then it lies, and moreover comes from a lying mouth, indeed from the father of lies. After his usual babbling, then, he [mentions?] [?] and her supplication, prayer and thanksgiving over the conception of Mary, "the mother," he says, "of Jesus"; and that she dedicated her in the temple, and that she was accepted by the Lord, he says, and taken in by Zachariah. Once, he says, when Zachariah entered the temple, he saw divine food beside her and asked where it had come from, and she said it came from God. He then asked God there for a child, and was promised that he would receive John, a man…

…righteous and a prophet. When Zechariah doubted how he could have a son in his old age, he received silence for three days as a penalty. Next he brings in the angels (62) saying to Mary, "God has chosen you above the women of all ages." And this, he tells Muhammad, comes from the explanation of a hidden matter, as the one speaking to him says: "This is what we have brought down to you, though you were not there (63), when the angels stretched out their arms (64) to see which of them would receive Mary; and you were not there." And the angels said to her: "God," he says, "announces to you the good news of his Word: Christ Jesus, son of Mary, successful in this life and existing in the life to come, one of those who draw near, and speaking to people from his swaddling clothes," he says, "and as a grown man, and one of the useful." Then (65) he brings her in trying to learn how she will have a son without a man, and they say: "What God wills, that also comes to be." He also says that Jesus learned from the angels wisdom and the Scripture and the Law and the Gospel, and was sent as an apostle to the sons of Israel. Then (66) he brings in Christ making birds out of clay, breathing on them and bringing them to life; healing the blind and lepers, raising the dead, and foreknowing things; and he says that Christ called the God of men his own God; that he chose the apostles for himself; and that God said to him: "I will subject you to death, and I will raise you up to me, and I will cleanse you of those who denied, and I will set those who followed you above those who denied on the day of the resurrection; but those who denied I will punish with a heavy punishment in the age to come, and they will have no avenger." And the form of Jesus' likeness, he says, follows the form of the first Adam, whom God fashioned. And he adds: "This is the true account [?]." 42. By calling this account true, he plainly rejected the divine Gospels as false. For where in the divine Gospels is Imran proclaimed as the father of the Theotokos? And what are we to do with the nine months of Zechariah's silence recorded in Luke, when this man says it lasted only three days? And where do we find birds fashioned of clay by Jesus and given life? Truly these things have been invented by the invisible minister of his madness. Is this the scripture that confirms those before it? But it seems he has forgotten what he promised. Or perhaps he is acting with malice here too, even though it has not gone unnoticed. Two ways lay open to him concerning our Lord Jesus Christ by which he might try to do away with his being true God: one was to strive to prove that he had never come at all; the other, to proclaim that the one who came was not God but a mere man. Since

refuting the first was very difficult for him, as it meant fighting against so manifest a fact, he takes refuge in the second. He runs down the account of the incarnation and hopes by this to do away with Christ's being God, and he mentions nothing of what proclaims his divinity. Consistently with what he set out before, he next brings in these statements about the humanity of Christ, saying (67): "O (68) people of the Scripture" (by which he here means those who live under the Gospel), "come to the word that stands in common between us and you: that we serve none but God, and set up no partner with him whatsoever." For since, as he thought, he had spoken of Christ in lowly terms in the way we have described, and had said that Christ too called the God of men his God, he now urges that, on the basis of the common invocation of the one God by Christ and men, by Christians and Hagarenes alike, Christ should no longer be confessed as a partner in the Father's glory, that is, as neither consubstantial nor sharing his throne. Grant him this, and nothing prevents Christians from turning Hagarene. This is the goal toward which, for him, the annunciation to Mary by the angels, the Father's conversations with Christ, and the miracles all lead. 43. What extreme of astonishment does this vain man's folly not surpass? He calls the Mother of Christ the sister of Moses (69), says the Christians were in the wilderness with Moses, and again that the Virgin received the good news of Christ's birth from angels in the temple of Solomon in the time of Zechariah! From this, the facts would follow in reverse order: Solomon would be older than Moses, Moses, Mary and Zechariah would be contemporaries, and Moses would wander in the wilderness many years after the temple was built. O demon-possessed man! O man drunk with the stupor of [?]! O wretched barbarians, who have believed such enormous lies against the divine Scripture! Let them ask those who are strangers to our faith, the Samaritans [?] and the Jews; let them ask the Persians, let them ask the writers and historians of the Greeks, these senseless, unreasoning people whose eyes of knowledge are darkened, and let them learn from them that Moses came before Solomon and not after. And if Moses came before Solomon, and Christ after Solomon, then Christ was not a contemporary of Moses; and if Christ was not a contemporary of Moses, neither was he the son of Moses' sister Mary. What then does he deserve who pronounces so great a lie against the truth of the true God? Truly wickedness is blind, whether it acts willingly or unwillingly. 44. Again, lying as usual, the wretch says that the first holy house was set up for men at

Mecca (70), and that there are manifest signs in it, in the mouth [so the manuscript] of Abraham. None of these things has been found to this day, as those of them who are baptized confess. But the godless man deceived the barbarians with his vain and empty talk. Truly, "the partridge has called out; it has gathered what it did not hatch." Then, after long babbling about himself, as if in the person of the savage demon who inspired him, he says: "Muhammad is nothing but an apostle (71)." It seems that because of his countless lies he was afraid that someone might form a higher opinion of him and suspect him of being an archangel or an angel. "Muhammad is nothing but an apostle; apostles have passed away before him. If he dies, the slaughter turns back (72)." Marvelous is the barbarian's god, who does not know for certain what will happen to his own apostle! "If he dies," he says, "the slaughter turns back." Then he says exactly [?]: "The barbarians, having kept the commandment of their God, turned back." But from this they ought to have perceived the error that the impostor had brought upon them, and, reckoning between two possibilities, to have adopted one of these views: either that it has fallen to us by some chance to rule so great a land (it would be no wonder for barbarians to suppose this), or that those who previously held these places deserved countless torments for their sins, and God, demanding satisfaction from them through us, made us prevail. Neither has anything to do with Muhammad, even if he thrust himself into the middle and seemed to be something while being nothing. But truly, "a senseless man will not know, and a fool will not understand." Next (73) he begins to send the barbarians off to war, and urges them to be always ready for it, saying: "If you fight in this, cowardice will seize your opponents." Having urged these and similar things, and sharpened them for manslaughter, he ended his drivel.

Refutation 3. 45. The third discourse of Muhammad's mythmaking is entitled "On Women." It prescribes with whom one may and may not have intercourse on grounds of kinship, not far from the old law. Afterward he again seizes on his labored [?] main point, that the barbarians must not think what is written to be human, but rather to come from the supreme nature (74). And he tries to train their reasoning: "If, as is likely, you are perplexed and ask, 'How shall we know that this scripture is from God?', do not bring any burden on yourselves by examining what is written or comparing it with other writings, but leave it to the day of judgment, and there you will learn whether these things are true or false." It is as if he said: "Keep nothing of what characterizes being made in the image

of God. Become irrational. Blind the eyes of your mind and follow me [?]. Do not exercise the discernment of good and evil." For he knew, he knew how worthless [?] his drivel was, differing in no way from the ravings of madmen, if it were set beside the divine Scripture or examined in any other way by human understanding. 46. What was said in the first fable too, that his god is the cause of those who perish, he says now as well (75): "Do you then want to guide the one whom God has led astray? Whoever God leads astray will find no way." It was fitting, as one might expect, that such a god should have such a herald. And if those taken captive by his deception refuse our argument, we must say to them [?]: If you call a deceiver God, the God of all things is no deceiver. He is the God of truth, and he is called so in the divine Scripture. Deception is a lie, and lying is not fitting [?] for a pious man, let alone for him who teaches man knowledge. But if this seems right to you as well, because your apostle said that God is a deceiver, then we too say that his god, the one who orders him to write such things, truly is one. And if they are still inflamed when we say that Muhammad has a god other than the one who truly is, we answer that this is shown not by our accusation but by his own confession. For a deceiver must be someone who is unable to do harm openly, or otherwise unable to take vengeance openly on those he wishes, and this has no place in the true God. So we are right to say that Muhammad's god is other than the true God, since he is a deceiver. This is clear from everything that Muhammad has sketched out [?], and also from this vehement accusation against God. If we say that this utterance was spoken by God, then God testifies against himself that he is a deceiver. But if this is impossible, and the apostle must be speaking the truth, it remains that it is the voice of Muhammad's god, and so Muhammad's god is a deceiver. But if his god is not a deceiver, then Muhammad lies when he says his god is a deceiver. And a lying prophet and apostle, being a deceiver, must be put to death when present and anathematized when absent. So Muhammad, if he tells the truth, is godless, and if he lies, abominable. 47. Going on, he again takes up some nonsense and babble so as not to be disbelieved, and he holds fear over the wretched barbarians in case they should try to obtain full assurance that these things were spoken by God. He knew that when he said, "I received these things from God," there would certainly be someone who doubted and demanded complete proof, saying: "If you truly received these things from God, and God is your friend, he can surely ask for some such thing and receive it while we watch." So he says (76), as if from the Python who inspired him: "The people

of the Scripture ask you to bring down upon them a writing from heaven. Indeed, they asked Moses for greater things than these, and said, 'Show us God openly'; and brimstone seized them because of their wrongdoing." Yet it is not written that they were destroyed by brimstone, but rather that they begged that the glory of God should not be shown to them. But this perverted man twisted everything in the divine Scripture toward his own error and destruction. He therefore persuaded those whose souls had already been captured [?] by his crooked fable that if they should seek anything of the kind from him, they would surely perish. This passage had, as he thought, another kind of plausibility [?] for the things he was eager to promote: one served this same point, that he must not be disbelieved when he raved in this way; the other emptied out the whole mystery of the Christians' hope. For while seeming to slander the Jews as having been disobedient to God and murderers of the prophets, he supposed that his own security would come from God's anger against them. He says (77): "Because of the wrongdoing of those who became Jews, we forbade them things that had been permitted to them [?]; and we have prepared for those of them a severe punishment; and because they murdered the prophets without justice." 48. And this is his trickery against the mystery of Christian piety. He pretends to champion Christ and to do away with the outrage done to him by the Jews, namely the cross and death, so that, once this is accepted and believed as coming from a well-wisher, the resurrection would be lost; and if the resurrection neither happened nor is believed, the hopes of Christians would come to nothing. So he says (78): "And of the Jews' saying, 'We killed Christ Jesus, son of Mary, the apostle of God': they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them (79). Those who dispute about him in doubt have no knowledge of him, but only follow supposition. They did not kill him in truth; rather, God raised him up to himself." From this we learn that the devil disguises himself as an angel of light, and it is no wonder if his servants do the same. Now is the right time [?] to recall the Lord's words, that if possible even the faithful would be deceived. For you see goodwill full of treachery, praise [?] full of accusation, and a doctrine that overturns the whole economy of God. Granted that he does not concede that Christ rose as Son of God, why does he not concede it at least of him as apostle of God, as you yourself call him? He acts so [?] for two reasons. The first is that he thought: "If I too am an apostle of God, the barbarians will surely demand that I rise as he did; and if this does not happen in my case, they will surely burn my bones

and the things written by me." The second: "If the resurrection is granted credence, my account does not hold up even so far as to call him an apostle. For if he truly rose, everything he says will also be believed; and by saying that he is the Son of God, he does away with Hagarism altogether." For Muhammad was inventing an error that admits only one person in God. So he consented to say that Christ was taken up like Elijah, rather than that he rose from the dead. Such is the malice of the devil. 49. A little later the vain man again disgraces himself, without even perceiving what was happening to him, and says (80): "Christ Jesus, son of Mary, is an apostle of God and his Word, which he cast to Mary, and a Spirit from him." O senseless and deranged man! If Christ is the Word of God, as you say, he will speak the truth in all that he says; and he says that he is the Son of God. You yourself said that he learned the Gospel from God. He must be believed; and once he is believed, your impiety will be overthrown by your own testimony. It is truly astonishing that while he calls Christ the Word of God and says that the Spirit is from him, he has been unable to understand that what proceeds from the essence of God, while having its own subsistence, is consubstantial with him, and so to worship one God in three hypostases. But blinded no less [?] by his lack of learning, he ends the discourse with some further brief nonsense.

Refutation 4. 50. The fourth discourse of Muhammad's mythology (81) is entitled "On the Table." It speaks about eating meat slaughtered with the knife, except pork, and in this way supposedly promises to declare the barbarians clean. It also condemns perjury and fornication (82), so that he may seem a good lawgiver. But he forgot what he said earlier: "Come together with your souls [?]." He also wants them to purify themselves when they go to prayer, with water if there is any, and if there is not, with dust, which everyone knows is not cleansing but filthy by nature. Again he seizes on his theme of fear. He had heard Christ saying that John was the end of the prophets, and the Apostle saying, "Christ is the fulfillment of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes." So he was afraid that some might say to him, "We have no promise of another prophet after Christ; how then do you call yourself an apostle of God and a prophet?", and that he would seem to be false. He himself confesses that he knows these things are so, and he gives as the reason for his coming: "So that you may not say," he says, "'No one has come to us bringing good news.'" From this he contrives the argument: "For your benefit Christ lied [?]; and he lied because he surely did not know the future. So when I came, he was shown to have lied; and having lied, he could not be God." (83) Sur. 13, 10.

Such is the misanthrope's show of love for mankind, and the stage set of his little fable. But he is refuted by the fact that no prophetic sign is found to have come from him. 51. With his customary falsehoods against the divine Scripture (83), he mentions the death of Abel and says that a raven buried his body while Cain watched, and that Cain was moved to remorse by this. These are things from the stage, from drunkards or madmen. Then, smoothing the hearts of the barbarians so that they would accept his blasphemies, he again mentions Christ and the Gospel, and does not see that he is refuting himself. For he says: "After them" (that is, after all the prophets) "we sent Jesus, the son of Mary, to confirm what came before him, the things of the law, and we brought down to him the Gospel, in which there is guidance, light and righteousness, in accordance with the power of the law before him, as guidance and promise for those who fear; and so that the people of the Gospel may judge by what God brought down in it. And whoever judges (84) by what God brought down, these are the lawless." Did the vain man understand what he was babbling? If Christ came to confirm what came before him, the things of the law, and gave the Gospel to men as light and guidance, as you confess, and he himself is going to carry out the judgment, what is left for you to bring to men? Nothing, except, by your own mouth, to falsify what came before you, to give men darkness and misguidance, and at the judgment to be condemned along with those who received you. 52. Not much further on, as though slipping back into his own madness, he says (85): "O you who have believed" (he is speaking to the barbarians), "do not become helpers of Jews or Christians; for whoever of you defends them is one of them." These are the rewards you pay, for their piety toward God, to the people who were guided, as you said, by the Gospel of Christ. Fittingly so, for what else will the devil and his servants grant their enemies? Granted, he orders that the Christians, who confess the holy Trinity that creates all things and is the source of life, should suffer this. But why does he procure the same for the Jews, who profess to preserve the faith of Abraham? This too is not beyond his malice. He knew that the law demonstrates the divinity of Christ, and so he orders hostility toward both, being through and through a fighter against God. That he wrote these things raving, as he did the earlier ones, or rather, to put it better, everything, is clear from what follows.
