For he attaches to these other similar things and addresses both Jews and Christians, saying: "O people of the Scriptures, you are nothing until you follow the law and the Gospel and what was brought down from your Lord; for there is added, from what was brought down to us from the (84) Arab.: does not judge.

Lord, error and denial." What more then shall we say to this, brothers? Truly our argument is with madmen, who [?] alike about good and bad. In the same way, besides these things, he tells a great many other lies and vanities (86). He thought he could shake Christ by means of the lowly things of the incarnation. He charged monks and priests with being filled with great compunction and tears at the reading of his scripture, which is absurd. Then he again takes up the subject of Christ, and brings him in being reminded by God of the signs which, he says (87), God had worked through him; and being asked whether he had permitted men to hold himself and his mother as gods; and supposedly denying it. By having Christ deny this, he means to show that Christ is not God, and to stop Christians from confessing Christ as God. Refutation [5?]. 54. The [fifth?] fable of Muhammad is entitled "On the [?]" (89), that is, on the [?] signs and proofs that this scripture was supposedly given to him by God. And right from the opening, the material demon who speaks to him chants this to him, so that he too might seem, as one would expect, to be ordered to say these things, and so that he might escape suspicion of deception. For he teaches (90) [?] the primal [origin?] of men

[?] …the substance [?], that they were made from clay according to the image, and that all the angels were commanded to worship Adam; and that while the rest worshipped, Beliar alone did not worship; and that when he was asked why he did not worship, he gave as the reason that Adam had been made from clay, but he himself from fire; and that he was rebuked by God; and that he talked back to God, threatening Adam because of the indignation shown toward himself, that he would leave him nothing except a few of his descendants who are saved; and the story about paradise, and Adam's banishment. You, then, who have been nourished on divine Scripture, surely understand the [?] and empty additions of the impostor.

55. His aim in this looks to the following: that those who set aside God's commandment, he says, perish, while those who keep it are saved and [?] their end. He builds this up from Adam and those who came after him, so that by this means acceptance of his own words would be believed. At once, then, he brings in some unintelligible drivel about obscure and nameless persons who came to preach before Noah: among those who believed them they procured the divine blessing, and among those who disbelieved them the greatest curse. After Noah he introduces a certain Zalet as a prophet and apostle, brother of Thamuth — a man who never existed and was never named by anyone else — who came for this same purpose and preached; and among those who believed him he too made God gracious, but those who disbelieved him, he says, were brought to ruin, wiped out by an earthquake in their dwellings. After this he speaks of another prophet, apostle and herald, sent to his own nation, the Midianites, whose name was Saik; likewise this one too bore witness and acted like those before him — men of whom neither Moses nor any learned man knows anything. And on top of these he mentions [?Moses] proclaiming God; and that among those, he says, by whom he was obeyed, God's help came first, while among those by whom he was disobeyed, justice destroyed the guilty. And having used this method, he readily says of himself: "O men, I am the apostle of God to you all." Well done indeed! Bringing forward no work of divine power, nor of wisdom, nor of any virtue worth mentioning, but self-appointed, without any proof or prior announcement, he carried off the dignity of apostle on his own authority. And which of the most utterly foolish and of those ignorant of God cannot do this? Because Moses is a lawgiver — why then is Pharaoh not a lawgiver too [?]? What you thought you were doing — badly, perhaps, but still you thought you were doing it — that you mentioned as an easy thing; but what you could not foretell, you passed over in silence. Yet I will remind you of this as well: Moses, besides being a lawgiver, is also a prophet, and every day we see the fulfillments of his prophecy. And what of yours shall we admire [?]: the debaucheries? the slaughters? the burnings? the plunderings? the blasphemies? and

the stonings of divine Scripture? For your impious words are worse than stones. "I am," he says, "an apostle of God." Indeed it is plain what sort of God you are apostle of: the one who fights against God, the liar, the slanderer. For the account of your mission teaches nothing more than this. Even if you try to put your hearers to shame with the name of the true God, you are refuted by the fact that you offer no opinion befitting God, that you blaspheme and overthrow God himself, and that you attribute to him what not even the nature of things allows. For how can the one who abolishes Satan be Satan, as you would have it? Or are not his commandments and his laws called the ways of God — the very things you say are the ways of Satan?

56. Then, in addition to this, as one who is the apostle and prophet of the father of lies, he brings in his spurious tales about the miracle at the flinty rock, so that he may seem both wiser than Moses and a more accurate interpreter, and he says: "And twelve springs gushed out of it." And a little later he adds: "When the Jews persisted in what they had been forbidden, we said to them, 'Become apes'; and some of them became apes, petrified [?]." For the moment, even if the strangeness of the story was not out of place, yet those who ordered it were more [?]. Again he brings up the blasphemy woven through his whole discourse, that God is the cause of evils, and says: "Whom God guides, he is the one who is guided; and those whom he leads astray, they are the losers." And a little after, confirming the same: "I have no power over my own soul for benefit or harm, except as God wills." And forgetting that shortly before he had proclaimed himself a prophet, he says: "And if I knew all things, I would have had abundance of good, and no harm could have touched me. I am nothing but a warner [?] and a bearer of good news to a believing people." Having made a show of condemning the idolaters a little — for this is the mask he always puts on after setting down some of his abominable and unacceptable things — he cuts short the drivel.

REFUTATION 7

57. The seventh tale of Muhammad is full of manslaughter and bloodshed; for it is entitled "On the Division [?]." He rouses and [?] the barbarians to stain themselves in every way with the blood of Christians, above all through the hope of the reward stored up, he says, with God in paradise for those who come to close quarters against them. And he tells them to give a fifth part of the spoils to God and to his apostle; for it was only fitting that the man who was the cause of their perdition should also share in their gains, and fitting that from a bloodthirsty people and a still more bloodthirsty apostle the deeds should be bloodthirsty. And being a dissembler himself, he also commands them to dissemble; when we make requests in these and similar matters, he has passed over the campaign in silence [?]. But this must be understood: that, perceiving [?]

the wrath brought upon us by God because of our measureless offenses, this godless barbarian seized the occasion for blasphemy against Christ, and says that we are handed over into their hands for no other reason than that we confess Christ as sharing the Father's throne. Hence he constantly declares: "For God does not guide the people of the lawless." But he can be refuted on many grounds for drawing this wrong conclusion, both from nature and from Scripture. From Scripture: from the pious Jacob and the profane Esau, from Joseph and Potiphar, from David and the ungrateful Saul, from Nebuchadnezzar and the captive prophets, and from very many other such cases. From nature: from sheep and wild beasts and the like; for the sheep do not endure capture by the beasts because they are worse and unfit for giving thanks to God, but it is so ordained for some other, secret reason.

REFUTATION 8

59. The eighth tale of Muhammad is entitled "On Repentance." He urges the barbarians to wait for the Christians for a fixed period of time, so that they might arrange their affairs as they wish. If, then, they become masters of themselves and break away from the barbarians' rule, they are to take up war against them; but if, he says, they change their minds and practice his impiety, they are to receive them as brothers. So he urges the Christians that it is better to repent and live than to die as Christians. And again he shamelessly lashes the wretched barbarians with threats, reproofs and reproaches for being negligent of his rites. And in addition, using the trick mentioned earlier, he tries with a single refutation to silence both Jews and Christians, babbling thus: "The Jews say that Israel is son of God, and the Christians say that Christ is the Son of God. This is their saying with their mouths; they echo the words of those who disbelieved before. May God slay them, because they deny [?]. They took their apostles and their priests as lords besides God, and Christ the son of Mary; yet they were commanded to serve none but the one God." The barbarian is dull-witted, because he is ignorant and uneducated. For if he had any rational understanding at all, he ought first to have stated what is meant by the name "son" according to the belief of each of the two nations, and to have rebuked more mildly those who are not so strongly opposed to him, and the reverse for those who fight him most. For the Jews do not call Israel a true son of God, except insofar as to show God's affection for them, surpassing that for the other nations, for the sake of the fathers. How then does the son of the father of

lies claim that they took Israel as their lord besides God? Let the Jews be asked whether they have ever thought this, or whether it is said in their Scriptures that Israel is their lord. And if the Christians do in very truth confess Christ as God's true Son, as befits God, and of the same essence as God the Father in the divine essence, in accordance with the Scripture of the Gospel, which even the barbarian himself confesses was given by God — for if, as he confesses, the Gospel was given by God, then it is written in it that God cried out three times from above concerning Christ: in one place, "This is my beloved Son"; in another, "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again" — what is absurd or strange in what the Christians do when they confess Christ as God and Son of God, since God himself bears witness to this very thing, and that from the book of the Gospels which he himself praises? But, I suppose, the barbarian never read the Scripture of the divine Gospels; hearing only their name, he extolled them as divine, and did not imagine it was written in them that Christ is truly the Son of God.

61. And there are proofs from the countless testimonies of the earlier Scripture of those who saw God and of the prophets — for one will find the proofs almost rivaling the stars in number, from the very first written book of Moses to Daniel the prophet and the rest. For that Moses knew the oneness of the divine nature and the distinction of the properties, that is, of the hypostases, is clear when he wrote, "Let us make man according to our image and likeness"; and when he said, "Behold, Adam has become like one of us." And also when he wrote, "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God, the Lord is one," it is clear that he knew the Trinity to be united in cause, essence and concord. Otherwise he wrote things contradicting himself: earlier presenting different persons in dialogue, and afterward proclaiming that there was only one person, the one who speaks and hears and acts — which is unthinkable. And Daniel, the most vivid of all the ancient prophets, clearly showed the time of Christ's coming and indicated his dignity when he says: "I looked, and behold, on the clouds of heaven one like a son of man; and to him was given honor and worship," and so on — and this while the Ancient of Days was seated on the throne.

62. But let the evidence from the ancient Scriptures be set aside. From Christ's own predictions and their fulfillment, if the foolish man had been capable of understanding, he would have grasped the reverence due to his divinity; and also from the testimony of John, whom he himself, when he proclaimed him, accepted as a prophet and a righteous man; or from the miracles that are his tokens — I mean the tomb and the resurrection. But Muhammad perceived none of these things; for he never had any concern for the knowledge of God, except insofar as

to ensnare his hearers with the name of the Scriptures. For, tell me, who that truly claims to follow his friend's word sets that friend's faith at naught when it is denied [?] in confirmation of certain matters? And if anyone of that kind is found anywhere, he is under a curse, according to the Scripture: "Woe," it says, "to the sinner who walks on two paths" — just as this senseless and inhuman man does. Some say that Israel is son of God, others that Christ is. What then? Do you always judge it a clear sign of falsehood that, when different persons dispute about something, the two sides do not agree? And do you suppose the matter is utterly abolished whenever some hold different opinions about it, and that by the denials of the other parties [?] either neither of them, or the whole thing, is refuted [?]? Bravo for your truth-loving knowledge! What then will you do, tell me, since we do not believe in your God but in our God, and you believe in your supposed God but not in ours? For it is yours, as the prophet says, to say in your folly, "There is no God," if each side has a different God. See where his own mighty refutation has overturned him: "Truly his mischief will return upon his own head, and his blasphemy will come down upon his own crown." And it is reasonable that the son of the slave girl, being by nature a slave, so to speak, cannot so much as imagine the title of son even by grace, as Israel did: slavishly brought up, slavishly initiated, and nothing more than that.

63. Next, the sign that the Apostle spoke of concerning the Antichrist can be clearly found in this passage: "Even though those who deny are displeased, it is he who sent his apostle for guidance and for the true faith, so that he may rule above every faith." This is the same as "who opposes and exalts himself above everything called god or object of worship" — simply, "so that he may rule above every faith." So in his eyes even the faith of Abraham was disparaged, the very faith he supposed he held; and not only the Law and the Gospel, for he says "above every faith"; and "true" is said in comparison with the rest. I do not hesitate from now on to consider that he too is truly an Antichrist. A little later it becomes plain where the whole aim of his fighting against God is heading. For the man who until now has insisted that God has no Son, not trusting himself as he contended for this, but reasoning that perhaps he does have one, does not shrink from attaching this role to himself, even if he brought it in obliquely; and he pretends, as it were, to adopt a most shameful stupidity, and says: "Some vex [?] the prophet and say that he himself is son of God." And he did not say that "the

Son" is, taking into account the one he is striving to destroy, lest, caught utterly stripped of [?], he be tripped up; but "that he himself is son" — as if he were saying, "If you want to confess a Son of God, I am nearer to what is being spoken of." Then, after babbling some things indecently, and priding himself on confirming the proofs of his nonsense by more nonsense, he mentions certain Thamud, and Midian, and Mateuchamat, to whom, he says, their apostles brought the manifestation — these being obscure and unproven, just as he himself is. And at once he leads the barbarians out on campaign against us, and after barking out the things that provoke them to it, he cuts short the drivel.

REFUTATION 9

64. The ninth tale of Muhammad is entitled "On Jonah," yet nothing about Jonah is contained in it. Instead, straight from the opening, as if fighting and accusing, or else mocking, he comes in saying: "Was it strange to men that God revealed to a man from among them that he should bear witness to men and bring good news to those who believed, that they have true advancement from their Lord?" He says this as if in the person of God, about himself. Then he brings in those who, as is likely, disbelieved and said, "This man is a sorcerer" — this he says on his own behalf. But to the first statement we reply that it is not at all strange for it to be revealed by God and proclaimed as good news to those who believe that they have true advancement from him; but whether "true advancement" could truly be said in his case [?] — since this has proved false, we turn away from the man who says that such a thing has been revealed, as truly lawless and, as he himself says, a sorcerer. For we know Abraham to have been such a one, and we are not surprised; for God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. From the ignorance of idols Abraham advanced to true progress in the knowledge of God, because this was revealed to him by God; and the works of his piety became more evident, confirming the knowledge of the truth. After him, again, we know that it was revealed to Moses by God to bear witness to men that there is true advancement from their Lord for those who believe; and this came to pass. For the law of God led Abraham's descendants up from the knowledge of God and way of life of Abraham's time, which was still imperfect, to a more perfect knowledge of God and way of life. If this is not granted, all the things of the law would be superfluous and pointless — the Sabbath and the sacrifices acceptable to God, which Abraham did not know — and that is impossible. After Moses — to stretch the word "revelation," until the outcome makes everything plain — God revealed to men through Jesus Christ that there is true advancement from the Lord for those who believe; and the word was fulfilled in deed. For the knowledge of God

became clearer and the way of life more exact; and this is evident from the fact that they were told not to murder, but we not to be angry.

65. Since, then, true advancement is to be seen — in Abraham's case from the ignorance of God among idols to God [?], and his own [?] is witness; from Abraham to the Law, true advancement, and the good order of the legislation bears witness; and from the Law to our Lord Jesus Christ, true advancement, and the exactness of the gospel way of life bears witness — it is not strange to men that God revealed to a man from among them that he should bear witness and bring good news to those who believe that there is true advancement. Let us now see whether this is said to have happened in Muhammad's case too. For he appears to extol Abraham's faith, the Law and the Gospel; and while he was under no obligation to add to Abraham and the Law, he necessarily had to add to the Gospel. Let us examine, then, which of Christ's commandments he enlarged upon. Was it those about poverty? Was it those about chastity? Those about freedom from anger [?]? But none of these is to be seen in him; on the contrary, he wrote and did the opposite of all of them. It remains, then, necessarily to conclude that he received no revelation from God, since he neither bore witness to men nor brought good news of true advancement to believers, but of regression — or rather of overthrow and destruction. See, then: taking his own statement as our measure and rule, we have refuted him by it as one who received no revelation from God. But, as he himself said, let him be a sorcerer if he likes; yet he received nothing from God. And having fallen from that, where he will be placed is not unclear; and the one who said, "Sinners shall fall into their own net," will prove true. The still more rotten little sayings that he sets down after these most feeble oracles of his we judged it reasonable to pass over, because of their utter emptiness and impotence. For he was of a nature truly wicked and garrulous, or rather babbling and old-womanish; and besides cowardly, irascible, deceitful and boastful; and I do not know what evil the devil had that he lacked. His whole discourse is entirely devoid of sound judgment and sensible thought. So we shall leave him, prattling away in these matters, to finish his drivel.

REFUTATION 10

66. The tenth tale of Muhammad is entitled "The Account of Hud," and its opening is full of elegant boasting: it was, he says, made wise, set in verses and distinguished by a wise man. For the moment, however, he admits that the scripture of his God needs knowledge supplied by men. And he begins again to terrify the barbarians by claiming that such trifles are laws of God; and he frightens them, if they do not obey, from

…of the punishment to come, and from the painful things that befall people unexpectedly. "For whatever happens to you," he says, "whether on land or at sea, you will suffer it because of your unbelief about these things." And he brings forward as witness Noah, who became a prophet and apostle, saying that when everyone rejected him, all perished; that one of his own sons did not believe and was drowned while the old man looked on; and that of each kind of animal he took with him not seven pairs and two pairs, but only one pair each. And he adds, as if from the one who supposedly inspires him: "From the accounts of things unseen we make these things known to you; you did not know them, neither you nor your people before this." See, he confesses about himself that he has not read the Scripture of Moses. He does not cite it correctly, but in a thoroughly distorted way that is inconsistent with itself. So it is plain that the discourse addressed to him, and this corruption of Scripture, do not come from the one who dictated Scripture. They come either from a Manichaean, or from a demon, or perhaps he does this mischief of his own accord, wishing to exalt himself above Moses. Besides these, he introduces Zaleth as a prophet and teacher of an unknown people. He says that Zaleth ordered them not to harm a certain camel grazing in the fields, but they disobeyed and killed it, and because of the camel they were left under the wrath of God, wiped out in their dwellings as though they had never existed. The barbarian's example is fearsome in every respect except for being true. He also mentions the vision of Abraham at the [?], and the [?], and he mangles and confuses everything; nevertheless, he set out the wrath brought down on Sodom. Again he mentions the obscure Shuaib the Midianite, if indeed such a man ever existed, and the events under Pharaoh. Then he attaches his own vain preaching: "Just as you accepted any one of these, accept my words too." And with this he cut his nonsense short. One must observe the barbarian's irrationality in such examples. He mentioned illustrious persons without fear, while walking the opposite road to theirs, and so one of two things happened to him: either he did not understand what he was doing, or he thought he would certainly escape notice. The first is simple folly; the second is derangement and shamelessness.

Refutation 11. § 67 [?]. The eleventh tale of Muhammad is entitled "On Joseph." It recounts the story of the chaste Joseph, in some places leaving things out, in others with insertions and expansions that are ridiculous and shameful. "And Rachel," he says, "fell at his feet together with Israel his father in Egypt." Yet Moses says that she had died earlier, in giving birth to Benjamin. This is how he always strives to show that the man who saw God was a liar. And he adds: "This, from the accounts of things unseen, we reveal to you in Arabic letters."

And yet elsewhere he says that he received these fabrications without writing. The aim of his discourse is this: "If Egypt received Joseph, how much more are you obliged to receive me!" Such is the excess of his madness. And with this he silenced his nonsense.

Refutation 12. § 68 [?]. The twelfth little tale of Muhammad is entitled "On the Thunder." In it he reminds his [?] that God made the heaven, and that he sends the rain and brings down the hail. It is as if no one had ever proclaimed before that God made these things and commanded them to act! Then, having laid these down as agreed first principles, he gathers in his own necromancy as though it must necessarily follow from them, and raves something like this: "God thunders; from this know that I am his prophet. God sends lightning; know that I am his prophet. God has placed animals and plants on the earth; know that I am his prophet." See how he captured the wretched barbarians! From now on, having learned from this and considering the particulars, we too can aptly say about him, following his own teaching: The donkey brays; know, barbarians, that Muhammad is the prophet of his God. The oxen low; know, barbarians, that Muhammad is the apostle of his God. And likewise with the barking of dogs, the buzzing of insects, and the like. To what impious thing might one liken him, for the excess of his fighting against God? [?] The deranged man does not even perceive his godless drivel, but actually takes great pride in it, since he supposedly hears God thundering and flashing lightning and tells these things to others. Let him boast of this great and extraordinary work, as from the mouth of the one who blinded his spiritual senses, in these words: "We have sent you to a nation before which nations have passed away, to recite to them what has been made known to you." O the wisdom from above [?] of Muhammad! Truly now is the right time to quote that saying of Scripture: "The fool will speak foolish things, and his heart will think vain things." About the thunder, from which the title comes, he says: "And the thunder glorifies with its thanksgiving" — that is, the thunder is a well-disposed and rational voice. This is not from the accepted Scripture, and rightly so. Otherwise one could think the same of the roar of the sea, the rush of the wind and many other things; yet there will be some very harsh noises to which the saying would not fit. Then, recalling still more shamelessly his blasphemous opinion that makes God the cause of evils just as of goods, he says: "For if God had willed [MS: 'had come'], he would have guided all men; and whom God leads astray, there is no guidance for him." Truly this man

was [?], as Solomon says, in places that the Most High does not watch over. Again he clings to his anxious premise that he must not be disbelieved, and says: "Those who deny say, 'You are not an apostle.' Say: God is sufficient for me as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Scripture." He puts forward God as witness of his apostleship, yet he offers no sign worthy of God: no miracle-working, no prophecy, no disciplined life, not even plain knowledge. Without any demonstration, he says, "God is witness." Then, sensing his slander against God and his own lie (for he had nothing to make it credible), he takes refuge in those who know the Scripture, having so far managed to mock the barbarians, who were ignorant, and escape notice. "And whoever has," he says, "knowledge of the Scripture." Which Scripture? Do you really think that Scripture is true and testifies about you? Perhaps what was said about the abomination of desolation was said about you; indeed, those who understand have nothing else left to think about you. But if he will not accept this and demands something more exalted, then you who study the divinely inspired Scripture, you yourselves know what prophecies God wrote about the apostle Muhammad and about the expectation of his coming! And you will also find in his own writing testimonies from the divine Scripture, aptly brought into his doctrines from the Law, the Prophets and the Gospel, which he appears to revere, and under the pretext of knowing them he [?] the barbarians unnoticed [?]

Refutation 13. § 70. The thirteenth little tale of Muhammad is entitled "On Abraham," but it tells nothing worth mentioning about the man. Instead, as in the preceding tale, he lists a few things about creation, that it is governed by the divine Spirit, and then brings in the things ordered by Him. And he utters his customary blasphemy, that God leads astray whom he wills and guides whom he wills. And again he mentions Thamud and Ad, following his old drivel [?], and says that for this reason I too ought to be believed as an apostle of God. As a token of his apostleship he gives this: "The faithful," he says, "will be in paradise, rejoicing with their wives and children. But the unbelievers," he says, "at the judgment: their shirts are of pitch, and the fire covers their faces." And so, mocking the fearful day, he left off his nonsense. One must note, however, that it is characteristic of evildoers not to set out their nets in plain sight, for otherwise they would rather be caught themselves. We should not be surprised, then, if something praiseworthy is seen even in him. Rather, we must examine the novelties he introduces, to see whether they do not fiercely conflict with the God-written laws from which his baits and deceptions were taken.

Refutation 14. § 71. The fourteenth little tale is entitled "On Hijr" [?]. He mentions it near the end of the tale, saying that it was an associate of the Sodomites. The whole aim of this tale is that he should not be disbelieved. He says: "They will surely say to you, 'You are possessed, you who claim to have received these things from God. For if you were truthful, you would have brought down an angel.'" He gives two reasons why an angel need not come: first, that there are some people on whose account this is prevented [?]; and second, that if angels came, the whole matter would be finished. And then what grace would there be for men? "And even if we opened heaven," he says, "those who saw it would stand amazed; for this reason none of these things happens. But instead of these," he says, as one who knows the heavenly things well, "look at the height of heaven and the stars, and the shooting stars that occur whenever Satan goes up wishing to eavesdrop on what is spoken in heaven. For this reason believe that I am an apostle, for no one else before me taught this." Then again he mentions the fashioning of Adam, the origin of Beliar and his disobedience, Abraham, and the story of Lot. He throws in some other extraneous matters, and having achieved, as he thought, from his exposition of these, that he would be believed, he then attacks those who give God a partner. And with this he puts an end to his nonsense.

Refutation 15. § 72. The fifteenth little tale is entitled "On the Bees." He mentions the bees around the middle of the tale, saying that they produce wax and honey. To this he adds his deception, that he received these things from God. He appears to run through God's mighty works in creation, saying that God made the cattle and governs all things. And he swears a dreadful oath by the name of God that those who say God has daughters, the angels, will be punished. You will see the full meaning of this pronouncement in his next tale and be astonished. Again he speaks about eating meat, and says: "Do not say, 'This is permitted and this is forbidden,' so as to utter a lie against God." In this way he calls the law of God blasphemy and a lie. And he urges belief in the faith of Abraham, in the one sole God. "For," he says, "the Sabbath was imposed on those who disputed about it." And yet Abraham knew nothing of Sabbath-keeping. One might conjecture from this that he wanted the barbarians to keep the Sabbath too, but perhaps, finding himself unheeded in this matter, he did not dare to add anything about it. And with this his nonsense came to an end.

[The sixteenth tale] is entitled "On the Children of Israel." Its composer declares: "We gave Moses the Scripture, and we decreed for the children of Israel in the Scripture that they would cause destruction in the land twice, and be exalted with a great exaltation." Consider from what follows whether this is truly the one who gave Moses the Scripture. For a little further on he babbles: "And for every man we have fastened his fate to his neck, and on the day of resurrection a writing will come out for him, meeting him: 'Read your writing.'" Nearly everyone knows that Moses not only did not teach the writing of fate and destiny, but could not even bear to mention them. Now, if accepting destiny contributes to God's glory, it is nothing strange if what was passed over in silence then was given to this man later. But this doctrine declares God the cause of evils as well as of goods, and so proves that the laws he gave and the punishments he threatened were laid down in vain. Since that is impossible, whoever wrote that this silly little tale comes from the one who gave Moses the law must certainly be lying. What follows also keeps to the same aim, for he says: "Whenever we wished to destroy a village, we commanded those who lived in it, and they lived in debauchery there; and the word was proved just against it, and we crushed them utterly; and how many [?] of the generations after Noah we destroyed!" To whom do these words better belong, to God who loves mankind or to the demon who hates mankind? Does God command debauchery, or the devil? Does anyone still look for clearer proof than this to be fully convinced that Satan produced the whole book of Muhammad? If some of them should say, "And how could Satan destroy many of the generations after Noah?", we will answer: by divine power and lordship, not at all; but by deceit, and by provoking them to anger God, he could, just as he is able to do even now. And it is fitting that here, of his own accord, he tells the truth in saying that he himself destroys men. § 74. If they are not persuaded by these refutations, they will believe from what follows. For as he continues his account of Noah, he adds this as well, about the sons of God and the daughters of men mentioned by Moses: "And our Lord chose children for you, and took females from among the angels; but you speak great words." See the impiety, see the folly of the [?]! Moses had said, "The sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves," and that the giants were among those born to them. This man did not know whom Moses calls God — that it is Enosh — and who his sons are, and he was at a loss. For after all his labor in the preceding passages,

all his hope collapses in this chapter, since Moses plainly speaks of sons of God, while his whole effort was to allow Him none. And as if seized by inspiration, he changes the characters of the persons and their kinds, and out of the daughters of men he fashions female angels, after the manner of the Greeks

[?] he proclaims that this happened. "For our Lord chose children for you, and took females from among the angels; but you speak great words." He means the words about God: that you proclaim that God has sons, and that he made them sons-in-law of men, when rather he gave female angels as brides to the sons of men. He says such things as though correcting the writings of Moses. This is why in the preceding tale he swears that the female angels are not God's daughters, while contending strenuously that they are female. But woe is me, more sinful than all flesh, that in my wish to refute the enemy of God I am compelled to speak of these things and the like! What, then, will the God-denying Saracens say to this? Will they still insist after this on calling Muhammad one who saw God? Or will they rather spit on him, now that he has been shown to be an enchanter, a sorcerer and a deceiver? After babbling and blaspheming much more of the same kind, as though he had already made his proofs clear and incontrovertible, he adds: "And say: I give thanks to God, who has not taken a son." And with this he puts an end to his nonsense.

Refutation 17. § 7[?]. The seventeenth little tale of Muhammad is entitled "On the Companions of the Cave." It relates how the seven holy youths of Ephesus fled to the cave, and their death and resurrection. This ignorant barbarian mentioned them for two reasons: first, to seem experienced in many writings; second, to claim for his own doctrine the miracle connected with them. But since he clearly knew that they were Christians, and that they were preserved intact after death for many years, he feigned a praiseworthy ignorance. He put on a safe opinion about God, that God knows what he does and how he does it, and so thinks to escape inquiry into the many matters he did not know, even had he wished to [?]. Yet he did not pass them by without reproach either, for he says: "You think them awake, while they are asleep; you turn them to the right and to the left, and their dog

stretches [MS: a variant form] its forelegs on the dust. The Lord knows what concerns them. Those who prevailed in their affair say: 'We will build a place of worship over them.' They will say, 'Three, and their dog the fourth,'" — supposing that they speak of things unseen — and so on, he says, up to seven. "The Lord knows their number, and none know them but a few." Then, after babbling some other strange things, he mentions paradise and describes it thus: "We do not cast away the reward of the one who has done good. For them there is a paradise in Eden, with rivers running beneath it. In it they are adorned with golden bracelets; they wear green garments of fine linen and figured silk, reclining in it on couches. Good is the reward, and fair the enjoyment." Next he babbles again what he said before about his father Beliar and Adam, and [?] some strange and deranged things. Then he mentions Alexander the Macedonian, and says that "he went as far as the setting of the sun, and found the sun setting into hot water"; that in the north he walled off Gog and Magog; and that Alexander was a monotheist in worship, like Abraham, and not a pagan. And he adds: "We relate this account to you in truth." What truth there is in these things all [?], even without our saying so. And having uttered his usual rotten talk, he ended the tale. § [?]. A refutation common to all the following little tales, setting out the blasphemies selected [?] from them. § [?]. We have passed over the tales between the eighteenth and the thirty-sixth, since they are full of his customary garrulity and marvel-mongering, or rather blasphemy and falsehood. For everything in them is topsy-turvy and absurd. He babbles about matters from both the Old and the New Testament. He says that Mary gave birth to Christ beside a palm tree, despairing of her life, and that Christ called out to her from her womb to shake the palm, bring down its fresh fruit and eat. He spins marvels about David and Solomon conversing with birds and irrational animals. He says that demons were helpers to Solomon, and that certain hosts [?] attended him; that he ruled the winds and understood the secrets of ants; that a wild cock was his teacher; and that the sun and moon are [?]. He says that the iron breastplate was first invented by David. He proclaims himself a judge alongside God when God judges the world. And he babbles other things still more shameful and irrational, or rather more demonic.

He introduces Muhammad's god swearing this oath: "By the [?] of the [?], and the additions of additions [?], and those that recite the remembrance: for your God is one, Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and Lord of the easts." Then he speaks as if in the person of many, saying: "We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of stars, and have guarded it from every rebellious Satan. They cannot listen in on the high assemblies, and they are pelted from every side and driven off." He says that paradise has four rivers: of unclouded water, of milk whose taste does not change [?], of sweet wine, and of strained honey. He goes on in this vein as far as the fiftieth. In the fiftieth fable he introduces his god swearing thus: "By those that winnow a winnowing, and those that carry loads [?]: for what is promised is true, and the judgment is bound to come." In the fifty-first fable he swears thus: "By the mountain, and a writing inscribed on fine parchment, and the house that is built, and the roof that is raised, and the sea that is [?]: the punishment of the Lord will come." 72. In the fifty-second fable, entitled "On the Star", he swears thus to the Arabs on behalf of Muhammad: "By the star that sets: your companion has not gone astray, nor has he transgressed; he has not spoken of his own will. It is nothing but a revelation revealed. One mighty in power showed him, the self-seen [?], and he sat, and he is in the highest firmament. And he drew near and hung suspended, and was at the distance of two bows or nearer, and he revealed to his servant what he revealed. He did not lie about the things within that he saw; for indeed he saw it at another descent, near the sidêritês tree; he gave way [?]." And a little later he declares, announcing thus: "And how many angels are in the heavens whose intercession avails nothing [?]!" In the fifty-third fable, wishing to speak about what happens to the moon, and not knowing that it is darkened by the shadow of the earth, he says: "The hour has drawn near and the moon has been split; and if they see a sign they turn away and say, 'It is sorcery that goes on and on', and they have called it a lie." And babbling in this way he goes on as far as the sixtieth fable. In the sixtieth fable, having veiled, as with darkness, the eyes of his wretched soul with folly or insensibility,

and having hurled himself over the cliff of unspeakable falsehood, he raves thus: "And when Jesus son of Mary said, 'O sons of Israel, I am an apostle of God to you, confirming what is before me of the law, and bringing good news of an apostle who comes after me, whose name is Muhammad'; and when he brought them the clear proof, they said, 'This is sorcery.' And who is more unjust than one who utters a lie against God?" He did not dare to name, even falsely, the one who wrote this down. For he knew that it was impossible for so great an announcement, if it had ever been proclaimed at all concerning Christ, to have been handed down in silence. That is why he neither attaches it to anyone by name, nor mentions place or time or any reasonable cause for which this man was to come. For in everything that is truly said, these things and others like them are preserved, but falsehood lacks them. Besides, he saw that none of Christ's sayings is abhorred among Christians. So he simply [?] declares, "When he said", mocking the barbarians as if they were foolish children. 80. In the sixty-seventh fable he swears thus: "By the pen and what they write: you are not, by his good gifts, possessed by a demon; and you have a reward without reproach, and you are of a great character." In the sixty-eighth fable, entitled "On the Hakka", he begins thus: "The hakka! What is the hakka? And how do you know what the hakka is? Thamud and [?] called the Hour a lie." He prattled all this to deceive the barbarians into thinking that he certainly knew some secret things. And he goes on stammering up to the seventy-fourth [perhaps: seventy-second]. In the seventy-fourth [perhaps: seventy-second] fable, entitled "On the Resurrection", he forswears thus: "I do not swear by the day of resurrection, and I do not swear by the formed [?] soul." The seventy-sixth little fable is entitled "On Those Sent Forth", and it begins thus: "By those sent forth in succession, and the storm of storms, and the spreading of those spread out, and the [?] separation, and those that cast a reminder of excuse and warning: for the coming is promised." The seventy-eighth little fable begins with an oath thus: "By those that draw out a [?] drawing,

[?]choud, the fire that has burning." The eighty-fifth little fable begins with an oath thus: "By the heaven and the altarik! And what do you know? What is the altarik? The piercing star: that every soul of beings has a guardian over it." The eighty-eighth little fable begins with this kind of oath: "By the dawn, and the ten nights, and the pair and the unpaired, and the night when it spreads out: is there in these an oath for those of [?]?" [81?]. The eighty-ninth little fable begins with this kind of forswearing: "I do not swear by this land, while you are in this land, and by a parent and what he begot; for we have formed man in strength." The ninetieth little fable begins with oaths like these: "By the sun and its rays, and the moon when it follows it, and the day when it reveals it, and the night when it [?] it, and the heaven and what created it, and the earth and what established it, and the soul and what fashioned it" — over all the earth now [?]. The ninety-first little fable begins with this kind of oath: "By the night when it [?], and the day when it shines clear, and him who made the male and the female: your life is manifold." The ninety-second little fable begins with an oath thus: "By the morning and the night when it is still: your Lord has not left you, nor has he grown weary." The ninety-third little fable he concludes with these words: "When you have leisure, strive, and pray to God." The ninety-fourth little fable begins thus: "By the figs and the olives, Sinai and the fearless land: for we formed man in fair stature, and turned him back below the lowest." How great is the oath of the Creator of mankind! But greater still is the feat for which he swears: "And we turned him back," he says, "below the lowest." Fittingly did such a one have to be Muhammad's god! The ninety-sixth little fable begins thus: "We brought it down on the appointed night. And what do you know of what the appointed night is? It is better than a thousand months. The angels and the spirit come down in it by permission of their Lord with every matter. Peace is that night, until the dawn rises." The ninety-seventh little fable is entitled "On Those Who Denied". In it he seems to persuade those who read his unphilosophical nonsense that he is from God, because he brought books that are purified, and in them are right writings. But let listeners judge their rightness. The ninety-eighth little fable [?]

is entitled "On the Earthquake of the Earth", because it will cry out against sinners — as if he himself were justified by these blasphemies! The ninety-ninth little fable is entitled "On the Runners", and it begins with an oath thus: "By those that ran panting, and those that strike sparks, and fall upon the dawn, and stir up in it a [?], and spew out in it [?]: for man is ungrateful [?] to the Lord." [82?]. The hundredth little fable is entitled "On the Karê", and it begins thus: "The karê! And what do you know of what the karê is? The day on which men become like scattered scab." The hundred and second little fable is entitled "On the Alexar", and it begins thus: "By the alexar: man is in a winding [?]." The hundred and fourth little fable is "On the Companions of the Elephant"; it is a short and pitiful piece of idle talk. The hundred and seventh little fable is "On the Kauthar", and it begins thus: "We have given you the kauthar; so pray to your Lord and sacrifice; for the one who hates you is himself the one cut off." But let us look into this matter of the kantharos! The hundred and tenth little fable is "On Abu Lahab", who, he declares, is burned in fire for having been unjust, while his wife kindles the furnace beneath. The hundred and eleventh little fable runs thus: "Say: He is God, one, God holosphyros, the all-solid; he did not beget, nor was he begotten, nor has anyone been like him." Even if holosphyros does not indicate the shape of a sphere, it at least indicates something dense and compacted, which is itself a property of a body. The hundred and twelfth is entitled "On 'I Will Flee'". It is a sorcerer's incantation, for it runs thus: "Say: I will flee to the Lord of the daybreak, from the evil of what he formed, and from the evil of the lightning when it spreads out, and from the evil of spittings into the cups [?], and from the evil of an envier when he envies." The hundred and thirteenth little fable is also a sorcerer's incantation. It is entitled "On 'I Will Flee'" and runs thus: "Say: I will flee to the Lord of men, the King of men, the God of men, from the evil of the whisperings of the demons into the hearts of men, from demons and men." And with this all his mythmaking and sorcery is muzzled, having brought an end fit for its blasphemous beginning. 83. From all the things that Muhammad's god takes up in his oaths, it is easier to see who his god was; or rather, through him the many [?]

From the ways in which he behaved outrageously toward the divine Scripture, the impieties he committed against the glory of God, the blasphemies he uttered against his holy angels, and from his deep ignorance, he is simply [?] — as I said, without any further refutation — plainly caught out as a worshipper of creatures and a superstitious man. In vain do the foolish Saracens boast of this sorcerer as one who taught them true knowledge of God. For he wrapped himself in the name of the only God merely as a veil, but covertly introduced to them the worship of creatures and paganism. This is clear, as I said, from such oaths of his. For how could the true God swear by a running dog, and the darkness of night, and things worse than these? But since it would have been burdensome and unacceptable to them if he had urged them outright to worship creation and the demons, he begins by proclaiming the knowledge of one God, so as to escape the suspicion of polytheism. Again, he does not shamelessly declare that created things are gods. Instead he keeps silent about the title "God", but attaches to them the reverence that is due to God — I mean swearing by them. So it necessarily follows that those who worship Muhammad's god worship, through him, creation and the demons. Moses does present the God of Abraham as swearing, but he says that he swears not by anything else, but by himself: "By myself I have sworn," he says. So whoever reveres the God of Abraham reveres no other god through him, but him alone. But those who worship Muhammad's god venerate, through that god, nights and dogs and figs and olives and all the fables mentioned above. Therefore, once they have perceived the error and understood the deceit, let them withdraw, if they will, from this vain man's misguidance. Let them keep in step with the divine Scripture alone, and be taught by it the perfect and only true knowledge of God. Compared with it, his counterfeit little fables are exposed as falling as far short as dung set beside refined gold.

REPLY 19. Against Muhammad, who takes the word "Word" in a bare sense when it is applied to the hypostatic Word and Son of God. 84. Things whose essences, that is, natures, are different are themselves wholly different in essence; and things that differ from one another in this way also have different and unlike essential properties of their natures. Therefore things whose essences, that is, natures, are different also have different and unlike essential properties of their natures. If, then, God, angel and man have different essences, they would also be different from one another; and if they differ from one another, their essential natural properties will also be different and entirely unlike one another. Therefore the rational faculty of God, of angels and of men differs from one

another, not only as that of a maker from that of a thing made, nor as that of the immaterial from that of the material, but in that the one has only the inner word, the second has the uttered word as well, and the third is beyond both the inner and the uttered word. In the case of creatures the word is without essence, for in creatures the word does not by nature subsist outside that in which it is, but exists as in a subject. His Word, however, is essential and truly existent, even though it does not depart from and is inseparable from him from whom it came forth and in whom it at the same time subsists; for it is also uncreated and ungenerated. Wrongly, then, did the ignorant Muhammad suppose one and the same [?] property of natures for things that differ in essence, and declare that the scattered and fleeting word of men is the same as the Word of God, which subsists in itself and has being. 20. Against the same, who says that God is the cause of evils just as of goods. 85. Among things that act without will, some act in virtue of themselves and some accidentally. For example, fire in virtue of itself heats, but accidentally, through counter-pressure, it cools; and again, in virtue of itself it gives light, but when some body is set in the way it produces darkness. Anyone who follows the analogy of their activity will find that the same holds for all other things. But things that act by will, except when they fail, do everything in virtue of themselves. If, then, God in his acting admits no failure, he does everything in virtue of himself; and acting in virtue of himself, he does, according to that man, both good and evil things. So according to Muhammad he does contrary things, and thus good and evil proceed from the same cause. But things that proceed in virtue of themselves from one cause cannot be contrary to one another, or else the cause from which the contraries proceed would be shown to be at once evil and good. If this is blasphemous and beyond cure, then evils are not from God — and by evils I mean sins, which are also the causes of punishments. Wrongly, then, did the impious Muhammad call God the cause of sin. 21. Against the same, who wrongly says that people will again live in pairs in paradise. 86. Every sentient nature, acting materially, has as the aim of its activity through the senses attachment to material things, and as its end, generation. But since to every change or motion there corresponds a rest, to which the change or motion is contrary, so also corruption is contrary to generation. And since revival is promised in the divine Scripture, it does not follow that, just as a human being now passes through birth into corruption, so too he will return again from corruption by way of the first birth. For corruption knows no unions, intercourse or births. Otherwise, let it be granted that it has these, and let corruption be divided into male and female — but that is impossible. So it is not the case that, as generation brings a human being forth, corruption likewise multiplies him through generation;

for then generation and corruption would be the same, which is impossible. If, then, a human being does not come forth by generation in the resurrection, neither will he exercise the functions of generation, since he no longer expects corruption. And if he does not exercise the functions of generation, what is the purpose of the sexual union of male and female? For where no end is set before it, the aim also disappears. If there is no need of the union of male and female after the resurrection, what will the camel-minded Muhammad say, and what will he do, when he orders human beings, divided into male and female, to live in pairs in paradise? And if anyone brings up the formation of Adam from the earth and the childbearing that came after, let him know that there it was a passage from non-being into being, and also took place so that the human race might be preserved because of the fall. Here, however, there is no need whatever of the first, because this is even beyond the first. For the resurrection, or re-formation, is deliverance from corruption and from the passions that cause corruption, and not birth and the passions of birth, which precede corruption, by which it necessarily [?]

22. Against the same, who ignorantly and impiously says that [angels] had intercourse with the people of Noah's time. 87. All things of different kinds that come together by way of generation either produce something wholly other than those from which it came, or else it comes forth partly sharing in them and partly differing from them; and it is either better or worse than those that produced it. If, then, as Muhammad fantastically claims, offspring came from the union of men and angels, either it must have been something wholly other than both — let the offspring be neither angel nor man, that is, neither mortal nor immortal, neither flesh-bearing nor bodiless, just as the mule neither neighs nor brays. But they were not even intermediate between mortal and immortal, or between material and immaterial; for the giants both died and were material, of man [?]. So when men came together with angels by generation, nothing other was born; or else the offspring partly share in their parents and partly differ from them. Then let it differ from man in mortality, or share with him in materiality; again, let it differ from the angel in immortality and share with him in bodilessness; and let it be mortal and immortal, material and bodiless. But that is impossible, for the giants were only material and only mortal men. So when men came together with angels, the offspring did not partly share in them and partly differ from them. And it has been shown that they were not something other than these either. Therefore nothing can be born from unions of men and angels, since nothing beyond the cases stated can be born of beings of different kinds; indeed, the thing has no place in nature. For even if it were granted — which is impossible — that a man had intercourse with an angel, in what womb will the bodiless being hold and give life to the [?]? And with what like

NICETAS OF BYZANTIUM [?] and suitable matter will it increase its bulk? How will it carry it in the womb? And how will a bloodless and immaterial nature suckle a living creature that is used to drawing nourishing juices? So an angel will not conceive by a man; nor indeed can a man come to an angel in intercourse. For the human body is tangible, but the angel is intangible; and what touch does not grasp is not partaken of by it; and if an angel cannot be partaken of by a man, neither can it come together with a man in intercourse. Wrongly and impiously, then, does Muhammad fantastically invent female angels, and blasphemously claim that men had intercourse with them. 23. Against the same, who says that the intercession of the saints in heaven is of no avail. 88. If he did not acknowledge the intercession of angels, one would ask whether he held such a belief at all. But since he grants it while declaring it useless, let us next ask what causes it to fail, if indeed it does fail. Either God is implacable toward every request, or the angels ask improperly. That he himself does not accept the first is clear from his exhorting people to pray. It remains, then, that he thinks the angels are not heard because they ask badly. But to ask badly is the same as to will badly, so on the same reasoning the angels are ill-willed. Now a person is ill-willed either from ignorance or from wickedness. How could any sensible person think that those who stand beside Wisdom itself are ignorant of the good? Or that those who are perpetually filled with the good are wicked? If these things are impossible, then Muhammad lies — or rather blasphemes — when he declares the intercessions of the holy angels useless. 24. Against the same, who says: "God is holosphyros; he did not beget, he was not begotten." 89. He who brought all things out of non-being would be in every way infinitely superior to the things made, in essence, power, will, eternity and activity. For if not, he does not bring them out of non-being. And if he does not bring them forth, [?] of the same eternal and unoriginate

and would be coextensive with the unoriginate; and if it were equal in power, the unoriginate would also be identical with all things. But we see all things being led not as all things, but as one; and although among all things some seem better and others worse, none of them is unalterable and unmoving. So if all things change, and are led not as all things but as one, then all things are not equal in power to the unoriginate. And if they are not equal in power, neither are they coeternal; and if they are not coeternal, yet exist, they were clearly brought forth by the unoriginate. And if he brings forth all things, then he is superior

…would be infinitely beyond the things brought into being, wholly and in every respect: in essence, power, eternity, will and activity. There are three kinds of essence: body, the incorporeal, and what is mixed from these two. Body is marked by extension in three dimensions, by density and by rarity. The incorporeal is marked by not being present everywhere and not being above all things, for even though it is incorporeal, it is still wholly circumscribed. But what shall we assign to the creating essence? Or rather, to put it this way: if these things are called essence, and are essence, then what will that be which made them, as has been shown, and what shall we name it? We will have nothing by which to define it, but because it surpasses these things we will call it superessential. If, then, the Creator is superessential, rarity, density and three-dimensional extension will be far removed from him, and Muhammad's "hammered-solid" God is done away with, since Muhammad feared that the procession of the Son and Word would empty him. The same holds for power, motion and activity: we must glorify what is above motion, above power and above activity. If this is so, let Muhammad not fear the Word who shares the Father's nature and eternity when he hears that he is the Creator and renewer of all creation, and Son, as having come forth from the mind as from a begetter. For he came forth without going out, and he remains in himself, not by relation, not by conjunction, not by memory, but beyond all these. For he is superessential, since he is from the superessential and is superessentially. 16. So let him not say, "If he was not begotten, neither did he beget." For see, we observe that just as he was not begotten, neither was he created, since the one without beginning necessarily has both of these. Yet we observe that, although he was not created, he did create. If, then, that man grants that God has done the one, and that this is a glory to him, why is God deprived of the other? Indeed, the glory brought to him by creation is not as great as the glory that comes through the Son. That glory is far greater, by as much as the Son's essence surpasses the essence of creatures. So it would have been better and more fitting for him to say, had he understood, "Since he was not begotten, for this very reason he begot," just as, not having been created, he created. And the proof that Christ, the Son and Word, is of one essence with God the Father is his own coming. For his coming took place after many prophecies, and this too is an indisputable sign of it: the change of human beings for the better, not only barbarians and Greeks, but also those who lived under the old law itself. Compared with the law, grace differs as much as an old man surpasses a child. Compared with the other nations, it differs as much as what is human by nature surpasses what is irrational by nature. For there was need of one who would teach and bring about things higher than nature and mere reason, such as the very Word of God who came. Besides these there is another sign: that the divine worship of the law, the priesthood, and

the anointing of kingship were transferred to grace. This is no small pledge of proof that the Son is heir of the Father's creatures. If these things now seem small to him, because he is sick with disobedience and barbarian [?] along with recklessness, then he will acknowledge them as great even against his will, when he sees fulfilled the word of the Father to the Son foretold through Isaiah the prophet: "And the rams of Nebaioth shall come to you." Clearly they do not now consent to submit to him, if indeed Nebaioth is interpreted as "firstborn of Ishmael." For if nothing Isaiah said had ever come to pass, neither will this. But if the rest did, this will too. And then the slander he so unreasonably hurls against us will [be turned back?] against him, and with good reason: that God does not guide [?] the one who goes astray.

[?] When God was initiating Abraham into the law of circumcision and promising him a son, Isaac, by [?] Sarah, what he showed Abraham was a cause for wonder and amazement: having children in the hundredth year of his life and the ninetieth of [Sarah's], so that he even laughed for joy. But before asking for Isaac, who was still only a promise, he asked for Ishmael, whom he already had, and spoke thus: "Let this Ishmael live before you." Then God said to Abraham: "Yes, behold, Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac; and I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this season next year." How far even the divine words themselves exceed every extreme of precision! "Behold," he says, "Sarah your wife." Yet Sarah was still childless, and Hagar, who had borne him Ishmael, should rather have been called his wife. But it is not the children of the flesh who are Abraham's children, nor is mere flesh Abraham's wife. "Behold," he says, "Sarah your wife": Sarah is your wife; Hagar is not your wife. "Shall bear to you" is also well said, meaning "one like you." "And you shall call his name Isaac": so the child is called by God. "And I will establish my covenant with him": this is a sign of belonging to God, for he added, "to be his God and the God of his seed after him." It is as though the Ishmaelites were set apart and not deemed worthy of God's covenant with them, nor of [?] and worship. For he added: "But concerning Ishmael." What does this mean? Is Ishmael the seed of another man, and not of your servant Abraham? "But concerning Ishmael": this is the beginning of another subject,

separated from the continuity of the first sequence. That sequence would have kept the belonging that comes from the covenant, had a new beginning not broken it off. And what do you say about Ishmael at all? "But concerning Ishmael," he says, "behold, I have blessed him, and I will increase him exceedingly." But you gave this same blessing to the birds of the sky and the fishes of the sea. This blessing is not yet one fit for human beings in particular. "He shall beget twelve nations": and what is that, when he is a stranger to the divine favour? He would not even have had his increase in number had Abraham not asked for it: "For behold," he says, "I have heard you." Besides, Ishmael is far inferior to Ham. And what is the use of great numbers when they are worthless? Fittingly he might hear from Isaiah: "You were born to me to excess." O the foreknowledge of God! Even when Abraham entreats God on Ishmael's behalf, Ishmael receives only increase in number. As a stranger and alien to God's covenant he is set apart by God himself, since Isaac alone was worthy to inherit it, because of the blessed Christ and God who was to come from him. This too is to be wondered at: concerning all the nations the prophecy says, "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord," but these people God himself judged to have no share in his covenant, surely because they serve the demon called the Adversary. 11. If, then, God himself excluded them from his covenant, and this is clear from the fact that even now they refuse to be taught the gospel of divine Scripture, where did the camel-like sorcerer [?] get the third covenant that he brought? He shamelessly lied against God, boasting that he received from heaven nonsense, myths, debauchery and babble, filled with every kind of ignorance and lack of learning. When he says that Mary, the sister of Moses, gave birth to Christ, is there any extreme of folly or height of ignorance left that this madman has not poured out upon himself? How much do you think he is laughed at for this by the Jews, by the Samaritans, by simply everyone who studies the Old or even the New Testament? Where, then, someone asks, did he find the nerve to call it a heavenly book? From being inspired by the one who said, "I will set my throne upon the clouds of heaven, and I will be like the Most High," who is, and is called, the father of lies. For who that has ever read divine Scripture will not be astounded at the size of the lie, when he says that Christ was born of Mary the sister of Moses? O the long old age of the Virgin! For nearly two thousand years had passed until the birth of Christ since Mary struck
the cymbals. And very [?] also David son of Jesse, from whom Christ is shown to be descended. Is this divine Scripture? Is this a heavenly book? O the irrationality and folly of the wretched [?]!

[?] So, both from the meaning of Scripture, since their accursed book is foreign and alien to divine Scripture, and from the fact that God judged them unworthy of his covenant, we can see that that camel-sacrificing book belongs to the demon who fell from heaven. For everything estranged from God passes over to the opposite, demonic lot. Isaac belongs to God, and the manifest sign of the true God is that he established his covenant with him ("For I will establish," he says, "my covenant with him, to be his God and the God of his seed after him"). So the sign that he is not the God of the Ishmaelites by belonging, even if he is their God by the principle of creation, is that God's covenant was not deemed fit to be established with them. The devil, then, who lies against God, is their god. For fear of failing in such an aim he has craftily kept his own name silent, because all people already hold it in ill repute, and he puts forward the title of the true God. Such scheming is the evil one's habit. If, then, the barbarians long to have the God of Abraham as their own God, let them renounce that lawless and deceitful book and the worthless man who clumsily wrote it, and let them walk by divine Scripture alone and be guided by it. Or else, if they prefer that book to this one and worship the adversary of the God of Abraham, let them hide their faces in shame, and let them be exposed as merely adorning themselves with the bare name of Abraham and mouthing empty words that do not fit the facts or the Scriptures. For whoever says that Pharaoh and Augustus reigned together at the same time is no different from a madman. Yet this must follow if Moses' sister conceived Christ: either Christ appeared to Pilate as an old man after two thousand years, or Mary lived that long, or even longer. [?] …to those who are circumcised and therefore think they have the God of Abraham as their God, in order to show whether their God is truly the God of Abraham. 45. Of a master's commands, some bring profit to the subjects when they are kept, some to the master, and some to both. Likewise, when they are rejected, some bring loss to the subjects, some to the masters, and some to both. Everyone knows that if a servant has broken any command of his master whatever, but still acknowledges him as his lord, he has hope of winning his master back to his former goodwill. But if he acknowledges another as his lord, he draws upon himself his master's unbearable anger, even if he diligently carries out all his commands. That servant does not make himself known as his master's slave by

doing what pleases him nearly as much as he shows himself an outsider by adopting another master. For what sign does a physician's servant give that the physician is now his lord, if he knows the matters of the art well and practises them as his master wishes, but enrols himself as the slave of another master? God's other commandments are nothing but healing and benefit for us. But faith in God brings glory to him, as we confirm that he is the true God and that the bond of lordship is kept unbroken. Breaking the other commandments brings ruin on ourselves, whereas repudiating his lordship insults the Lord himself. When, then, will he be more vehemently angry with us? When he is rejected, I think, as everyone knows. Let us test this argument about God in the cases of Abraham and Muhammad. God said to Abraham: "Circumcise the foreskin of your flesh"; he does so. "You shall not worship another god, except the Lord your God"; this Muhammad will not do. For he worships Chousar, a very ancient idol in the desert of Yathrib, and Makach, which they say was fashioned in the likeness of Aphrodite. So Muhammad cannot have the God of Abraham as his God, even though he brings in circumcision as a token of God's command, because he transfers himself to another god. For God had said, "except the Lord your God." [?] For circumcision in itself is only a removal of flesh from

the one circumcised, not a bond of slavery and lordship. In the same way, if a servant ran away from a physician and went over to another master, his use of medicine would be no proof that he was the physician's servant. So the Hagarenes call the God of Abraham their God in vain; they have been shown to be lying. For even if he was once their God, [now they belong to?] Chousar and Muhammad; he is not their God. 27. Another on the same subject. [?] Everything that truly exists is known from its name and its reality together. If these are divided in two, into name alone and reality alone, it misleads. By "name alone" I mean a name bereft of the reality truly proper to it; by "reality alone" I mean a reality bereft of the name truly proper to it, though not nameless. From both together true knowledge arises; from either one alone, deception. This is what makes people agree with one another about something, or be at odds. The deception of the name alone is twofold: when it signifies nothing at all, and when it is taken from its proper reality and attached to something unlike it. A name that signifies several true things may be called the proper name of each and of all together. A true reality is, and is called, that which preserves the definition of what belongs to its essence, without lack or excess. A true name is what the definition of the reality means to signify. So the reality, as reality, does not mislead, nor does the name, as the name of its proper reality,

deceive. Deception arises when the name of one reality is applied to another reality, and when the reality of one name is placed under another name. [?] This being so, it is easy to refute this barbarian race: they deceive themselves in vain with the name of the God of Abraham, since he is not truly worshipped by them, even if they bear and confess some partial marks of him, such as circumcision and their claim to be the people of the God of Abraham. Saying "two-footed and mortal" does not suffice to convey knowledge of man, although man truly is two-footed and mortal; these words do not at once indicate man, because they do not state the distinguishing feature that properly presents human nature. In the same way, their saying that they have the God of Abraham as their God and that they are circumcised in the flesh does not show that he is their God properly and truly, since they have neglected the tokens that could characterize him. For when the leader of their nation commands things contrary to the laws of the God of Abraham, does he not bring another god in under that God's name, in just the way we said deception arises? Consider this: the God of Abraham said to his sons, "You shall not worship any likeness, nor serve them," that is, as God [so the manuscript]. God said to the Hagarenes, so they claim, through his apostle: "Worship Chousar as God," though it is an idol and a likeness of Aphrodite. Let us see, then, what Abraham and Muhammad have in common and in what they differ. Let us see also in what things God is most clearly characterized, as God is known among human beings; in what things he seems to be so but is not; and in what things he is provoked to anger.

[?] In the commandments by which we ourselves alone are adorned, the manifestation of the Divine is lesser and dim, and sometimes not even lesser, when he himself is rejected. But in those by which his glory is established, it is true and surpassingly greater. The reverse holds as well. Abraham received circumcision after first coming to know God, and he renounced his father's idols. When, then, did he please God more: in renouncing idols, or in circumcising the flesh? Clearly in renouncing idolatry, for he received circumcision as a sign of the faith he had while uncircumcised. The sorcerer, the apostle of the Hagarenes, also introduces circumcision, but idolatry as well. Did he, then, please God as Abraham did, or did he rather provoke him, or, as it seems, both? But if both, did he please God by circumcising, or did he provoke him far more by worshipping idols? Clearly he provoked him more, for where success is greater, failure is surely greater too. The nature of things is shown either from what belongs to them in themselves or from what surrounds them. What is shown from their surroundings is not of the same kind; what is shown from what they are in themselves is more secure and more reliable. One shows the nature of slavery and lordship in itself when the bond is kept unshaken. One does not show it in itself when one displays something that surrounds the matter but does not have

the bond itself. So circumcision has to do with the bond of slavery, but is not the bond itself. Idolatry, on the other hand, is not only no part of the divine bond, whether in itself or in its surroundings; it even rebels against the bond itself and tears it apart. From this it is clear who is near to God, Abraham or Muhammad, and which law brings in the God of Abraham: the one that says, "You shall not worship another god, but the Lord God," or the one whose follower worships Chousar, an idol of Aphrodite. So let them not take pride in the name of the God of Abraham while thinking contrary to the God of Abraham, and so deceive themselves into believing that they have the God of Abraham as their own and well disposed to them. For they have been exposed as revering a name alone, without the reality, falsely applied to something unlike it. They are deceived because they have knowledge from what surrounds the reality, and they are convicted of being estranged from what the reality is in itself. Unless, perhaps, we appear to be forcing ourselves [?] in order to have God, while they confess two utterly opposed gods, true and false, or rather, to speak more truly, have neither. 28. Proof that [?] the God whom Muhammad introduces is not [?], and that it is not him the Hagarenes worship, but the apostate who appropriated the divine [title?] to himself. [?] The Divine is set apart from all beings in a surpassing way, and if anything characterizes it clearly, it is its unchangeability and immutability: in its very being, in its thinking, in its speaking, and in its doing.
