Hence the sayings, "They shall all be changed, but you are the same"; "The counsel of the Lord abides forever"; "Your word, O Lord, endures forever"; and "All your works are true" — these being understood, of course, in a manner more divine than human. We must now examine whether the camel-like apostle of the evil one, in his fable of a third and newer covenant, allows these to have been preserved for the Divine. 100 [?]. It is confessed that the Divine is wholly immaterial and incorporeal. It is contemplated, by analogy, from its own works as well. It is recognized from the divine words, when the words agree with the works, and it is hymned from wills befitting God, when he makes these manifest, and these too clearly keep to the aim of the words and works. So whenever any one of these is found to be opposed to the rest, whoever holds to this deception would be convicted of impiety, as having fallen away from what befits the Divine. Let this be examined in the case of the Arab. He too accepted the events of Pharaoh and the Red Sea; how, I do not know, but as far as I can understand, it was in keeping with the saying that "sinners shall fall into their own net." Yet he dismisses the law of the one who parted the sea as nothing, evidently rejecting his wills together with his words. It is clear that he adopts for himself a god of his own appointing.

[?] …but not the true God. For the one who split that sea did it for no other reason than that his own words might be kept. Whoever sets aside his words, then, first sets aside him; and in setting him aside, he also denies that the miracle was done by him. Or, if he admits that the miracle happened at all, he must say that someone else did it, not the one who wrote the words in which this miracle is also written. So his impiety is twofold, or rather threefold: he takes the miracle away from God who performed it, and he does not credit it to the one who performed it [?]. We know clearly who it is that has exalted himself against the divine glory from the beginning; so anyone who thinks this way must be worshipping him. Otherwise, by his account, the Divine has been altered and changed; his word does not abide forever, and not all his works are true. But let that absurdity be thrown back on the heads of those who are guilty of the blasphemy. And if the Divine remains unchangeable and unalterable, then he himself will stand overthrown as impious, because he blasphemes the Divine as something that alters and changes, and because he has set aside God's words. We, however, will share by grace in God's changelessness: we who have accepted the miracle, who fulfil and perfect the laws, and who are taught by them the godly lessons and prophecies about Christ and about all things that are and will be.

101. From all this it follows that he has been caught saying one of two things. Either God is not God and some other being is god, or, if he is God, he does not always remain the same and unchanging, but leaves his own state and changes over time, like things subject to coming into being and passing away. It is easy to see how impious this is. So let every lover of truth use this rule, even if he accepts something else from the Old or even the New Testament. For the man even dares to acknowledge the virgin birth, though he does not want to. Let the lover of truth overturn him from his own admission, for the barbarian is very ignorant and uneducated.

29. That those who say the nation of the Hagarenes keeps true piety toward God the Father are mistaken.

102. Our Lord Jesus Christ is called the Truth and is the Truth. Those who believe this, then, must not concede that the God of Abraham, the God of Moses and Aaron, is worshipped by the Hagarene nation. For the Lord says, 'Whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father either.' Clearly all those holy patriarchs and prophets kept in mind and revered the knowledge of the Son of God. For he says, 'Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad.' Moses wrote of him, and the prophets after him revealed him in a hidden way, whether by deed or by word. How then could this impious

nation [?], which champions the complete abolition of the Son, worship his Father? Or how could the Father himself accept them, when he sees his own Son, who truly exists, his Word and God, blasphemed by them out of existence? No father is a friend to the enemies of his only son. If they had worshipped the Father, the Father himself would have revealed the Son to them. For the Lord says, 'No one knows the Son except the Father, and anyone to whom he chooses to reveal him.' We see that this happened with the saints of old, who left their knowledge of and faith in the Son in writings, as if inscribed on pillars. Besides, how could they know the Father unless the Son revealed him to them? 'No one knows the Father except the Son.' So all the approved and righteous men of the Old Testament, in worshipping God the Father, kept in mind the knowledge of the Son of God and initiated others into it.

103. The Son also gave this as a clear sign of those who worship the Father, both of those men and of those who came after them: that they honour the Son. And we see that this is truly so, both under the Law and under grace. It is plain, then, that the Hagarenes, who deny the knowledge of the Only-begotten, do not worship the God of Abraham and Moses, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. They worship the father of lies, as follows of necessity, because they do not worship the Father of truth. For whoever turns away from the one falls into the other. And the Lord's word does not lie: 'Whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father either.' Those who believe in Christ, then, must not be allowed to say that the Hagarenes worship the true God. If they say this, they will be forced to say three things. First, that Abraham, Moses and their company did not worship the true God. Second, that the Lord lies, which Truth itself cannot suffer. Third, that the Scripture of the ancients does not also signify the person of the Son, distinct from the Father, in passages such as 'From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you,' and 'Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a sceptre of uprightness is the sceptre of your kingdom. You loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you' forever, and the like. But if they confess that Truth does not lie and that Abraham and his company were godly, they will certainly declare the Hagarenes impious and godless, and in no way godly.

30. A reply to the Hagarenes who blaspheme the divinity of Christ and foolishly say, 'There is no God,' and who therefore think that God has handed the land of the Christians over to them as plunder.

104. It would be fitting to rebuke them from the outset, but this must be passed over, since there is one who will rebuke them as they deserve. Instead we will first lay down common notions for solving this difficulty, and refute them from what they themselves admit, showing that they think wrongly in this, as in everything else. They have learned from us, and they admit, that the Divine must be good, loving toward humankind,

wise, just and powerful, or whatever else they revere under his name. As good, then, he wants to benefit both our souls and, if possible, our bodies, and he stirs the soul up from things perceived by the senses to things grasped by the mind. But as wise, just and powerful, he always ranks the soul above the body. Among human beings, some are godly and others impious. Among the godly, some are useful and others useless. Among the useless, again, some can be cured and others cannot. Among those who can be cured, some are healed through prosperity and others through adversity. Some are healed through themselves, while others are corrected through others. Among the useless [?], some are granted relief, those whom relief saves, while others are given hardships. Among these, some suffer for their own sake, and others both for the sake of others and for their own, either because they will become more proven or because they still have shortcomings. Among the impious, some perhaps prosper [?], namely those who are not wicked in disposition, since the punishment there is cut short by the distress here. Others, utterly wicked [?] through their wickedness, are given over on both counts. And the impious prosper so that every excuse may be taken away from them.

Affliction and delight are opposites that both occur within one and the same human race, and this has misled many into thinking that those who please God are always cheerful while those hateful to God are distressed. But one should not think this way. Rather, one must understand that cheerfulness is twofold: one kind is perceived by the senses and is temporary, while the other is grasped by the mind and is eternal. The same holds for affliction. So the righteous are cheerful, like Abraham, and the unrighteous are cheerful too, like those [?] with Pharaoh. Again, the righteous are distressed, like Jacob fleeing from Esau and serving Laban, and the unrighteous are distressed too, like Amalek and the Egyptian. See, then: in one and the same character of the righteous man there is affliction and despondency [?], and in one and the same state of the unrighteous man there is affliction and despondency. Someone may say, 'What is this inequality among equals, and where does it come from? After all, cold and heat are not both seen in fire.' I too will say: neither is the just both equal and unequal. Rather, affliction and delight belong to beings capable of justice and injustice.

105. It has been said that affliction is either temporary and very easy to bear, or eternal and unbearable, and that joy is either temporary and pleasing for only a short while, or eternal and greatly pleasing. The Lord who loves souls, whose gifts are ineffable and everlasting, arranges each of these in wisdom by exchange: eternal affliction in return for temporary joy, and eternal joy in return for temporary affliction. Because of the pleasure that led Adam into unbelief, he did not hesitate [?] to lead him from joy to joy, and to send Cain on from affliction to affliction [?]. This is what perplexes the barbarians and leads them to make irrational pronouncements. Whether the Christians are godly is not a question to put to the barbarians, for 'the sons of men are false,' and indeed 'every man is a liar.' It must be put to Truth itself, which is Christ, and to the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, who spoke in the Law and the Prophets, and who

perfected grace. That those people are impious has already been shown, is being shown, and will be shown. But we ourselves see, and confess, that among us too some are useful and others useless. Our affairs are governed by the wisdom and goodness of God. (Surely he has not been stripped, on our account, of being good, wise, just and powerful in reason [?], as we have said, for the whole of divine Scripture teaches this.) How then will the ignorant barbarians, who have barely grasped one judgment of the division, and that most wretchedly, be able in their ignorance to confine the divine wisdom to this, as though God knew no more than the Hagarenes? If, then, Christians are godly, and some of them are useful and others useless, and God provides for the salvation of both, it is not then [?] … that the Hagarenes plunder them [?]. Rather, they are being disciplined by God: when they rebel, when they are strengthened while growing faint, when they are humbled while being arrogant, and when they are reproved by his incomprehensible understanding in many and varied ways. Nor, on the other hand, are those people godly because they enjoy temporary prosperity, for neither were the Egyptians godly when they enslaved the Lord's good people. Someone may truly say that passing from place to place is motion, but that will not make him believable when he says there is no other kind of motion. In naming one kind, he has left out the many others. In the same way, the righteous have indeed conquered the impious, as Israel conquered the land of Canaan, but that will not make these people believable when they say they rule over us as Israel did over them. For the impious have also been found to have overpowered the godly, and quite harshly. The Psalmist is a witness: 'O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple.' It is not, then, because the Christians hold a wrong belief about the Divine that the descendants of Hagar now plunder their land and that it has been handed over to them as spoil. Rather, to tell the truth, as the word of truth has shown, it is because the Christians are being disciplined for their sins.

106. These, then, are the blows that we, weak as we are, have struck like so many slaps against the utterly shameless face of the lying doctrine of Muhammad, following reason, which loves the truth and refutes falsehood. Those who have greater strength and boldness on behalf of the real truth will surely be commanded by the unerring Word to subject what Muhammad blasphemed [?] to the fitting scourges and tortures it deserves, and finally to lock it away in unbreakable fetters and inaccessible prisons and condemn it to voiceless silence. Then the saying will be fulfilled: 'The mouth of those who speak unjust things has been stopped.'

End of the refutation of the impious Muhammad.

NICETAS OF BYZANTIUM

BY THE SAME NICETAS OF BYZANTIUM

A constructive exposition, with demonstration, of Christian doctrine, developed from common notions, dialectical method, natural arguments, and a rich variety of sharp reasoning; and a reply to the letter sent by the Hagarenes to the emperor Michael, son of Theophilus, to slander the [?] of the Christians. [?]

1. Truth is a thing hard to hunt down, able to escape even the very sharp-sighted. The exception may be a soul that has broken right through the thickness of this bodily darkness and persuaded the senses to close or rest; such a soul may manage to reach some trace of truth. But as long as the eye of the mind still perceives the smoke of material things, which stings it like smoke [?], that is, the attachment to [?] them, it will not recognize truth even when it lies at its feet, let alone when it dwells far away. And the more keenly it perceives those things, the deeper its ignorance of truth will become. Truth is twofold: one kind is seen in creation, and the other concerns the Creator. As far as created things fall short of their Maker, so far does pure knowledge of the Maker surpass them. Hence all who have entrusted the knowledge of all things to reasoning alone have been found to have strayed far from it. But those who have bidden farewell to every comfort of life and devoted themselves to the search for truth alone have, with the divine hand helping them, both grasped it securely themselves and led those who follow in their footsteps straight to it. When the first way is found among those who wish to speak of divine things, the second will undoubtedly follow; but it will not follow if the first does not appear. As long as those held by ignorance and sloth follow those who have arrived there, they will enjoy the same divinity [?] no less than those others. But when the first way has been put off and they will not pursue even the second-best course, they will certainly no longer be able to escape the charge of wrongdoing. If they take no care for a disciplined life by which they might reach the measure of unerring knowledge of God, are not persuaded by those who have reached it, and rely only on their own reasonings, how will they attain, by running down another road, what is reached by a different one? Yet free will is truly unforced in all things. You, my most experienced friend, in your learning, are more concerned to submit the proofs of religious doctrines to natural reasoning; your letter shows this clearly in its opening. The doctrine of our faith does not primarily allow this,

because the Divine transcends every conception, not only human but even angelic. Even so, for your sake, we will first set out our belief about the Divine constructively, from arguments of this kind, as far as we can. Then we will examine the strength of the problems you raise to slander our religion. I shall begin here, namely: 'The all-wise and good…' and so on.

72. It is now time to examine the slanders against our faith in your writing, and to see whether they hit the mark. I shall begin here. Your letter runs as follows: 'And God gave them,' that is, the human beings he created, 'a mind to know that the creation is separate and stands far from likeness to the Creator, and that everything made is inferior to its maker.' I agree with this too: everything brought into being is foreign to the essential likeness of the one who brought it into being. So let this be taken as agreed by us as well. Then comes the next statement, joined to this one, which says: 'Every begetter is prior to his own offspring.' Stated without qualification, this is true in some cases and false in others. Since in God it is foreign and has no place, I will neither accept it nor concede it. Instead I will refute it, and show where it does have a place. Having taken this as agreed, you think you are tripping us up, either about consubstantiality or about the relation between begetter and begotten. I will explain how. We confess that the Father and the Son are consubstantial and the same, and that the one is called Father because he has begotten, and the other Son because he has been begotten. You take from our side the axiom that says 'Every begetter is prior to his own offspring,' and wrongly attach it to the divine nature. Yet it applies rather to a nature that has come into being and been created, and has no force in God. (To tell the truth, many things apply among us [?] that are wholly foreign to God.) Taking this as true of God, you argue somewhat like this: if every begetter is prior to his own offspring, the Son we believe in will not be coeternal and consubstantial with the Father; and if, on the other hand, the Son is coeternal with the Father, and the saying 'Every begetter is prior to his own offspring' is true, then the relation is forced to come apart.

3. It is nothing strange, my good friend, that once one absurdity is granted, countless others follow. If someone were to claim that a human being is a stone, he would saddle that human being with many absurdities, or rather with infinitely many. You have done something similar. You took a little premise about God that says 'Every begetter is prior

NICETAS OF BYZANTIUM

to his own offspring,' and on it you built your fallacy. Once this premise has been refuted, and it has no place at all in what is said of God, we will escape the absurdity on both sides. For where a cause is present, its opposite is absent [?]. The premise 'every begetter,' wrongly taken over from created nature, leads the argument into absurdity. Since it has no place in God, we will clearly escape the absurdities and keep both coeternity and consubstantiality, and the relation of fatherhood and sonship, unharmed. 'Every begetter is prior to his own offspring.' What a marvel! This is true of you and me. In actuality we are human beings or [?] or something else, and we become what we are potentially, such as begetters or people with knowledge or something else. But in cases where potentiality has no place, it is clear that being prior, that is, prior and posterior, [?]… it is evident that

impassible and simultaneous [?]. This is what the methods of logic tell us.

4. 'Every begetter is prior to his own offspring.' This is someone laying down the law about God, not speaking the truth at all. The term 'begetter' belongs either to absolute terms or to relative terms. It does not belong to absolute terms, since then it would not refer to an offspring. Clearly, then, it is a relative term. Relative terms are simultaneous by nature, and things simultaneous by nature exist together and cease to exist together. So the begetter, insofar as he is a begetter, has no 'before' and 'after' with respect to what he is related to. If, then, a begetter has no 'before' and 'after', and yet you said that every begetter is prior to his own offspring, it is evident that the begetter is prior not insofar as he is a begetter but in some other respect, the respect in which he is Socrates or Peter. In God the Father, the term 'begetter' is hypostatic, and the property of his hypostasis is characterized by this alone. This has been shown to have no 'before' and 'after' with respect to what it is related to. It is evident, then, that God the Father, though he is the begetter of his own offspring, will not be prior. If he is not prior, clearly they are simultaneous; and if simultaneous, then also coeternal. Therefore the Son is coeternal with the Father. So the very means by which you thought to trip us up has tripped you up instead. 'Every begetter is prior to his own offspring.' This applies among us, and the following makes it clear that it does: every potentiality, for the sake of something…

For if it is not for the sake of something, it is in vain; but neither God nor nature does anything in vain. Clearly, then, it is for the sake of something. If, then, the power exists for the sake of something, clearly the ability does too; and everything that is able to do something will also do it, unless something hinders it. So if there is in us an innate power of begetting children, but we are prevented, clearly something is hindering us. But in God there is nothing opposing or hindering. It is evident, then, that the begetting too is connatural with him; and if connatural, then simultaneous; and if simultaneous, there is no before and after. So it is clear that before and after have no place in God. "Each begetter is prior to his own offspring." Where, my good man, did you get your premises? For those who posit nothing in common between the Creator and his creatures deceive themselves when they take the divine words in the same sense of God and of creatures. The first premise is banished by the second, and again the second by the first. For if every thing made is inferior to its maker, according to the first axiom, while your argument from the begetter reasons from things made that the maker is prior, then it is both inferior and not inferior, and every thing made is both the same as its maker and not the same, which is impossible. 5. Let us look also at what follows. It runs thus: "Since, if you suppose there to be one principle for both, the Father and the Son, the order of relation that runs from the begetter to the offspring is destroyed; and the designation of the two is forced to be separated, that of the one who has begotten and that of the offspring, that of the pre-existent and that of the later-born." You have relieved us of trouble, my friend, by blurting out the secret. For if I saw that the little premise you put forward, which says "Each begetter is prior to his own offspring," had any place in God, perhaps, drawn along by the truth even against my will, I would have conceded the second as well. But since the argument has shown this to be stale, wholly false and foreign in the case of God, no argument will compel me to posit what follows from it either. For if there are two things, and one is taken in the position of antecedent and the other in that of consequent, clearly when the antecedent is granted, the consequent will follow; but it will not follow when the antecedent is in no way granted. This is clear from the following: let there be man and animal, and let man be taken as the antecedent and animal as the consequent. Evidently, when man is posited, animal will necessarily follow; but it will not follow when man is not posited. Such too is the drama you have staged. Therefore, if "Each begetter is prior to his own offspring" had a place in God, then, since we confess that the Father and the Son are coeternal, evidently the designations would be forced to be separated from each other. But since the first is not true, neither is the second; and so what you said has proved foolish. 6. And otherwise: if you say that because of the coeternity of the Father and the Son the relations are necessarily separated, the argument will rather compel, because of the relation,

that coeternity also be introduced. And this is clear as follows: the name "begetter," being one of the relatives, has its reference to a son; relatives are simultaneous by nature; and things simultaneous by nature both exist together and cease to exist together. It follows, then, that because of the relation they exist simultaneously, which is true. So how is it, my friend, that you introduce the opposite, and seem to lead us astray through coeternity into the relation of fatherhood and sonship, but through the relation of begetter and offspring into coeternity and consubstantiality? And otherwise: if the name "begetter" confers simultaneous existence, and things taken as simultaneous in existence, according to you, destroy the relation that runs from the begetter to the offspring, it follows that the name "begetter" and the offspring, though they are in relation, are without relation; which is
[?] vol. II, p. 79: "Enhypostatic: that which really subsists according to [?], and not [?]"

clearly showed it to be both Word and Son, constituted the universe, and made manifest his own creation in his works; and that there is one God over all, beyond being, just as one of our theologians somewhere said in agreement with this: "For his invisible things are clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things made, even his eternal divinity," and what goes with these words. So even if you do not wish it, you are in harmony with our confessions. But going on a little, concerning the monarchy of God and his transcendence of being, you write thus: "Because if he had a partner in his kingdom, he would be liable to opposition, or he would have to be in need of a helper to govern his creation." I am amazed that you write such things. For I do not see what necessity there is, in the case of God, to introduce either partners in the kingdom or a need of assistance for governing his own world, and all the rest you add to these. For God the Father has his own Son like him in all things, except unbegottenness and begottenness; and since we in no way confess the Son to be a partner of the Father, I do not know how you mislead us, or rather are caught by your own feathers. Your sophism is of this sort: if there are two things, one more universal and the other particular, such as raining and the earth being wet — for raining is narrower than being wet, since the two do not convert — then when the former is the case, clearly the other will be too, as with raining and being wet; but if, when the latter is the case, someone says that the former is too, he commits the fallacy so called "from the non-convertible" and "of the consequent." 9. You yourself have done something of this kind in your writings. For there are two things, "common" and "partner"; the one is wider, namely "common," the other narrower, namely "partner." For a partner is called a partner as having something in common; but it is not necessary that whatever has something in common with another should be called its partner. A stone is not called the partner of a stone, though the substance of both is common; likewise a horse and a horse, though they have a common and single substance, are not called partners. If, then, "common" is wider and "partner" narrower, and we say that the Father has his kingdom in common and undivided with his own Son, you shift the term and write: "If kingship and authority are common with the Son, the Son will certainly also be a partner of the Father in his kingdom." And you mislead yourself rather than us, committing the fallacy called "from the non-convertible." In doing this you seem rather to be ignorant of to whom the name "partner" fittingly applies and is properly said, and for this reason you wrongly transfer it to God. For the name "partner" does not seem to be applied to any but those in whom the work of each one is accomplished separately and distinctly, and when, by voluntary agreement and mutual persuasion, in the same

matter, two or three or more of them come together into the same [?] undertaking. For example, someone practises rhetoric on his own, carrying out his own pursuit; if another person comes to him, and by voluntary agreement and mutual persuasion they join with one mind in the work of rhetoric, each of them would be called a partner in it. But in those in whom work and will, wish and activity and concord are naturally present without division, how could the name "partner" have any place? Not at all. Therefore, when we say that the Father does something, we say that the Son and the Holy Spirit act together with him, inseparably; and the activity of the one is in some way that of the three, undivided. For every activity that reaches out from God, and is named according to manifold conceptions, sets out from the Father, proceeds through the Son, and is perfected in the Holy Spirit. For this reason it is not right to apply the name "partner" to the Holy Trinity. 10. You go on, writing about the partner thus: "He would be liable to opposition and strife." What senselessness in your words! For if the name "partner" had a place in God, perhaps opposition and strife would also be found; but since this is not granted, neither will what depends on it be granted. And so, unwillingly and against your intention, by what you add you have made plain to us the point we proposed, namely to whom the term properly applies. For if the name "partner," when posited, has opposition and strife following it, it is surely evident that "partner" will have a place among those who proceed by voluntary agreement and mutual persuasion, among whom strife and opposition also [?] arise. For only these are capable of admitting strife and opposition, because of the changeability of choice. But in those whose goodness is unchangeable, how could opposition and strife creep in? And shortly afterwards you write thus: "Or he would have to be in need of a helper to govern his creation." Well said, my friend! For if the name "partner" had a place in the case of the Son, then according to you there would also be opposition and strife and the need of assistance. But since that has been shown to be stale and feeble, clearly these are too. For if certain things are posited by the positing of something, clearly they are removed along with its removal. 11. Again, your letter runs thus: "And through the extension of the ages and their opposition to one another, his lordship over the creatures would be abolished, one would master the other, and the harmony of created things would be cut off." This charge of two principles and of opposition, my friend, does not apply to us; you ought rather to bring it against others, those who introduce two principles and two gods, a good one and an evil one, and say that the one created, holds together and rules the sensible world, and the other the intelligible world. This opinion we abhor and utterly reject, and those who extol it we

condemn to capital punishment (2); but you even welcome and cherish [?] it. For to us the one principle is the object of worship, since there is also one God, even if he is believed to be three in properties, that is, in hypostases. And if the difference of hypostases leads you to think of a difference of nature as well, and to introduce as many natures as there are hypostases, that is the mark of one who is ignorant rather than of one who knows. For nature and hypostasis are not the same; otherwise nothing that exists would be of the same nature, and the common and the particular would be one and the same thing, which is not found to be so. 12. And otherwise: if the difference of hypostases leads to the introduction of a difference of nature as well, then necessarily what is not different in nature must not be established as different in hypostasis either. It follows, then, that things the same in nature are the same in hypostases too. Paul and Peter, then, being the same in nature and without difference, will also be the same in hypostasis, which is laughable. For your sophism is the one so called "from homonymy." For since "one" is said in many ways, as the methods of logic teach — in genus, in species, in number, or by analogy — clearly "many" is too; for in as many ways as the proposed term [?] is said, in so many ways is its opposite said as well; this is what we have been taught. But while we attribute the three to the hypostases, you introduce a difference of natures as well. This is not how things are; for the evidence of the facts is plain, and the disciplines teach it. And so all your slanders against our faith have been shown to be stale, implausible and false; and once the slanders have plainly been removed, all the rest will follow along with them. And this is already beyond measure, since a surfeit of words is hostile to the ears. These things, then, are sufficient for those who wish to perceive even a little, and by comparison with what is better to pursue the truth and to thrust away falsehood. Therefore I shall bring my discourse to a stop here (5).

By the same Niketas: Refutation and overthrow of the second letter [?] sent by the Hagarenes to the emperor Michael, son of Theophilus, in slander of the faith of the Christians. 1. I would have wished, my friend, first to subject the true account of our faith — I mean the Christian doctrine — to the necessities of demonstration, and as far as possible to present it, on the basis of natural reasonings, as firm and most exact; and then to refute what you have written so strangely in slander of our religion. For a polemical discourse absolutely demands this.

But since, in reply to your other letter, our own doctrine has already, as was fitting, been set out constructively with demonstrations at great length (4), and clearly accomplished, we shall, so as not to seem now to be writing to you superfluously, make our rebuttals only of what was sent to us for the overthrow of our blameless faith. Let us therefore examine here whether the slanders against our faith and your other objections are well aimed. Your letter runs thus: "God is one, having no partner in his authority; and because he has no partner, he has not had a child either." I am amazed that you write such things. For I do not see what necessity there is, in the case of God the Father, for his own Son to be introduced as some partner or co-worker in his kingdom, and all the things of this kind that you often write. For God the Father has his own Son like him in all things, except unbegottenness and begottenness; and since we in no way confess the Son to be a partner of the Father, I do not know how you mislead us, or rather are caught by your own feathers. For your sophism is of this sort: if there are two things, one wider and the other narrower, such as man and animal — for man is narrower than animal, since they do not convert, while animal is wider — then when the one, namely man, is the case, clearly animal is too; but not, when animal is the case, man as well. If, then, when animal is the case, someone should say that man is too, he commits the fallacy so called "from the non-convertible" and "of the consequent." [?] to be applied to the Holy Trinity. [?] 2. And otherwise: "God is one, having no partner in his authority." That there is one God over all, granting to all beings both simple being and well-being, and possessing no partner or co-worker whatever among beings, as you say, has been shown above by us, and is confessed and believed. But that the Son of God whom we believe in, being himself also true God, just as the Father is, and rightly confessed by us in theology as one God with the Father and the Spirit, is not a partner of God the Father, nor of the one principle and the one God contemplated in Father and Son and Holy Spirit, is also [?] by us [?] (in the earlier letter),

confessed. If this were so, it would follow that the Son is his own partner, which is absurd; for nothing that exists is said to be its own partner. Therefore the Son is not a partner of the one principle and the one God contemplated in Father and Son and Holy Spirit, nor indeed of God the Father. For only among those can one find a son called a partner of his own father in whom a divergence of judgment creeps in, a difference of will is present, need summons them to the task, and an activity cut off and separate belongs to each. But where there is one mind, a will ever unbroken, identity of nature, one authority and an unchangeable willing, how could a partner creep in? So those who in theology speak of [?] and Spirit do not bring in a partner alongside the one God, even if they are wrongly so labeled by you [ms. "us"]. 3. And otherwise: "God is one, having no partner in his authority; and because he has no partner, he has not had a child either." You have relieved us of trouble by blurting out the secret. For if I saw that "partner" followed from and had a place in the divine begetting, perhaps, drawn along by the truth even against my will, I would have removed the antecedent along with the removal of this — that is, I would have disowned the Son in theology. But since the argument has shown this to be stale, wholly false and not following in the case of the divine begetting, no argument will compel me to deny the antecedent either, that is, the Son, in theology. For in the case of things that follow necessarily, when these are removed, clearly the antecedents are removed with them; but not so with things that do not follow at all, as the disciplines teach. Your syllogism, then, was in effect this: "If a Son is believed in theology, the one God will be found to have a partner; but God is one over all, having no partner; therefore no Son is found in theology either." First, as the philosophical methods teach us, the consequent is mistaken. For it has been shown that in the divine begetting it does not follow that the Son is called the partner of the Father; and for this very reason the argument proceeds without proof. Next, let us briefly examine our theology, so that we may show all the more clearly to everyone how feeble and implausible is the argument you set forth as doctrine. 4. Now of the things truly said by us in theology, some are said in common of the three hypostases, as of one substance or godhead and one God — I mean, for example, the name "God," and "Lord," and "lover of mankind," and the like — and these are not counted together, because they are said in a unitary way, as has been shown. Others are said properly, and these belong primarily and properly to the hypostases — I mean, for example, "Father" and "Son" and "Holy Spirit"; and because these are said properly, they are counted together. For counting together belongs properly to things said properly, not to things said in common, as has been shown elsewhere. Sometimes a term is also found applied to two

[?] of the divine hypostases, such as "caused" and [?]. Things said in common are said in common of the Father together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, as of one God who is and is so understood, and they are also predicated properly of each of the hypostases in turn. For the Father is truly God; and the Son is God as God from God, and as light from light; and likewise the Holy Spirit. But things said properly of the hypostases are said properly, and not in common, since what is narrower cannot be predicated of what is wider and be made equal to it. You would find this said of created nature too; for example, for the sake of clarity, "man" and "mortal" and "articulate-voiced": each of them is said both in common of individual men taken together and properly of each one considered by himself. For Peter and Paul and individual men are all together called "man" by a common account, and each one is so called properly; for Peter is called a man, and Paul, and the like. 5. But even if in our theology some things are said in common of the three hypostases and others properly, and those said in common are predicated both in common together and properly of each in turn — for whenever the name "God" or "Lord" is said in common of Father and Son and Holy Spirit together, clearly the three are called one God, in whom the godhead is, and so we rightly confess in theology — yet whenever the name "God" or "Lord" is said properly and individually, as of the Father, or of the Son or the Spirit, then the Father is indeed called God, but it is not that the Father is one God separately, individually and with a different nature, and again the Son another God, and likewise the Holy Spirit. Away with such polytheism and blasphemy from us! For to us the one principle is the object of worship, and one God, even if he is believed to be three in properties, that is, in hypostases. Hence, in speaking of the Son of God in theology, we say that he is other than the Father in hypostasis, but not other in substance and godhead; rather he is one and the same, as was shown in the earlier letter. 6. Indeed our theology, depending on common notions and on the divine prophets, and having secured firmness and stability, confesses Father and Son and Holy Spirit in theology, the three as one God. But you did not take it so; rather, supposing and understanding "one God" to be said properly and individually of the Father, and then reckoning the Son as something intruded from outside the one God, you contrived the fallacy. That is why you falsely conclude thus: "If there is a Son with God, he is also a partner; but there is no partner with God; therefore there is no Son either." In saying this you have fallen into many absurdities. First, you make hypostasis and nature the same in [?] God, which has already been refuted; then you do not allow the Son to be one God with the Father and the Spirit, as is rightly confessed by us in theology, and this too has already been demonstrated by us. For this very reason

…and it showed that what you teach is foolish. [?] Let us also look at what you add next. It runs like this: “He made the faith of the Saracens a light, and there is no other faith through which anyone can draw near to God,” along with everything else you write to glorify your own faith. Anyone who wanted to could easily and effortlessly attack someone else's faith with bare insults and no proof, and give great praise to his own. But to show by demonstration that one's own faith is beneficial and useful and given by God is the work of a pious and sensible man. So you too should have done this, rather than simply declaring, full of pride, that your faith is a light made and given by God. We, for our part, will try instead to set out with demonstration the error and falsehood of your faith and the truth and beauty of ours.

6. All sensible people agree on the following. A faith is beneficial and useful, and stands as a light, when it pledges that those who embrace it are brought close to God. Its ordinances command the putting away of the worst and most harmful things, [?] and move the human race from what is contrary to nature to what is according to nature and above nature. But a faith whose ordinances proclaim the putting away of good things and the embracing of base ones, and which drags the human race down from what is according to nature, or even above nature, to what is contrary to nature, is certainly unprofitable and harmful. Through it a person can hardly be brought close to God. Your faith commands the embracing of base things and the putting away of good ones, and it drags those who embrace it down from what is above nature, or according to nature, to what is contrary to nature. It is therefore evident that your faith is unprofitable and harmful, and that no one is brought close to God through it. You can see that this is true from the following. Everyone knows that “contrary to nature” means a shift from what is natural to what is worse, while “above nature” means a shift from what is natural to what is better. Now man was created somehow in the middle, between the sensible creation, I mean, and the intelligible one. For this reason he shares in both natures, the irrational and the angelic. He shares in the angelic through his reasoning and discerning faculty, and in the irrational through his spirited and appetitive faculties. Man is preserved and kept in accordance with nature when the reasoning faculty rules the spirited and appetitive ones. More than that, he is brought nearer to the angelic nature and rises to what is above nature when the irrational part of the soul is subdued and kept under. But whenever the opposite is seen in him, so that the passions prevail over reason and reason serves them, he plainly descends to what is contrary to nature, from what is according to nature or even above nature, as he does what is worse. This happens without doubt in those who live licentiously or murderously. So the more free rein the spirited and appetitive faculties have, the more the passions leap about; and the more they leap about, the more they grow; and

NICETAS OF BYZANTIUM

the more they grow, the more man shares in the life of the irrational animals, and by doing this he hurries to become a beast. That is why the prophetic word speaks this way about the man who wallows in his passions [?] and has become like the beasts: “Man, though he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them.”

8. Your faith promises and prescribes the licentious life, and the growth and dominance of the passions rather than of reason, and it pushes people to gape after what is worse. That is, it drags people down from what is according to nature and above nature to what is contrary to nature. We have agreed that a faith whose ordinances are of this kind is harmful and unprofitable, and that no one is brought close to God through it. It follows, then, that your faith, the faith of the Saracens, is darkness rather than light, and that no one is brought close to God through it. If so, then it was not given by God either, and it is in vain that you boast and pride yourself in this falsely named faith (or rather, to tell the truth, this unbelief) and invite us to it. Our faith, however, promises the opposite of yours. Yours promises licentiousness, ours self-control; yours gluttony, ours temperance; yours prodigality, ours generosity. Yours has been shown to be unprofitable and harmful and not to bring anyone close to God, because it prepares people instead to share in the life of the irrational beasts. It is therefore evident that ours is beneficial and useful and brings people close to God, because it joins them instead to the angels. So it is rather we who can firmly declare that there is no faith apart from ours, the faith of the Christians, through which anyone can be brought close to God and come to share in what is good. Let this be enough to say about your faith and ours.

9. Going on a little further, you try to show that man was not formed according to the image and likeness of God, as we wrote to you, persuaded both by the history according to Moses and by the facts themselves. You seem to think you have good reason to write as follows: “God is indescribable and unlimited and incomprehensible. For God always was, and there was none like him, for his height is boundless. He formed his creature without likeness to himself.” From this you seem to infer that man was not formed according to the image and likeness of God. Your reasoning is that since God is incomprehensible, invisible, boundless and so on, and nothing that exists resembles him, man clearly does not resemble him either, since he too is one of the things that exist. If so, man was not made according to the image and likeness of God. These are the words of someone laying down laws about God and his creatures, not of someone speaking the truth at all. If, in saying that man was made according to the image and likeness of God, we meant a likeness of essence, one involving an identical and indistinguishable essence with God,

and then, at the same time, confessed that God is indescribable, unlimited, incomprehensible and infinite, and that nothing that exists is like this, we might perhaps have contradicted ourselves, and what you write would have been reasonable. But when we say that man was made according to God's image and likeness, we do not understand this as a likeness of essence. We mean a likeness that bears an analogy to God, of the kind that is also found among created things. So there is nothing unreasonable in our writing that man was formed according to the image and likeness of God. The account of the creation of the world according to Moses also persuades us to confess this. We say “according to the image,” then, with respect to his ruling [so the manuscript] and self-determining faculty. Moreover, in man there are mind, word and spirit. The mind is the begetter of the word in us; the word is the offspring of the mind; and the spirit is sent forth through the word. Just as the mind is never without word, so the word is never found without mind. They exist together, and neither comes before the other. In the same way the word does not exist without spirit, nor does the spirit (the breath that is shaped into voice) exist without word.

10. The supersubstantial and uncreated essence, which is God, is contemplated in three hypostases: in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, as we have demonstrated and as is rightly believed. Accordingly, the mind in us, as the begetter of the word in us, is analogous to God the Father, who begot his own Word eternally and timelessly. The word in us, as the offspring of the mind in us, is analogous to the Son, who was begotten from God without flux and without passion and is true God. And the spirit in us is analogous to the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and is poured out and imparted to existing things through the Son. In this respect, again, man is said to have been formed according to the image of God. Again, we say that man was made according to the likeness of God because of the perfection of the virtues and the participation in good things. Whatever the creative cause, which is God, is primarily and without a cause, man is secondarily, by participation, and as something caused. For example, the First and supersubstantial is life, light, wise, mighty, good, gentle and just; and man too is wise, and life, and mighty, and good, and gentle, and just. But God is so by nature and essentially, while man is so by adoption and grace, as something added to his essence. If so, we rightly say that man was made according to the likeness of God, since he bears a last echo of God by reflection [so the manuscript]. And so, once again, what [?] from you was shown to be foolish.
11. Passing on to another of the things we wrote, and trying to refute this too, you write again: “We see among the kinds of wild beasts that the stronger rises up against the weaker, and the

greater against the smaller, and the superior against the inferior, and it often makes the other its food. Sometimes it even destroys it, out of jealousy, lest it be driven from its lair,” and so on. Here you seem not to know how demonstrations should proceed and how they should not. Suppose what we wrote had claimed, of every irrational animal, that it gathers and unites with its own kind or with another kind out of gentleness toward one another, as if they cared for each other's safety. Then suppose you had found that this was not seen in some animals, and that instead the opposite happened: the stronger rose up against the weaker, destroyed it and drove it away, and the superior did the same to the inferior. You set out such cases in your letter, I mean the lion, the bear and the like. In that case you could have refuted our argument handsomely. But what we wrote makes no such claim about every irrational animal, and so you are talking idly, staging a badly contrived drama and play-acting. Who, even among those who can see just a little, has failed to notice that not all kinds of animals are naturally disposed to gather and live together? Some animals are solitary and others live in herds. Of those that live in herds, some are ranged under a leader and others are not. And among each of these, some are social and others are not, as the books of natural history and the inquiries about them teach. So if some are solitary and others are not, it is evident that some are naturally disposed to gather with their own kind and others are not. If this is so, no one with an undistorted mind either thinks or writes, “All animals gather and live together with one another.” Neither did we. Reason, prudence and judgment guided by reason are the most distinctive and characteristic mark of the animal that is social in the proper sense. That is why man also needed outward speech, so that thoughts lying in the depths could be brought out into the light and shared with his neighbors. Man, then, is a gentle animal by nature, and in this respect he is properly a social animal. In the irrational animals as a whole, sociability and natural gentleness are not present in the proper sense. Yet in some irrational animals we do find this gathering, living together and sharing in common. All the more, then, would it be right among human beings. For if what seems less likely to exist does exist, all the more does what is more likely. This is what is fitting, and what man ought all the more to do: to gather and live together with his own kind, since he is properly a social animal and gentle by nature. It was with this in view that we wrote to you.

12. Again, passing on to another of the things we wrote and likewise trying to overturn it, you write as follows: “Some killings are lawful and others unlawful. It is unlawful, and forbidden by God, to kill one who is faithful by his own choice. But it is permitted and lawful to kill one who glorifies a partner of God and fashions one

equal to him in power.” In writing this you show yourself ignorant and completely uninitiated in these matters. You did not understand that every killing, insofar as it is killing, is to be shunned and abhorred, since it is evil, and nothing evil is lawful. That killing is evil is clear from the following. Every killing, insofar as it is killing, is either the destruction of a man or something that brings about the destruction of a man. But man is the finest and best of the things on earth, since he is the very first of God's creatures on earth. It follows, then, that every killing, insofar as it is killing, is either the destruction of something good or something that brings about such destruction. If so, it is evil in itself. For the destruction of good things, and whatever destroys them, is entirely evil, just as the destruction of evils, and whatever destroys them, is good. This is what the common notions and the teachings of philosophy [?] teach us. If, then, every killing, insofar as it is killing, has been shown to be evil, it is clearly not lawful either, for nothing evil is lawful. Yet sometimes it becomes good incidentally. Among things that exist, some are good in themselves but become evil incidentally, such as almsgiving. Others are evil in themselves but become good incidentally, such as lying. Others are in themselves neither, but incidentally go either way, such as wealth, strength and the like. Things good in themselves ought to happen always, or for the most part, for such is the nature of things good in themselves. With things evil in themselves it is the reverse: they ought never to happen, or for the most part not, but only rarely, for such is their nature. Things that in themselves are neither are equally disposed to happen or not. Now killing is among the things evil in themselves, as we have demonstrated. What is evil in itself, by the primary principle, ought not to happen at all, or for the most part not, and this is the primary good. Only rarely does it become good incidentally, and that is a secondary and lesser good. And the good that holds by the primary principle and in most cases is more choiceworthy and better than the good that is secondary and lesser, as the methods of logic teach us. Therefore not killing is better and more choiceworthy than killing, even if killing is sometimes good incidentally. If so, those who aim to remove killing from among men would be shown to be far better and more honorable than those who do not choose to do this, since they aim at the better good. We, then, have been shown by demonstration to be the better ones, since we choose to put killing out of the way altogether.

13. The killing that you carry out against us every day cannot be counted even among the incidental goods. This is clear from the following.

What becomes good incidentally does so by dispensation, and what happens by dispensation happens for the sake of something good. So what happens incidentally happens for the sake of something good. But the killing you do against us is done for no other reason, as you yourselves say, than that you are Saracens and practice the Saracen religion. And this is not good. It follows, then, that the killing you do against us is not even among the incidental goods. That being a Saracen is not good is clear as follows. To be a Saracen is nothing other than to drag people down from what is according to nature and above nature to what is contrary to nature. This we have demonstrated. And it is plain to everyone that doing this is not good. So, since it is not among the things good in themselves,

nor among the incidental goods, that the killing you carry out against us belongs, and since what is good neither in itself nor incidentally ought not to happen at all, the killing that you carry out against us every day ought not to happen. If so, it is not lawful either, for what ought not to happen is not lawful. “Some killings are lawful and others unlawful.” I too agree that some killings are lawful, clearly incidentally, since they belong to the incidental goods. Others are unlawful, clearly in themselves, since killing, insofar as it is killing, has been shown to be among the things evil in themselves. Hence also as agreed by us [?].

14. Next comes the short clause joined to this, which says: “But it is permitted and lawful to kill one who glorifies a partner of God and fashions one equal to him in power.” What arrogance and conceit, or more fittingly, what stupefaction and bewilderment you must be full of! Out of great simple-mindedness and unbelief, you irrationally hold an opinion from who knows where, not the one we preach. You shadow-box and belch out vanities, and in your fictions you mock us as people who bring in partners and equals in power alongside the one God and the one sovereign principle. Who among us, small or great, ever conceived or invented a partner equal in power to the one God and the one sovereign principle, so that the killing carried out against us might be lawful, as you say? Among us the Son of God is indeed confessed and glorified as true God, since he is of one nature with God the Father. Yet he is not spoken of as God in the sense of a partner of the one sovereign principle, [?] a God brought in from outside, as you imagine (this too we have demonstrated). He is spoken of as one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and so he is, and so he is rightly believed and glorified by us Christians. If so, it is in vain that you smear us with this reproach of having a “partner.” Moreover, you reckon the killing you carry out against us to be godly and lawful, as you write. For if it is lawful for you to kill us because we [?] a partner and equal in power of God, as you yourselves say,

then, since this charge is clearly made against us falsely, it is evident that our being killed by you is not lawful either. But perhaps the distinction of the hypostases of Father, Son and Holy Spirit troubles and disturbs you. You may think that among us the Son is introduced as a partner from outside the one God and the one sovereign principle, and that he differs in nature from God the Father. If so, this is the mark of someone ignorant rather than someone who knows. For nature and hypostasis are not the same. Otherwise nothing that exists would share one nature, and the common and the particular would be one and the same thing, which is never found.

15. To argue it another way: if a distinction of hypostases requires introducing a distinction of nature, then necessarily what is not distinct in nature cannot be distinct in hypostasis either. It follows, then, that things identical in nature will also be identical in hypostasis. Socrates and Peter, being identical and undifferentiated in nature, would then also be identical in hypostasis, which is ridiculous. This kind of sophism is called the fallacy of equivocation. As the methods of logic teach us, “one” is said in many ways: in genus, in species or in number. Clearly, then, “many” is said in many ways too, for a term is said in as many ways as its opposite. This we have been taught. But while we apply “three” to the hypostases, you bring in a difference of natures as well. These things are so: the evidence of the facts makes it plain, and the teachings of the schools instruct us. And so all your slanders against our faith and all your objections against us have been shown to be stale, unconvincing and false. With the slanders refuted, everything else will follow for you. And this has gone beyond due measure, for too much talk is an enemy to the ears. So this is enough for those who are willing to see even a little, and who, by comparing it with what is better, will pursue the truth and reject falsehood. Hence at this point our discourse

…participating in divinity, is god. [?] …none of those [?] God, as the Lord Jesus Christ is…

…to rule her [?]. But since he was wicked and spoke with guile, he deceived her and married her, though he himself was possessed. When she learned this she was distressed and vexed, and said: “I am ruined, for I have taken a poor man and a demoniac.” And she was about to drive him away. When the wicked man realized this, he went to a friend of his who was a monk and had been exiled from the great city. He gave him these instructions: “I know that you are acquainted with my wife, and that she wants to tell you about me and about how I fall down in fits of dizziness. When she does, back me up and say this: that it was nothing other than a vision of an angel of God, Gabriel I mean, [?] and that I am a prophet of God upon [?]…” [?] the woman [?] was pleased, and from then on [?] it has prevailed in Arabia until now.
